title: 〜なし
meaning: without; with no ~ (noun suffix)
summary: なし attaches to a noun to say 'without / with no ~'. It is the noun form of the negative ない, so 予約なし = 'no reservation', 砂糖なし = 'no sugar'. It often appears as なしで or なしに ('without ~') before a clause. Use it to mark the absence of a thing.
pitfalls: なし attaches to a noun; to say 'without doing (a verb)', use 〜ずに or 〜ないで, not なし.

examples.ja: 予約なしでこのレストランに入れますか。
examples.en: Can I get into this restaurant without a reservation?
examples.f: ｜予約[よやく]なしでこのレストランに｜入[い]れますか。

examples.ja: 彼は文句なしで、頼んだ仕事を全部やってくれた。
examples.en: Without a single complaint, he did all the work I asked of him.
examples.f: ｜彼[かれ]は｜文句[もんく]なしで、｜頼[たの]んだ｜仕事[しごと]を｜全部[ぜんぶ]やってくれた。

synonyms.note: 抜きで also means 'leaving out / without'; なし simply states a noun's absence.

related.note: なしに is the same word before a clause, often 'without (doing) ~'; なし stands as a plain noun suffix.

title: 合う
meaning: to do an action to one another; to do mutually / together
summary: 〜合う attaches to the ます-stem and says that two or more people do the action to or with each other — 話し合う = talk it over together, 助け合う = help one another, 分かり合う = understand each other. The nuance is reciprocal: the action goes both ways. The compound conjugates like an ordinary う-verb (合った, 合って).
pitfalls: Attach it to the stem, not the dictionary form: 話し合う, not 話す合う.
It implies a two-way, mutual action between people; a plain 話す is just 'talk', while 話し合う is 'talk it through with each other'.
Don't confuse this compound suffix with the standalone verb 会う ('to meet someone'), which sounds the same but is written differently.

examples.ja: 家族でよく話し合って、留学することを決めました。
examples.en: We talked it over as a family and decided that I would study abroad.
examples.f: ｜家族[かぞく]でよく｜話し合[はなしあ]って、｜留学[りゅうがく]することを｜決[き]めました。

examples.ja: 困ったときは、友達と助け合うことが大切です。
examples.en: When you're in trouble, it's important to help each other out with your friends.
examples.f: ｜困[こま]ったときは、｜友達[ともだち]と｜助け合[たすけあ]うことが｜大切[たいせつ]です。

title: 上がる・上げる
meaning: to finish doing something completely; to carry an action through to completion
summary: 〜上げる and 〜上がる attach to the ます-stem to say an action is carried all the way to completion, often producing a finished result — 書き上げる = finish writing, 作り上げる = build/complete, 出来上がる = be finished. 〜上げる is transitive (you complete it); 〜上がる is intransitive (it comes to be finished). This is a compound suffix, unrelated to the N5 verb あげる 'to give'.
pitfalls: Attach it to the stem: 書き上げる, not 書く上げる.
Use 〜上げる when someone completes the action (料理を作り上げる) and 〜上がる when it comes out finished on its own (料理ができ上がる).
This 'finish' suffix is not the N5 あげる ('to give') nor the N4 てあげる ('do for someone').

examples.ja: レポートをやっと書き上げて、ほっとしました。
examples.en: I finally finished writing the report and felt relieved.
examples.f: レポートをやっと｜書き上[かきあ]げて、ほっとしました。

examples.ja: 三年かけて、この作品を作り上げました。
examples.en: Over three years, I built this work all the way to completion.
examples.f: ｜三[さん]｜年[ねん]かけて、この｜作品[さくひん]を｜作り上[つくりあ]げました。

antonyms.note: 〜かけ・かける is an action left half-done; 〜上げる・上がる is one carried through to a finished result.

related.note: 〜終わる neutrally marks finishing an action; 〜上げる adds the sense of completing it into a finished product.
〜切る stresses doing something thoroughly to the very end; 〜上げる stresses arriving at a completed result.

title: 〜当たり
meaning: per; apiece; for each (unit)
summary: 〜当たり attaches to a counter or unit noun to express a rate — 'per one of that unit'. 一箱当たり = per box, 一時間当たり = per hour. It is used when dividing a total across units, much like English 'per'. Here 当たり has nothing to do with 'hitting' or 'winning'; it is a fixed suffix meaning 'per'.
pitfalls: This 当たり means 'per each ~' and follows a unit; it is unrelated to 当たる in the senses of 'to hit' or 'to win'.
It states a rate, so it usually pairs with a following amount or number (ひとり当たり三千円 = 3,000 yen per person).

examples.ja: この駐車場は、一時間当たり三百円かかります。
examples.en: This parking lot costs 300 yen per hour.
examples.f: この｜駐車[ちゅうしゃ]｜場[じょう]は、｜一[いち]｜時間[じかん]｜当[あ]たり｜三[さん]｜百[ひゃく]｜円[えん]かかります。

examples.ja: パーティーの参加費は、ひとり当たり三千円です。
examples.en: The fee to join the party is 3,000 yen per person.
examples.f: パーティーの｜参加[さんか]｜費[ひ]は、ひとり｜当[あ]たり｜三[さん]｜千[せん]｜円[えん]です。

synonyms.note: につき also means 'per' in this rate sense; it additionally has a separate meaning 'due to', which 〜当たり never carries.

title: あまり
meaning: so much ~ that; out of an excess of (a feeling)
summary: 〜のあまり (after a noun of feeling) or 〜あまり (after a verb) means an emotion or state was so extreme that it caused the result that follows — 緊張のあまり = out of too much nervousness, 心配のあまり = from worrying too much. It presents an overpowering cause leading to an often unexpected or unwanted outcome.
pitfalls: This あまり ('so much that') usually follows a feeling-noun + の or a verb; it is not the adverb あまり〜ない ('not very'), which needs a negative verb.
It tends to introduce an extreme cause and a striking or negative consequence, not a neutral 'because'.

examples.ja: うれしさのあまり、涙が出てしまいました。
examples.en: I was so overjoyed that the tears came.
examples.f: うれしさのあまり、｜涙[なみだ]が｜出[で]てしまいました。

examples.ja: 緊張のあまり、自分の名前を言い間違えました。
examples.en: I was so nervous that I got my own name wrong.
examples.f: ｜緊張[きんちょう]のあまり、｜自分[じぶん]の｜名前[なまえ]を｜言[い]い｜間違[まちが]えました。

synonyms.note: あまりに（も）is an adverb placed before an adjective/verb ('excessively ~'); 〜のあまり follows a feeling-noun to give the cause of a result.

related.note: 〜ほど also builds 'so ~ that' by giving a yardstick; 〜のあまり frames an excess of feeling as the cause.

title: あまりに・あまりにも
kana: あまりに・あまりにも
meaning: excessively; far too; so ~ (that)
summary: あまりに and あまりにも are adverbs placed directly before an adjective or verb to say something is excessive — 'far too ~'. あまりにも高い = far too expensive, あまりに忙しい = terribly busy. The も is optional and just strengthens the emphasis. It often leads into a result: 'so ~ that…'.
structure: あまりに（も）＋ い-adjective ／ な-adjective ／ Verb
pitfalls: あまりに（も）is an adverb and goes in front of the word it intensifies; it does not follow a noun the way 〜のあまり does.
The も is optional — あまりに and あまりにも mean the same thing, with も adding a touch more emphasis.

examples.ja: この店の服はあまりにも高くて、何も買えませんでした。
examples.en: The clothes at this shop were so expensive that I couldn't buy anything.
examples.f: この｜店[みせ]の｜服[ふく]はあまりにも｜高[たか]くて、｜何[なに]も｜買[か]えませんでした。

examples.ja: あまりに忙しくて、昼ご飯を食べる時間もなかった。
examples.en: I was so busy that I didn't even have time for lunch.
examples.f: あまりに｜忙[いそが]しくて、｜昼[ひる]ご｜飯[はん]を｜食[た]べる｜時間[じかん]もなかった。

synonyms.note: 〜のあまり follows a feeling-noun to name the cause of a result; あまりに（も）is an adverb that intensifies the following word.
〜すぎる attaches to a stem and says the thing itself is overdone (高すぎる); あまりに（も）is a free adverb placed before it (あまりにも高い).

title: 〜あり
meaning: with ~; having ~; ~ included
summary: 〜あり is a noun-like suffix built from ある that labels something as 'having ~' or 'with ~' — 駐車場あり = parking available, わけあり = with (special) circumstances. You see it on notices, listings, and menus. Its opposite is 〜なし ('without ~').
pitfalls: Here あり is a fixed label, not the conjugating verb ある; it sits at the end like a noun (エアコンあり).
It is common in written, sign-style Japanese; in full sentences you would normally say ～がある instead.

examples.ja: このアパートはエアコンありで、すぐに住めます。
examples.en: This apartment comes with an air conditioner, so you can move in right away.
examples.f: このアパートはエアコンありで、すぐに｜住[す]めます。

examples.ja: 「わけあり」の商品は、少し安く売られています。
examples.en: "With-issues" items are sold a little cheaper.
examples.f: 「わけあり」の｜商品[しょうひん]は、｜少[すこ]し｜安[やす]く｜売[う]られています。

antonyms.note: 〜なし is the exact opposite — 'without ~'; 〜あり marks that something is present or included.

title: あるいは
meaning: or; or else; alternatively; possibly
summary: あるいは joins two options ('A あるいは B' = A or B) and can also work as an adverb meaning 'possibly / perhaps', often with かもしれない. It is fairly formal and belongs to written or careful spoken Japanese. Between choices it functions like または; as 'perhaps' it flags one uncertain possibility.
pitfalls: あるいは is on the formal, written side; in casual speech または (between choices) or それとも (in questions) sound more natural.
In its 'perhaps' meaning it often pairs with かもしれない to mark one uncertain possibility.

examples.ja: お電話、あるいはメールでご連絡ください。
examples.en: Please contact us by phone or e-mail.
examples.f: お｜電話[でんわ]、あるいはメールでご｜連絡[れんらく]ください。

examples.ja: 彼はもう家に着いているか、あるいはまだ電車の中かもしれない。
examples.en: He may already be home, or possibly still on the train.
examples.f: ｜彼[かれ]はもう｜家[いえ]に｜着[つ]いているか、あるいはまだ｜電車[でんしゃ]の｜中[なか]かもしれない。

synonyms.note: それとも offers a choice inside a question ('A, or B?'); あるいは is more formal and also works in statements and as 'possibly'.

title: 言うまでもない
meaning: it goes without saying; needless to say; obviously
summary: 言うまでもない presents something as too obvious to need stating — 'it goes without saying'. As a final phrase it closes a sentence (〜のは言うまでもない), and as 言うまでもなく it leads into the main point at the front of a sentence. It signals that what follows is common knowledge or beyond question.
pitfalls: 言うまでもなく (adverbial) sets up the following statement; 言うまでもない (final) rounds one off — pick the form by where it sits in the sentence.
It frames the content as self-evident, so avoid it for genuinely new or debatable information.

examples.ja: 健康が何より大切なのは、言うまでもないことです。
examples.en: It goes without saying that health matters more than anything.
examples.f: ｜健康[けんこう]が｜何[なに]より｜大切[たいせつ]なのは、｜言[い]うまでもないことです。

examples.ja: 言うまでもなく、締め切りは必ず守ってください。
examples.en: Needless to say, please be sure to meet the deadline.
examples.f: ｜言[い]うまでもなく、｜締め切[しめき]りは｜必[かなら]ず｜守[まも]ってください。

synonyms.note: は言うまでもない is the topic-marked version ('as for X, it needs no saying'); this entry is the plainer 言うまでもない / 言うまでもなく.

related.note: 〜までもない (N1) attaches to a verb to say 'no need to go so far as to ~'; 言うまでもない is the fixed 'it goes without saying'.

title: いくら〜ても・いくら〜でも
kana: いくら〜ても・いくら〜でも
meaning: no matter how (much) ~; however ~
summary: いくら sets up a concession that is completed by 〜ても / 〜でも, giving 'no matter how much ~'. いくら頼んでも = no matter how much I ask, いくら便利でも = however convenient it may be. The pattern says the result holds regardless of the degree of the first part.
structure: いくら＋い-adjective［て form くて］＋も
pitfalls: いくら on its own is unfinished — it needs a matching 〜ても／〜でも later in the sentence.
Use でも after nouns and な-adjectives (いくら元気でも), and ても after verbs and い-adjectives (いくら安くても).
It is close in meaning to どんなに〜ても, which stresses the manner rather than the amount.

examples.ja: いくら頼んでも、彼は手伝ってくれませんでした。
examples.en: No matter how much I asked, he wouldn't help me.
examples.f: いくら｜頼[たの]んでも、｜彼[かれ]は｜手伝[てつだ]ってくれませんでした。

examples.ja: いくら安くても、要らない物は買いません。
examples.en: However cheap it is, I don't buy things I don't need.
examples.f: いくら｜安[やす]くても、｜要[い]らない｜物[もの]は｜買[か]いません。

related.note: 〜ても alone means 'even if ~'; いくら〜ても adds いくら to stress 'no matter how much', a whole concessive frame.

title: 一度に
meaning: all at once; at one time; in a single go
summary: 一度に is an adverb meaning several things happen or are done together on a single occasion — 'all at once'. たくさんの仕事を一度に = a lot of work all at once. The focus is on multiple items being handled at the same time rather than one after another.
pitfalls: 一度に stresses handling many things together on one occasion; 一気に stresses doing one thing in a single unbroken burst.
It describes doing things simultaneously, not repeating them — for 'once' as a count use 一度 without に.

examples.ja: そんなにたくさんの仕事を、一度に頼まないでください。
examples.en: Please don't pile that much work on me all at once.
examples.f: そんなにたくさんの｜仕事[しごと]を、｜一[いち]｜度[ど]に｜頼[たの]まないでください。

examples.ja: お皿を一度に運ぼうとして、落としてしまいました。
examples.en: I tried to carry all the plates at once and ended up dropping them.
examples.f: お｜皿[さら]を｜一[いち]｜度[ど]に｜運[はこ]ぼうとして、｜落[お]としてしまいました。

synonyms.note: 一気に is doing something in one continuous rush without stopping; 一度に is doing several things together on the same occasion.

title: 一体
meaning: (just) what / who / why on earth ~ (question emphasis)
summary: 一体 is an adverb that adds force to a question, coloring it with surprise, puzzlement, or irritation — 'what on earth', 'why in the world'. It teams up with a question word such as 何・誰・どうして and the sentence usually ends in か or だろう. It intensifies the asking, not the answer.
structure: 一体＋ question word（何／誰／どうして…）＋ … か
pitfalls: 一体 needs a question word to lean on (一体どうして…); it does not go in plain statements.
It carries an emotional charge — bafflement or frustration — so it is stronger than a neutral question.

examples.ja: 一体どうして、こんなことになったのですか。
examples.en: How on earth did things end up like this?
examples.f: ｜一体[いったい]どうして、こんなことになったのですか。

examples.ja: さっきから待っているのに、彼は一体どこにいるんだろう。
examples.en: I've been waiting all this time — where in the world is he?
examples.f: さっきから｜待[ま]っているのに、｜彼[かれ]は｜一体[いったい]どこにいるんだろう。

title: 一方だ
meaning: to keep ~ing more and more (a one-way, ongoing change)
summary: Verb［dictionary form］＋一方だ says a situation keeps moving in a single direction — it only ~s more and more. 値段は上がる一方だ = prices just keep rising, 実力は落ちる一方だ = one's ability only declines. The change is one-way and continuous, and it often describes an unwanted trend.
pitfalls: It follows the dictionary form and describes a one-directional change; it does not mean 'on the other hand' — that is 一方で.
It usually paints a steadily worsening or intensifying trend, not a two-sided comparison.

examples.ja: 最近、物の値段は上がる一方です。
examples.en: Lately, prices just keep going up and up.
examples.f: ｜最近[さいきん]、｜物[もの]の｜値段[ねだん]は｜上[あ]がる｜一方[いっぽう]です。

examples.ja: 毎日練習しないと、実力は落ちる一方だ。
examples.en: If you don't practice every day, your skills will only keep declining.
examples.f: ｜毎日[まいにち]｜練習[れんしゅう]しないと、｜実力[じつりょく]は｜落[お]ちる｜一方[いっぽう]だ。

related.note: 〜つつある marks a change that is currently in progress; 一方だ stresses that the change keeps going one way, more and more.
一方で uses the same 一方 but means 'on the other hand'; 一方だ means a situation only keeps ~ing.

title: 一方で
meaning: on one hand ~, on the other hand ~; while
summary: 〜一方（で） contrasts two sides of a situation that hold at the same time — 'on one hand…, while on the other…'. 明るい一方で = cheerful, while (on the other hand)…. It links two coexisting facts that pull in different directions, often about the same person or thing.
pitfalls: 一方で sets up a contrast between two coexisting sides; don't mix it up with 一方だ ('keeps ~ing more and more').
The two sides usually pull in opposite directions, so it is not just neutral addition.

examples.ja: 兄は明るい一方で、弟はとても静かです。
examples.en: My older brother is cheerful, while my younger brother is very quiet.
examples.f: ｜兄[あに]は｜明[あか]るい｜一方[いっぽう]で、｜弟[おとうと]はとても｜静[しず]かです。

examples.ja: この仕事は大変な一方で、やりがいもあります。
examples.en: This job is hard, but on the other hand it's rewarding.
examples.f: この｜仕事[しごと]は｜大変[たいへん]な｜一方[いっぽう]で、やりがいもあります。

synonyms.note: 〜反面 also contrasts two sides of the same thing; 一方で can present two separate subjects side by side as well.

related.note: 逆に flips to the opposite ('conversely'); 一方で holds up two coexisting sides at once.
一方だ uses the same 一方 but means a situation only keeps ~ing; 一方で marks a two-sided contrast.

title: 上で
meaning: after doing ~ and then; upon ~; in the course of ~
summary: With the past form or a noun + の, 〜上で means 'after deliberately doing X, then do Y' — 相談した上で = after discussing it, then… . With the dictionary form it means 'in the course of / for the purpose of' (生きる上で = in living / in life). The 'after' use marks a considered step taken before the next action.
pitfalls: With the past form (確認した上で) it means 'after taking step X, then do Y', and is more formal and deliberate than 〜てから.
With the dictionary form (働く上で) it shifts to 'in the course of / for the purpose of', not 'after'.

examples.ja: 家族とよく相談した上で、お返事します。
examples.en: I'll give you my answer after discussing it thoroughly with my family.
examples.f: ｜家族[かぞく]とよく｜相談[そうだん]した｜上[うえ]で、お｜返事[へんじ]します。

examples.ja: 契約書の内容をよく確認した上で、サインしてください。
examples.en: Please sign only after carefully checking the contents of the contract.
examples.f: ｜契約[けいやく]｜書[しょ]の｜内容[ないよう]をよく｜確認[かくにん]した｜上[うえ]で、サインしてください。

related.note: 〜てから is the everyday 'after doing'; 〜た上で is more formal and stresses X as a deliberate step taken before Y.
〜後で just orders two events in time; 〜た上で implies you do X on purpose as a basis for doing Y.

title: 上に
meaning: on top of that; besides; not only ~ but also
summary: 〜上に adds a second point in the same direction as the first — 'and on top of that'. 駅から近い上に = close to the station, and on top of that…. Both points lean the same way (both good, or both bad), so it stacks reasons rather than contrasting them.
pitfalls: 〜上に piles on a point in the same direction (good + good, or bad + bad); it does not contrast the way 一方で does.
Watch the attachment by word type: 近い上に (い-adj), 静かな上に (な-adj), 病気の上に (noun).

examples.ja: この部屋は駅から近い上に、家賃も安いです。
examples.en: This room is close to the station, and on top of that the rent is cheap.
examples.f: この｜部屋[へや]は｜駅[えき]から｜近[ちか]い｜上[うえ]に、｜家賃[やちん]も｜安[やす]いです。

examples.ja: 彼は約束の時間に遅れた上に、謝りもしませんでした。
examples.en: He was late for our appointment, and on top of that he didn't even apologize.
examples.f: ｜彼[かれ]は｜約束[やくそく]の｜時間[じかん]に｜遅[おく]れた｜上[うえ]に、｜謝[あやま]りもしませんでした。

synonyms.note: 〜だけでなく ('not only ~ but also') adds a second item too; 〜上に leans more on 'and worse/better still, on top of that'.
〜のみならず is the stiff, written 'not only ~ but also'; 〜上に is everyday and stresses stacking a further point.
〜ばかりか adds a surprising further point ('not only ~ but even ~'); 〜上に simply piles on more of the same tendency.

related.note: 〜し loosely lists reasons or points; 〜上に more tightly stacks a second point on top of the first.

title: うちに
meaning: while (still) ~; before ~ changes
summary: 〜うちに picks out a window of time and says to act within it. After a plain state it means 'while ~ still holds' (熱いうちに = while it's still hot); after a ない-form it means 'before ~ happens' (忘れないうちに = before I forget). The nuance is that the window will close, so do it now.
pitfalls: 〜ないうちに means 'before ~ happens' (暗くならないうちに = before it gets dark); plain 〜うちに means 'while the state still lasts'.
It carries the sense that the window will end, so act during it — it is not a neutral 'while'.

examples.ja: 熱いうちに、どうぞ召し上がってください。
examples.en: Please eat it while it's still hot.
examples.f: ｜熱[あつ]いうちに、どうぞ｜召し上[めしあ]がってください。

examples.ja: 忘れないうちに、メモしておきます。
examples.en: I'll jot it down before I forget.
examples.f: ｜忘[わす]れないうちに、メモしておきます。

related.note: 〜間に marks a defined span and something happening within it; 〜うちに adds the sense that the state may change, so act now.
〜ないうちに is the negative pattern of this point — 'before ~ happens'; plain 〜うちに is 'while ~ still lasts'.
〜前に just says 'before' a point in time; 〜ないうちに adds 'while it hasn't yet happened, take the chance'.

title: おかげで
meaning: thanks to; owing to; because of (a good result)
summary: 〜おかげで credits a cause with a good outcome — 'thanks to ~'. 先生のおかげで = thanks to my teacher, 天気が良かったおかげで = thanks to the good weather. The default tone is gratitude, so it normally pairs a cause with a welcome result.
structure: Verb ／ い-adjective ／ な-adjective［plain form］＋おかげで
pitfalls: 〜おかげで normally credits a good result; for a bad result you blame on something, use 〜せいで.
It can be turned ironic ('thanks a lot…') for a bad outcome, but its plain meaning is genuine thanks.

examples.ja: 先生のおかげで、試験に合格できました。
examples.en: Thanks to my teacher, I was able to pass the exam.
examples.f: ｜先生[せんせい]のおかげで、｜試験[しけん]に｜合格[ごうかく]できました。

examples.ja: 天気が良かったおかげで、旅行はとても楽しかったです。
examples.en: Thanks to the good weather, the trip was a lot of fun.
examples.f: ｜天気[てんき]が｜良[よ]かったおかげで、｜旅行[りょこう]はとても｜楽[たの]しかったです。

antonyms.note: 〜せいで pins a bad result on a cause ('because of ~, unfortunately'); 〜おかげで credits a good result.

related.note: 〜ために gives a neutral cause or purpose; 〜おかげで specifically thanks a cause for a good outcome.

title: かえって
meaning: on the contrary; rather; if anything (contrary to expectation)
summary: かえって is an adverb marking a result that is the opposite of what you'd naturally expect — you do something meant to help, but かえって it makes things worse. くすりを飲んだのに、かえって具合が悪くなった = took medicine, but if anything felt worse. It flags a reversal against common sense.
pitfalls: かえって signals a reversal of what you'd expect, so there is usually an implied 'you'd think X, but instead…'.
It is close to 逆に, but かえって leans on the sense of an unexpected, backfiring result.

examples.ja: くすりを飲んだのに、かえって具合が悪くなりました。
examples.en: Even though I took some medicine, I actually felt worse.
examples.f: くすりを｜飲[の]んだのに、かえって｜具合[ぐあい]が｜悪[わる]くなりました。

examples.ja: 手伝ってもらったら、かえって時間がかかってしまった。
examples.en: When I got some help, it ended up taking even more time.
examples.f: ｜手伝[てつだ]ってもらったら、かえって｜時間[じかん]がかかってしまった。

synonyms.note: 逆に flatly states the opposite ('conversely'); かえって adds the flavor of a result that backfires against expectation.

related.note: むしろ picks the better of two options ('rather / if anything'); かえって points to an unexpected reverse outcome.

title: かける・かけ
meaning: half-done; not yet finished; on the point of ~ing
summary: 〜かける attaches to the ます-stem to mean an action is only half carried out or is just about to happen — 言いかける = start to say, 倒れかける = be on the verge of falling. The noun form 〜かけ describes a left-unfinished thing — 食べかけ = half-eaten, 読みかけ = half-read. Either way, the action is not seen through to the end.
pitfalls: Attach it to the stem: 読みかける, not 読むかける.
〜かけ (noun) labels something left half-done (読みかけの本); 〜かける (verb) also means 'be on the point of ~ing' (泣きかける).

examples.ja: 食べかけのケーキが、テーブルに置いてあります。
examples.en: There's a half-eaten cake sitting on the table.
examples.f: ｜食[た]べかけのケーキが、テーブルに｜置[お]いてあります。

examples.ja: 何か言いかけて、彼は急に黙ってしまいました。
examples.en: He started to say something, then suddenly fell silent.
examples.f: ｜何[なに]か｜言[い]いかけて、｜彼[かれ]は｜急[きゅう]に｜黙[だま]ってしまいました。

antonyms.note: 〜終わる is an action carried all the way to the finish; 〜かけ・かける is one left half-done.

related.note: 〜切る is doing something thoroughly to the very end; 〜かける is stopping partway or only starting.
〜途中で marks being partway through on the way somewhere; 〜かけ marks a thing itself left half-finished.

title: 〜型
meaning: type; model; -sized; -pattern (noun suffix)
summary: 〜型 attaches to a noun to classify by type, model, or size — 血液型 = blood type, 最新型 = latest model, 大型 = large-size. It sorts things into categories or grades. In these everyday compounds it is read 〜がた.
pitfalls: Don't confuse 型 ('type / model / mold') with the similar-looking 形 ('shape / form') — they carry different meanings.
It classifies by kind, model, or size (大型・小型), so it needs a base noun that names such a category.

examples.ja: 私の血液型はA型です。
examples.en: My blood type is A.
examples.f: ｜私[わたし]の｜血液[けつえき]｜型[がた]はA｜型[がた]です。

examples.ja: この会社は、最新型のロボットを作っています。
examples.en: This company makes the latest-model robots.
examples.f: この｜会社[かいしゃ]は、｜最新[さいしん]｜型[がた]のロボットを｜作[つく]っています。

related.note: 〜風 means '-style / in the manner of ~' (和風 = Japanese-style); 〜型 sorts things into a type, model, or size.

title: がたい
meaning: hard to bring oneself to; difficult (almost impossible) to do
summary: 〜がたい attaches to the ます-stem and marks an action as hard, sometimes nearly impossible, to do — 信じがたい = hard to believe, 忘れがたい = unforgettable. It is formal and rather literary, and pairs with a limited set of verbs of thinking, feeling, and perception. The whole compound behaves like an い-adjective.
pitfalls: It joins only a narrow set of verbs (信じる, 想像する, 理解する, 忘れる, 認める); it does not combine freely with any verb the way にくい does.
More formal and written than 〜にくい; in casual speech people usually say にくい or づらい instead.
Attach it to the stem: 信じがたい, not 信じるがたい.

examples.ja: 彼が嘘をついたなんて、信じがたい話だ。
examples.en: The idea that he told a lie is hard to believe.
examples.f: ｜彼[かれ]が｜嘘[うそ]をついたなんて、｜信[しん]じがたい｜話[はなし]だ。

examples.ja: あの日の景色は、今でも忘れがたい。
examples.en: The scenery of that day is unforgettable even now.
examples.f: あの｜日[ひ]の｜景色[けしき]は、｜今[いま]でも｜忘[わす]れがたい。

synonyms.note: 〜にくい is the everyday 'hard to do'; がたい is formal and limited to a few verbs of thought and perception.
〜づらい is 'hard/uncomfortable to do', often physical or social; がたい is a more abstract 'hard to bring oneself to'.

antonyms.note: 〜やすい 'easy to do' is the plain opposite of this difficulty family.

title: がち
meaning: tends to; apt to; prone to (usually something unwanted)
summary: 〜がち says something tends to happen often, usually with an unwanted flavor — 忘れがち = apt to forget, 病気がち = prone to illness. It attaches to a verb stem or a noun and describes a recurring tendency, not a single event.
pitfalls: It leans negative (遅れがち, 忘れがち, 曇りがち); for a neutral or positive 'tends to', it sounds off.
It describes a habitual tendency, not what is happening right at this moment.
Attach it to the stem, not the dictionary form: 遅れがち, not 遅れるがち.

examples.ja: 忙しいと、朝ごはんを抜きがちになる。
examples.en: When I'm busy, I tend to skip breakfast.
examples.f: ｜忙[いそが]しいと、｜朝[あさ]ごはんを｜抜[ぬ]きがちになる。

examples.ja: 最近、曇りがちの天気が続いている。
examples.en: Lately there's been a stretch of cloudy weather.
examples.f: ｜最近[さいきん]、｜曇[くも]りがちの｜天気[てんき]が｜続[つづ]いている。

synonyms.note: 〜気味 marks a slight touch of something (degree); がち marks how frequently it happens.
〜っぽい 'tends to / -ish' overlaps but is more colloquial and also covers 'looks like'.

related.note: 〜やすい 'prone to' rates the ease/likelihood of one instance; がち is about frequency of occurrence.

title: かというと
meaning: as for why…; the reason is…
summary: なぜ〜かというと sets up a question — typically 'why?' — and then answers it, a smooth way to introduce an explanation. It usually closes with からだ／のだ. Think of it as 'if you ask why…, it's because…'.
structure: なぜ ＋ Sentence［plain form］＋ かというと ＋ …からだ
pitfalls: It typically opens with a question word (なぜ, どうして) and closes with からだ／ためだ; dropping that closing reason feels unfinished.
Keep this 'explaining a reason' use apart from かというと meaning 'if I had to choose' — the reason use hinges on a why-question.

examples.ja: なぜこの仕事を選んだかというと、人と話すのが好きだからです。
examples.en: If you ask why I chose this job, it's because I like talking with people.
examples.f: なぜこの｜仕事[しごと]を｜選[えら]んだかというと、｜人[ひと]と｜話[はな]すのが｜好[す]きだからです。

examples.ja: どうして遅れたかというと、電車が止まっていたからです。
examples.en: As for why I was late, it's because the train had stopped.
examples.f: どうして｜遅[おく]れたかというと、｜電車[でんしゃ]が｜止[と]まっていたからです。

related.note: Same shape, but that one hedges a choice ('if anything'); this one answers a 'why' question.
ので states a reason directly; かというと first raises the why-question, then answers it.

title: かというと
meaning: if I had to say; if anything; rather
summary: かというと, most often as どちらかというと, hedges a choice — 'if I had to pick, I'd lean toward…'. It softens a statement into a mild preference rather than a firm claim.
structure: どちらかというと ＋ Sentence
pitfalls: It most often appears as the set phrase どちらかというと ('if anything / rather'); learn it as a chunk.
This hedging use does not answer a 'why' question — that is the separate reason use of かというと.

examples.ja: どちらかというと、私は夜より朝のほうが元気だ。
examples.en: If anything, I have more energy in the morning than at night.
examples.f: どちらかというと、｜私[わたし]は｜夜[よる]より｜朝[あさ]のほうが｜元気[げんき]だ。

examples.ja: 甘いものは、どちらかというと苦手です。
examples.en: If I had to say, I'm not really into sweet things.
examples.f: ｜甘[あま]いものは、どちらかというと｜苦手[にがて]です。

related.note: Identical form, but that one introduces and answers a 'why'; this one softens a preference.

title: か何か
meaning: or something (like it)
summary: 〜か何か attaches to a noun to say 'or something like it', leaving the exact item vague — お茶か何か = tea or something. Use it when you don't need to pin down which thing you mean.
pitfalls: It follows a noun; for a vague 'do something or other' you would restructure rather than tack か何か on.
It leaves the category open ('X or something similar'); it is not just listing two set choices like AかB.

examples.ja: のどが渇いたので、お茶か何か飲みたい。
examples.en: I'm thirsty, so I'd like to drink tea or something.
examples.f: のどが｜渇[かわ]いたので、お｜茶[ちゃ]か｜何[なに]か｜飲[の]みたい。

examples.ja: 疲れているみたいだね。風邪か何かじゃない？
examples.en: You look tired. Is it a cold or something?
examples.f: ｜疲[つか]れているみたいだね。｜風邪[かぜ]か｜何[なに]かじゃない？

related.note: など lists examples 'and so on'; か何か offers one vague alternative 'or something like it'.

title: 必ずしも
meaning: not necessarily; not always (paired with a negative)
summary: 必ずしも is an adverb that teams up with a later negative to mean 'not necessarily, not always' — 必ずしも〜とは限らない, 必ずしも〜ない. It qualifies a general claim, saying it does not hold in every case.
pitfalls: It must be answered by a negative later in the sentence (ない, とは限らない, わけではない); with a plain positive verb it is ungrammatical.
It very often pairs with とは限らない for 'isn't necessarily the case'.

examples.ja: 高いものが、必ずしもいいとは限らない。
examples.en: Expensive things aren't necessarily good.
examples.f: ｜高[たか]いものが、｜必[かなら]ずしもいいとは｜限[かぎ]らない。

examples.ja: お金があれば必ずしも幸せになれるわけではない。
examples.en: Having money doesn't necessarily make you happy.
examples.f: お｜金[かね]があれば｜必[かなら]ずしも｜幸[しあわ]せになれるわけではない。

synonyms.note: とは限らない is the clause 'not necessarily so'; 必ずしも is the adverb that often sets it up.

title: 〜かは〜によって違う
meaning: whether/what ~ depends on ~; varies depending on
summary: 〜かは〜によって違う says the answer to an embedded question varies depending on something — 何を選ぶかは人によって違う = what you pick depends on the person. The first part is a question clause ending in か; the second names what it varies with.
structure: Sentence［question, ending in か］＋ は ＋ Noun ＋ によって違う
pitfalls: The first blank is an embedded question ending in か (何を…か, どうする…か), not a plain noun.
によって here means 'depending on'; don't confuse it with によって 'by means of' in a passive sentence.

examples.ja: どの方法がいいかは、状況によって違う。
examples.en: Which method is best depends on the situation.
examples.f: どの｜方法[ほうほう]がいいかは、｜状況[じょうきょう]によって｜違[ちが]う。

examples.ja: 何を大切にするかは、人によって違います。
examples.en: What one values differs from person to person.
examples.f: ｜何[なに]を｜大切[たいせつ]にするかは、｜人[ひと]によって｜違[ちが]います。

related.note: によって・による on its own is 'by means of / depending on'; this pattern frames a whole question clause as varying.

title: から〜にかけて
meaning: from ~ through ~ (a continuous span of time or space)
summary: 〜から〜にかけて marks a continuous stretch from one point to another across time or space — 春から夏にかけて = from spring through summer. The boundaries are approximate; it describes a broad range rather than exact endpoints.
structure: Noun ＋ から ＋ Noun ＋ にかけて
pitfalls: The endpoints are vague and the span is one continuous stretch; for a precise 'from X to Y' with clear limits, use から〜まで.
にかけて takes each side as a broad region or period, so exact clock times sound better with まで.

examples.ja: この地方では、夏から秋にかけて雨が多い。
examples.en: In this region there is a lot of rain from summer through autumn.
examples.f: この｜地方[ちほう]では、｜夏[なつ]から｜秋[あき]にかけて｜雨[あめ]が｜多[おお]い。

examples.ja: 今夜から明日の朝にかけて、雪になるでしょう。
examples.en: From tonight through tomorrow morning, it will likely turn to snow.
examples.f: ｜今夜[こんや]から｜明日[あした]の｜朝[あさ]にかけて、｜雪[ゆき]になるでしょう。

related.note: まで marks a clear endpoint 'until'; にかけて spans a vague stretch to an approximate end.

title: から言うと
meaning: from the standpoint of; judging from; in terms of
summary: 〜から言うと presents a judgment made from a particular standpoint or basis — 私の経験から言うと = speaking from my experience. It names the angle you are judging from, then gives the conclusion that follows.
structure: Noun ＋ から言うと／から言えば
pitfalls: It follows a noun naming a viewpoint or basis (経験, 立場, 結果); it doesn't attach to plain verbs directly.
Close to からすると／からすれば; から言うと foregrounds 'putting it into words from this angle'.

examples.ja: 私の経験から言うと、この方法はうまくいかない。
examples.en: From my experience, this method won't go well.
examples.f: ｜私[わたし]の｜経験[けいけん]から｜言[い]うと、この｜方法[ほうほう]はうまくいかない。

examples.ja: 値段から言うと、この店はけっして安くない。
examples.en: In terms of price, this shop is by no means cheap.
examples.f: ｜値段[ねだん]から｜言[い]うと、この｜店[みせ]はけっして｜安[やす]くない。

synonyms.note: として states a role or capacity 'as X'; から言うと gives a judgment from X's standpoint.

title: からこそ
meaning: precisely because; it is exactly because ~ that ~
summary: 〜からこそ emphasizes that this reason, and no other, is the real cause — 家族がいるからこそがんばれる = it's precisely because I have a family that I can keep going. こそ highlights the から clause as the one decisive reason, often for something positive.
pitfalls: It stresses one reason as the true, decisive one; plain から just states a reason without that emphasis.
The main clause often takes のだ／んです to complete the 'that's exactly why…' feel.

examples.ja: 家族がいるからこそ、毎日がんばれる。
examples.en: It's precisely because I have a family that I can give it my all every day.
examples.f: ｜家族[かぞく]がいるからこそ、｜毎日[まいにち]がんばれる。

examples.ja: 難しいからこそ、挑戦する価値がある。
examples.en: Precisely because it's hard, it's worth taking on.
examples.f: ｜難[むずか]しいからこそ、｜挑戦[ちょうせん]する｜価値[かち]がある。

related.note: から just gives a reason; からこそ marks it as the one decisive reason.
こそ is the emphasis particle; からこそ applies that emphasis to a reason clause.

title: 代わりに
meaning: instead of; in place of; in exchange for
summary: 〜代わりに carries two linked senses: 'instead of / in place of' (substitution) and 'in exchange for / to make up for' (compensation) — バターの代わりにオイルを使う = use oil instead of butter; 手伝う代わりに昼ごはんをおごる = treat someone to lunch in return for help. Context tells you which.
pitfalls: After a noun it takes の: 私の代わりに, not 私代わりに.
The same form covers both 'instead of' and 'in exchange for'; read the context to tell substitution from compensation.

examples.ja: 今日は父の代わりに、私が会議に出た。
examples.en: Today I attended the meeting in place of my father.
examples.f: ｜今日[きょう]は｜父[ちち]の｜代[か]わりに、｜私[わたし]が｜会議[かいぎ]に｜出[で]た。

examples.ja: 手伝ってくれる代わりに、晩ごはんをごちそうするよ。
examples.en: In exchange for helping me, I'll treat you to dinner.
examples.f: ｜手伝[てつだ]ってくれる｜代[か]わりに、｜晩[ばん]ごはんをごちそうするよ。

title: 考えられない
meaning: unthinkable; inconceivable; can't imagine
summary: 考えられない is the negative potential of 考える, used as a set phrase meaning 'unthinkable, inconceivable' — a strong reaction that something couldn't possibly be so. It often follows なんて: 〜なんて考えられない = 'I can't imagine…'.
structure: Noun ＋ なんて ＋ 考えられない
Sentence ＋ なんて ＋ 考えられない
pitfalls: As this expression it means 'unthinkable / can't imagine', a judgment — not the literal 'am unable to use my head'.
It usually follows なんて or a quoted situation: 〜なんて考えられない.

examples.ja: スマホなしの生活なんて、今の私には考えられない。
examples.en: A life without a smartphone is unthinkable for me now.
examples.f: スマホなしの｜生活[せいかつ]なんて、｜今[いま]の｜私[わたし]には｜考[かんが]えられない。

examples.ja: こんなに寒い夏があるなんて、考えられない。
examples.en: It's inconceivable that there could be a summer this cold.
examples.f: こんなに｜寒[さむ]い｜夏[なつ]があるなんて、｜考[かんが]えられない。

synonyms.note: わけがない 'there's no way' also denies possibility; 考えられない frames it as 'unimaginable' from the speaker's reaction.

title: 関係がある
meaning: to be connected with / involved in; (negative) to have nothing to do with
summary: 〜と関係がある says two things are connected or that someone is involved with something; the negative 関係がない means 'has nothing to do with it'. It is everyday phrasing for stating a connection or, very often, denying one.
structure: Noun ＋ と／に ＋ 関係がある／関係がない
pitfalls: The thing connected is marked with と (or に): 事件と関係がある.
The negative 関係ない is very common in speech to brush something off ('that's none of my business / irrelevant').

examples.ja: その問題は、私とは関係がありません。
examples.en: That problem has nothing to do with me.
examples.f: その｜問題[もんだい]は、｜私[わたし]とは｜関係[かんけい]がありません。

examples.ja: 天気は農業と深い関係がある。
examples.en: Weather is deeply connected with farming.
examples.f: ｜天気[てんき]は｜農業[のうぎょう]と｜深[ふか]い｜関係[かんけい]がある。

title: 気味
meaning: a touch of; a bit; tending toward (a slight sign of)
summary: 〜気味 attaches to a noun or verb stem to say there is a slight touch or trace of something — 風邪気味 = a touch of a cold, 疲れ気味 = a bit tired. It marks a mild sign or leaning, usually of something not great.
pitfalls: It marks a slight degree ('a bit, a touch'), not a full-blown state; 風邪気味 is coming down with a cold, not having a bad one.
It tends toward negative or unwanted conditions (疲れ気味, 太り気味, 遅れ気味).

examples.ja: 少し疲れ気味なので、今日は早く寝ます。
examples.en: I'm feeling a bit tired, so I'll go to bed early today.
examples.f: ｜少[すこ]し｜疲[つか]れ｜気味[ぎみ]なので、｜今日[きょう]は｜早[はや]く｜寝[ね]ます。

examples.ja: 最近、体重が増え気味で心配だ。
examples.en: Lately my weight has been creeping up, and I'm a little worried.
examples.f: ｜最近[さいきん]、｜体重[たいじゅう]が｜増[ふ]え｜気味[ぎみ]で｜心配[しんぱい]だ。

synonyms.note: がち is 'frequently, apt to' (how often); 気味 is 'a slight touch of' (degree).
っぽい '-ish' overlaps loosely but is broader and more casual.

title: きり
meaning: only; just; (after た-form) ~ and nothing since
summary: きり has two senses: after a noun it means 'only, just' (二人きり = just the two of us), and after a た-form verb it means 'since ~, and nothing has changed since' (出かけたきり = went out and hasn't come back). Both narrow things down to a single case.
pitfalls: With a た-form it implies the expected next action never followed: 寝たきり = bedridden (lay down and stayed that way).
In the 'only' sense it overlaps with だけ but feels more exclusive and is a bit colloquial.

examples.ja: 彼とは一度会ったきり、その後会っていない。
examples.en: I met him just once, and I haven't seen him since.
examples.f: ｜彼[かれ]とは｜一度[いちど]｜会[あ]ったきり、その｜後[ご]｜会[あ]っていない。

examples.ja: 祖母は病気で、もう何年も寝たきりだ。
examples.en: My grandmother is ill and has been bedridden for years now.
examples.f: ｜祖母[そぼ]は｜病気[びょうき]で、もう｜何[なん]｜年[ねん]も｜寝[ね]たきりだ。

synonyms.note: だけ 'only' is the neutral limiter; きり is more exclusive/colloquial and also has the た-form 'since' use.

related.note: ばかり 'nothing but / just' overlaps in the 'only' sense; きり adds the 'and nothing since' meaning.

title: 切る
meaning: to do completely, all the way to the end (or to the limit)
summary: 〜切る attaches to the ます-stem to say you do an action completely, all the way to the end or the limit — 使い切る = use up entirely, 読み切る = read through to the finish. It can also stress reaching an extreme (疲れ切る = be utterly exhausted).
pitfalls: Attach it to the stem: 食べ切る, not 食べる切る.
Beyond 'finish', it can mean 'to the utter limit' (困り切る = be at a total loss); the sense is completeness or extremeness, not just stopping.

examples.ja: 買った食べ物を、家族みんなで食べ切った。
examples.en: The whole family finished off all the food we bought.
examples.f: ｜買[か]った｜食べ物[たべもの]を、｜家族[かぞく]みんなで｜食[た]べ｜切[き]った。

examples.ja: 長いマラソンを、最後まで走り切った。
examples.en: I ran the long marathon all the way to the finish.
examples.f: ｜長[なが]いマラソンを、｜最後[さいご]まで｜走[はし]り｜切[き]った。

antonyms.note: 切れない is its negative — 'can't finish / too much to get through'.

related.note: 〜終わる neutrally marks finishing an action; 〜切る adds 'completely, to the very limit'.

title: 切れない
meaning: can't finish; too much/many to ~ (all the way)
summary: 〜切れない is the negative potential of 〜切る — an action can't be carried through to the end, usually because the amount is too great. 数え切れない = too many to count, 食べ切れない = can't finish eating it all.
pitfalls: It usually means 'too much/many to complete', not simply 'I chose not to'.
Attach it to the stem: 使い切れない, not 使う切れない.

examples.ja: 料理が多すぎて、とても食べ切れない。
examples.en: There's too much food; there's no way I can finish it all.
examples.f: ｜料理[りょうり]が｜多[おお]すぎて、とても｜食[た]べ｜切[き]れない。

examples.ja: 空には、数え切れないほどの星が見えた。
examples.en: Countless stars were visible in the sky — too many to count.
examples.f: ｜空[そら]には、｜数え切[かぞえき]れないほどの｜星[ほし]が｜見[み]えた。

antonyms.note: 切る is the positive 'do completely'; 切れない is 'can't get through it all'.

related.note: ほど 'to the extent' pairs naturally as 数え切れないほど 'so many you can't count'.

title: くせに
meaning: even though; despite (with blame or contempt)
summary: 〜くせに means 'even though', but always with a critical, reproachful edge — you are blaming or looking down on someone for the contradiction. 知っているくせに教えてくれない = he won't tell me even though he knows. Both clauses usually share the same subject.
pitfalls: It carries blame or contempt, so it is rude toward the person described; for a neutral 'even though', use のに.
It connects to nouns with の and な-adjectives with な: 子供のくせに, 下手なくせに.

examples.ja: 知っているくせに、彼は何も教えてくれなかった。
examples.en: Even though he knew, he told me nothing.
examples.f: ｜知[し]っているくせに、｜彼[かれ]は｜何[なに]も｜教[おし]えてくれなかった。

examples.ja: 自分ではやらないくせに、文句ばかり言う。
examples.en: He does nothing himself, yet he's all complaints.
examples.f: ｜自分[じぶん]ではやらないくせに、｜文句[もんく]ばかり｜言[い]う。

synonyms.note: のに is the neutral 'even though'; くせに adds blame and can't be used approvingly.

title: くらい・ぐらい
meaning: about, approximately; to the extent that ~
summary: くらい・ぐらい has two jobs: with quantities it means 'about, approximately' (千円くらい = about 1,000 yen), and after a clause it marks a degree by example — 'to the extent that…' (泣きたいくらい = to the point of wanting to cry). くらい and ぐらい are interchangeable.
structure: Verb［plain form］＋ くらい・ぐらい
pitfalls: In the extent sense it gives a vivid example of a degree (立てないくらい疲れた = so tired I couldn't stand), not a precise measure.
くらい and ぐらい mean the same thing; ぐらい just tends to follow certain sounds. Both are fine.

examples.ja: 駅までは、歩いて15分くらいかかります。
examples.en: It takes about fifteen minutes on foot to the station.
examples.f: ｜駅[えき]までは、｜歩[ある]いて15｜分[ふん]くらいかかります。

examples.ja: お腹が痛くて、動けないくらいだった。
examples.en: My stomach hurt so much that I could barely move.
examples.f: お｜腹[なか]が｜痛[いた]くて、｜動[うご]けないくらいだった。

synonyms.note: ほど also marks extent and approximation; it is a bit more formal and common in negative comparisons.

related.note: The standalone N5 くらい covers just the basic 'about' (approximation) sense.

title: 結果
meaning: as a result of; as the outcome of ~
summary: 〜結果 means 'as the result of ~', linking an effort or process to its outcome — 話し合った結果 = as a result of discussing it; 努力の結果 = as a result of effort. It presents what actually followed from the preceding action.
pitfalls: After a verb use the た-form: 調べた結果, not 調べる結果; after a noun use の: 検査の結果.
It reports an outcome that genuinely followed; it is not a plain 'after (in time)' like た後で.

examples.ja: よく考えた結果、留学することに決めた。
examples.en: After thinking it over carefully, I decided to study abroad.
examples.f: よく｜考[かんが]えた｜結果[けっか]、｜留学[りゅうがく]することに｜決[き]めた。

examples.ja: 努力の結果、試験に合格できた。
examples.en: As a result of my efforts, I was able to pass the exam.
examples.f: ｜努力[どりょく]の｜結果[けっか]、｜試験[しけん]に｜合格[ごうかく]できた。

related.note: た末に also means 'after (much) ~, finally'; 末に stresses a long, hard process, while 結果 stresses the outcome that resulted.

title: 結局
meaning: after all; in the end; when all is said and done
summary: 結局 is an adverb that sums up the final outcome after a stretch of effort, wavering, or twists and turns. You lay out the process, then use 結局 to state how it actually turned out — often against expectations. It frequently pairs with a result clause like 〜ことになった or a negative 〜なかった.
pitfalls: 結局 points to the end result of a process; it does not mean 'finally, after a long wait' with a sense of relief — that is やっと.
It usually reports how things settled out, so it often precedes a past-tense result (結局〜た／結局〜なかった).

examples.ja: いろいろ考えたが、結局行かないことにした。
examples.en: I thought it over from every angle, but in the end I decided not to go.
examples.f: いろいろ｜考[かんが]えたが、｜結局[けっきょく]｜行[い]かないことにした。

examples.ja: みんなで待っていたが、結局彼は来なかった。
examples.en: We all waited, but in the end he never showed up.
examples.f: みんなで｜待[ま]っていたが、｜結局[けっきょく]｜彼[かれ]は｜来[こ]なかった。

related.note: ついに marks a long-awaited or feared point finally being reached; 結局 states the outcome after a process, often an unexpected one.
た末に sums up the result reached after much effort or deliberation; 結局 simply states how things ended up, effort or not.
つまり restates a meaning in other words; 結局 reports how a situation actually ended up.

title: 決して〜ない
meaning: never; by no means; not at all (strong, firm denial)
summary: 決して sets up an emphatic negative that follows later in the sentence, expressing the speaker's firm will or an absolute denial — 'never, no matter what.' It is stronger and more formal than ぜんぜん and often signals a promise or conviction.
pitfalls: 決して must be answered by a negative later in the sentence: 決して忘れない, never 決して忘れる.
It conveys the speaker's determination or a categorical 'no'; it is not a neutral 'not really,' which is ぜんぜん or あまり〜ない.

examples.ja: この約束は決して忘れません。
examples.en: I will never forget this promise.
examples.f: この｜約束[やくそく]は｜決[けっ]して｜忘[わす]れません。

examples.ja: 彼は決してうそをつく人ではない。
examples.en: He is by no means the kind of person who tells lies.
examples.f: ｜彼[かれ]は｜決[けっ]してうそをつく｜人[ひと]ではない。

synonyms.note: ぜんぜん〜ない is a neutral, conversational 'not at all'; 決して〜ない adds firm will and a formal, categorical tone.

related.note: 必ずしも〜ない softens to 'not necessarily'; 決して〜ない is an absolute 'never.'
なかなか〜ない means 'not easily / not readily'; 決して〜ない is a flat denial regardless of effort.

title: こそ
meaning: precisely; for sure; this very one (emphasis)
summary: こそ spotlights the word right before it, singling it out as 'this one, precisely, and not another.' Attached to a noun or phrase it says 'this is the one that really counts' — 今度こそ (this time for sure), こちらこそ (no, thank YOU). It highlights rather than contrasts.
pitfalls: こそ spotlights one item as 'precisely this'; unlike は it does not set up a topic-and-contrast, it simply emphasizes.
In reply exchanges こちらこそ means 'the feeling is mine, precisely' — the emphasis lands on こちら, not on thanking again.

examples.ja: 今年こそ日本語能力試験に合格したい。
examples.en: This year for sure, I want to pass the Japanese Language Proficiency Test.
examples.f: ｜今年[ことし]こそ｜日本語[にほんご]｜能力[のうりょく]｜試験[しけん]に｜合格[ごうかく]したい。

examples.ja: 「手伝ってくれてありがとう。」「いいえ、こちらこそ。」
examples.en: "Thanks for helping me." "No, thank YOU."
examples.f: 「｜手伝[てつだ]ってくれてありがとう。」「いいえ、こちらこそ。」

related.note: からこそ means 'precisely because'; here こそ is fused with the reason から, while plain こそ can spotlight any noun.
さえ emphasizes by giving an extreme example ('even this'); こそ emphasizes by singling one thing out as the very one.
だけ limits to 'only this'; こそ spotlights 'this, precisely,' without excluding others.

title: ことか
meaning: how …!; what …! (deep emotion)
summary: ことか turns a statement into a heartfelt exclamation, usually paired with a question word like どんなに, どれほど, or なんと. It voices strong emotion — how happy, how worried, how long — rather than asking a real question. It has a slightly literary, emotional ring.
structure: どんなに／どれほど／なんと ＋ ［plain form］＋ ことか
pitfalls: It normally needs a degree word (どんなに, どれほど, なんと) to carry the exclamation; ことか alone does not do the job.
Despite the か, it is not a question — it is an emphatic outpouring of feeling.

examples.ja: 合格の知らせを聞いて、どんなにうれしかったことか。
examples.en: When I heard I had passed, oh, how happy I was!
examples.f: ｜合格[ごうかく]の｜知[し]らせを｜聞[き]いて、どんなにうれしかったことか。

examples.ja: この日をどれほど待っていたことか。
examples.en: How long I have waited for this day!
examples.f: この｜日[ひ]をどれほど｜待[ま]っていたことか。

related.note: ことに front-loads the emotion word to color a fact ('to my surprise, …'); ことか makes the whole line an exclamation of degree.
ものだ can voice deep feeling or fond recollection; ことか is specifically an exclamation of 'how much.'

title: ことから
meaning: from the fact that; judging from; owing to the fact that
summary: ことから presents a fact as the grounds you reason from — 'from the fact that A, we can tell / it came about that B.' It often explains how a conclusion is reached, or how a name or reputation arose. The B clause is a judgment, result, or naming that follows from A.
pitfalls: ことから frames A as evidence you infer B from; plain から simply gives a cause, without that 'judging from' nuance.
な-adjectives and nouns take な／である before ことから (静かなことから, 有名であることから).

examples.ja: 窓が割れていたことから、どろぼうが入ったことが分かった。
examples.en: From the fact that the window was broken, we knew a burglar had gotten in.
examples.f: ｜窓[まど]が｜割[わ]れていたことから、どろぼうが｜入[はい]ったことが｜分[わ]かった。

examples.ja: 空が急に暗くなったことから、もうすぐ雨になると思った。
examples.en: Judging from how suddenly the sky darkened, I figured it would rain soon.
examples.f: ｜空[そら]が｜急[きゅう]に｜暗[くら]くなったことから、もうすぐ｜雨[あめ]になると｜思[おも]った。

related.note: から states a straightforward reason; ことから presents a fact as evidence you draw a conclusion from.
ので gives an objective cause for a result; ことから emphasizes reasoning outward from a known fact.
ことだから reasons from someone's known character; ことから reasons from an observed fact or circumstance.

title: ことだ
meaning: should; the thing to do is to ~ (direct advice)
summary: Attached to a verb, ことだ delivers direct advice or a recommendation — 'the best thing is to do X.' It sounds firm and a little instructive, as if handing down the sensible course of action. Use the dictionary form for what to do, the ない-form for what to avoid.
structure: Verb［dictionary form］／［ない form］＋ ことだ
pitfalls: This advice sense attaches to a verb; when ことだ follows a feeling word (うれしいことだ) it is instead an exclamation, a different use.
It can sound top-down, like giving a lesson; for gentler suggestions use ほうがいい or 〜といい.

examples.ja: 上手になりたいなら、毎日練習することだ。
examples.en: If you want to get good, the thing to do is practice every day.
examples.f: ｜上手[じょうず]になりたいなら、｜毎日[まいにち]｜練習[れんしゅう]することだ。

examples.ja: 風邪のときは、無理をせずにゆっくり休むことだ。
examples.en: When you have a cold, you should take it easy and rest well.
examples.f: ｜風邪[かぜ]のときは、｜無理[むり]をせずにゆっくり｜休[やす]むことだ。

synonyms.note: ほうがいい gently suggests one option is better; ことだ states more forcefully what one really ought to do.

antonyms.note: ことはない says there is no need to do something; ことだ says doing it is exactly what one should do.

related.note: べきだ frames a should as a matter of principle or duty; ことだ gives practical, situational advice.

title: ことなの
meaning: it means (doing) ~; it comes down to ~; what it is, is ~
summary: ことなのだ (casual ことなの, polite ことなのです) restates a topic as what it fundamentally amounts to. It takes a plain clause, packages it as a こと — a matter or act — and equates the topic with it, explaining 'what X really is / what it means.' The な comes from こと being treated with the explanatory の.
structure: Noun／〜というのは ＋ Verb［plain form］＋ ことなのだ／ことなの
pitfalls: The な is required because こと takes the explanatory の: ことなのだ, not ことのだ.
This is a defining 'it means that ~,' distinct from the advice ことだ that attaches to a verb ('you should ~').

examples.ja: 東京で働くというのは、日本語を毎日使うことなのだ。
examples.en: Working in Tokyo means using Japanese every single day.
examples.f: ｜東京[とうきょう]で｜働[はたら]くというのは、｜日本語[にほんご]を｜毎日[まいにち]｜使[つか]うことなのだ。

examples.ja: 大人になるというのは、自分で責任を持つことなのだ。
examples.en: Becoming an adult means taking responsibility for yourself.
examples.f: ｜大人[おとな]になるというのは、｜自分[じぶん]で｜責任[せきにん]を｜持[も]つことなのだ。

synonyms.note: ということだ also restates a meaning ('that is to say'); ことなのだ frames the whole thing as one defining matter with explanatory の.

related.note: ことだ after a verb gives advice; ことなのだ defines or explains what something amounts to.

title: ことに
meaning: to my ~ (surprise, delight, regret); ~ enough
summary: ことに puts a feeling word up front to color the fact that follows — 驚いたことに (to my surprise), 残念なことに (regrettably). The emotion is the speaker's reaction to what comes next, delivered as a lead-in before the main clause.
structure: Verb［た form］／い-adjective／な-adjective［な］＋ ことに、＋ Sentence
pitfalls: Only emotion words fit (驚いた, うれしい, 残念な); a neutral verb like 食べた does not work here.
The feeling comes first as a reaction; the fact that caused it follows after ことに.

examples.ja: 驚いたことに、彼女は私の名前をまだ覚えていた。
examples.en: To my surprise, she still remembered my name.
examples.f: ｜驚[おどろ]いたことに、｜彼女[かのじょ]は｜私[わたし]の｜名前[なまえ]をまだ｜覚[おぼ]えていた。

examples.ja: 残念なことに、試合は雨で中止になった。
examples.en: Sadly, the match was called off because of rain.
examples.f: ｜残念[ざんねん]なことに、｜試合[しあい]は｜雨[あめ]で｜中止[ちゅうし]になった。

related.note: ことか makes the whole line an exclamation of degree; ことに tags one feeling onto a fact that follows.
ものだ voices general feeling or nostalgia; ことに names a specific reaction to a specific fact.

title: ことになっている
meaning: it is a rule / arrangement / custom that ~; is supposed to ~
summary: ことになっている describes a rule, arrangement, or custom that is already in place and expected to hold — a school regulation, a schedule, a standing plan. It presents the situation as an established norm rather than a fresh decision.
structure: Verb［dictionary form］／［ない form］＋ ことになっている
pitfalls: ことになっている is a standing rule or arrangement in place; ことになる is a decision or outcome coming about at some point.
Do not confuse it with ことにしている, which is a personal habit you keep by choice, not an external rule.

examples.ja: この学校では、教室で物を食べてはいけないことになっている。
examples.en: At this school, the rule is that you may not eat in the classroom.
examples.f: この｜学校[がっこう]では、｜教室[きょうしつ]で｜物[もの]を｜食[た]べてはいけないことになっている。

examples.ja: 来週、社長と会うことになっている。
examples.en: I'm scheduled to meet with the company president next week.
examples.f: ｜来週[らいしゅう]、｜社長[しゃちょう]と｜会[あ]うことになっている。

related.note: ことになる is the moment a decision or result comes about; ことになっている is the rule or arrangement that then stands.
ことにする is deciding to do something yourself; ことになっている is a norm set from outside.

title: ことは〜が
meaning: it's true that ~, but; ~, yes, but ~ (partial concession)
summary: By repeating the same predicate around ことは and following with が, you concede a point partway before qualifying it — 話せることは話せるが (I can speak it, sure, but…). It admits the first half is true, then adds a reservation.
structure: ［plain form］＋ ことは ＋ ［same word, plain form］＋ が／けれど ＋ Sentence
pitfalls: Repeat the same predicate on both sides of ことは (高いことは高いが), not two different words.
It grants the point only partly; the real message lands in the が clause that follows.

examples.ja: 日本語が話せることは話せるが、まだ上手ではない。
examples.en: It's true I can speak Japanese, but I'm still not good at it.
examples.f: ｜日本語[にほんご]が｜話[はな]せることは｜話[はな]せるが、まだ｜上手[じょうず]ではない。

examples.ja: このかばんは、高いことは高いが、丈夫で長く使える。
examples.en: This bag is expensive, yes, but it's sturdy and lasts a long time.
examples.f: このかばんは、｜高[たか]いことは｜高[たか]いが、｜丈夫[じょうぶ]で｜長[なが]く｜使[つか]える。

related.note: けど simply joins a 'but' clause; ことは〜が specifically concedes the point half-heartedly before qualifying it.
ものの concedes an established fact then adds a contrary result; ことは〜が repeats the predicate to grant it only partly.
とはいえ is a formal 'that said'; ことは〜が is a colloquial 'true, but' built by repeating the word.

title: ことはない
meaning: there is no need to ~; no reason to ~
summary: Verb-dictionary + ことはない reassures someone that a certain action isn't necessary — 'you don't need to (do that).' It is gentle, encouraging advice, often used to talk someone out of worrying or overreacting.
pitfalls: Verb-dictionary + ことはない means 'no need to do'; do not mix it up with たことがない, which means 'have never done' (past experience).
It reassures or reduces a burden, so it pairs with actions the listener need not take on.

examples.ja: そんなに心配することはないよ。きっと大丈夫だから。
examples.en: There's no need to worry so much — it'll surely be fine.
examples.f: そんなに｜心配[しんぱい]することはないよ。きっと｜大丈夫[だいじょうぶ]だから。

examples.ja: 一度の失敗で諦めることはない。
examples.en: There's no reason to give up over a single failure.
examples.f: ｜一[いち]｜度[ど]の｜失敗[しっぱい]で｜諦[あきら]めることはない。

antonyms.note: ことだ says doing something is exactly what you should do; ことはない says there's no need to do it.

related.note: ほうがいい recommends doing something; ことはない reassures that you don't have to.
べきだ frames a duty to act; ことはない removes any such obligation.

title: 込む
meaning: to ~ into (inward); to ~ deeply / thoroughly
summary: 込む attaches to a verb stem in two related senses: moving something inward (飛び込む jump in, 押し込む shove in) and doing an action deeply, hard, or over a long stretch (考え込む sink into thought, 使い込む use extensively). Context makes clear which sense is meant. The compound conjugates as an ordinary う-verb.
pitfalls: Attach it to the stem: 飛び込む, not 飛ぶ込む.
It covers two senses — moving inward and doing thoroughly — so read the base verb and context to tell 押し込む (shove in) from 考え込む (become lost in thought).

examples.ja: 子どもたちが次々にプールに飛び込んだ。
examples.en: The children jumped into the pool one after another.
examples.f: ｜子[こ]どもたちが｜次々[つぎつぎ]にプールに｜飛び込[とびこ]んだ。

examples.ja: 彼は難しい問題を前に、しばらく考え込んでいた。
examples.en: Faced with a hard problem, he sank into thought for a while.
examples.f: ｜彼[かれ]は｜難[むずか]しい｜問題[もんだい]を｜前[まえ]に、しばらく｜考え込[かんがえこ]んでいた。

antonyms.note: 〜出す points an action outward or marks a sudden start; 込む (in the inward sense) moves things in.

related.note: 〜切る stresses completing an action fully to the end; 込む (thorough sense) stresses doing it deeply or at length.
〜抜く means pushing an action through to the very end despite difficulty; 込む (thorough sense) is doing it intensively or repeatedly.

title: さ
meaning: well now; come on; all right (prompting)
summary: Used at the start of an utterance (often lengthened to さあ), this さ urges or invites — 'come on,' 'all right, let's…,' 'now then.' It rallies the listener toward the next action rather than adding meaning to the sentence.
pitfalls: This prompting さ(あ) opens an utterance; keep it apart from sentence-final さ (casual assertion) and the mid-sentence filler さ.
Lengthening to さあ makes the invitation stronger and more natural.

examples.ja: さあ、そろそろ始めましょう。
examples.en: All right, let's get started soon.
examples.f: さあ、そろそろ｜始[はじ]めましょう。

examples.ja: さあ、みんな、行くよ。
examples.en: Come on everyone, let's go.
examples.f: さあ、みんな、｜行[い]くよ。

related.note: The filler さ drops into the middle of casual speech; this さ opens an utterance to urge someone on.
Sentence-final さ asserts casually; sentence-initial さ prompts action.

title: さ
meaning: like; you know; I mean (casual filler)
summary: In casual talk, さ can be dropped in after phrases to buy a beat or keep the listener's attention — much like English 'like' or 'you know.' It adds no meaning; it softens the flow and marks the rhythm of chatty speech.
structure: …さ、… （inserted after a phrase in casual speech）
pitfalls: It is casual and can sound blunt or immature if overused; it carries no content of its own.
Distinct from the opening さあ (urging) and the sentence-final さ (offhand assertion).

examples.ja: あのさ、ちょっと聞きたいことがあるんだけど。
examples.en: Hey, um, there's something I kind of want to ask you.
examples.f: あのさ、ちょっと｜聞[き]きたいことがあるんだけど。

examples.ja: 昨日さ、駅で偶然先生に会ったんだ。
examples.en: So yesterday, you know, I ran into my teacher at the station.
examples.f: ｜昨日[きのう]さ、｜駅[えき]で｜偶然[ぐうぜん]｜先生[せんせい]に｜会[あ]ったんだ。

related.note: The opening さ(あ) urges someone to act; the filler さ just keeps casual speech flowing.
Sentence-final さ closes a line with a light assertion; the filler さ sits mid-sentence.

title: さ
meaning: casual sentence-final particle; a light, offhand よ
summary: At the end of a sentence, さ makes a relaxed, offhand assertion — a softer, more casual cousin of よ. It states a view or reassures in a light, matter-of-fact way, and has a somewhat masculine, easygoing feel.
pitfalls: It is casual and a bit offhand — softer and less insistent than よ; it can sound too breezy in polite settings.
Not the same as the opening さあ (urging) or the mid-sentence filler さ.

examples.ja: 心配ないさ、きっとうまくいくよ。
examples.en: No worries — it'll work out for sure.
examples.f: ｜心配[しんぱい]ないさ、きっとうまくいくよ。

examples.ja: そんなの簡単さ。
examples.en: Something like that is easy.
examples.f: そんなの｜簡単[かんたん]さ。

related.note: Sentence-initial さ(あ) prompts action; this sentence-final さ makes a casual assertion.
The filler さ sits mid-sentence and adds no meaning; this さ closes a line with a light claim.
The N4 suffix さ turns an adjective into a noun (高さ, height); this さ is a sentence-final particle — same spelling, different job.

title: 最中に
meaning: right in the middle of; in the very midst of
summary: 最中に marks the peak of an ongoing action, often the moment something cuts in — 食事の最中に (right in the middle of dinner), 話している最中に (right as I was talking). It stresses that the action was at full swing when interruption or an event occurred.
pitfalls: 最中に highlights the height of an action in progress, usually broken into by something; it suits continuing actions, not instantaneous ones.
A noun takes の before it: 会議の最中に, not 会議最中に.

examples.ja: 食事の最中に、電話がかかってきた。
examples.en: Right in the middle of dinner, a phone call came in.
examples.f: ｜食事[しょくじ]の｜最中[さいちゅう]に、｜電話[でんわ]がかかってきた。

examples.ja: 話している最中に、急に電気が消えた。
examples.en: Right as I was in the middle of talking, the lights suddenly went out.
examples.f: ｜話[はな]している｜最中[さいちゅう]に、｜急[きゅう]に｜電気[でんき]が｜消[き]えた。

related.note: ているところ marks the stage of an action ('in the middle of doing'); 最中に stresses its very peak, often interrupted.
間に marks a span during which something happens; 最中に zooms in on the height of one ongoing action.
うちに means 'while a state lasts / before it changes'; 最中に is 'right at the peak of an action.'

title: 際に
meaning: when; on the occasion of; at the time of
summary: 際に is a formal 'when' for notable occasions or special situations — applying for something, visiting on business, a ceremony. You meet it often in written notices and polite speech; in everyday conversation とき does the same job more plainly.
pitfalls: 際に is formal and suits special or official occasions; for ordinary everyday 'when,' use とき.
A noun takes の before it: 卒業の際に, not 卒業際に.

examples.ja: お申し込みの際に、身分証明書が必要です。
examples.en: When you apply, you will need a form of identification.
examples.f: お｜申し込[もうしこ]みの｜際[さい]に、｜身分[みぶん]｜証明[しょうめい]｜書[しょ]が｜必要[ひつよう]です。

examples.ja: 東京へ出張した際に、旧友と会った。
examples.en: When I was in Tokyo on a business trip, I met up with an old friend.
examples.f: ｜東京[とうきょう]へ｜出張[しゅっちょう]した｜際[さい]に、｜旧友[きゅうゆう]と｜会[あ]った。

related.note: とき is the neutral, everyday 'when'; 際に is its formal counterpart for notable occasions.
最中に means 'right in the middle of an ongoing action'; 際に marks the occasion or moment when you do something.

title: さえ
meaning: even; so much as; not even
summary: さえ singles out an extreme or surprising example to imply the rest follows — 子どもでさえ知っている (even a child knows), 時間さえない (I don't even have time). The idea is 'if even this, then surely everything else.' It is emphatic and often a touch more formal than も.
pitfalls: さえ picks an extreme case to make its point; it is more emphatic and often more written-sounding than も.
Do not confuse plain さえ ('even') with the conditional さえ〜ば ('if only').

examples.ja: そんなことは子どもでさえ知っている。
examples.en: Even a child knows something like that.
examples.f: そんなことは｜子[こ]どもでさえ｜知[し]っている。

examples.ja: 忙しくて、食事をする時間さえない。
examples.en: I'm so busy I don't even have time to eat.
examples.f: ｜忙[いそが]しくて、｜食事[しょくじ]をする｜時間[じかん]さえない。

synonyms.note: すら is a more formal, literary 'even'; さえ is the everyday emphatic 'even.'

related.note: まで stresses reaching an unexpected extreme ('to the point of even'); さえ picks a minimal example to imply the rest.
さえ〜ば uses さえ to mark the one sufficient condition; plain さえ just highlights an extreme example.

title: さえ〜ば
meaning: if only ~; as long as (just) ~
summary: さえ〜ば names the one and only condition needed for a result — 'just do X, and that's all it takes.' A noun takes さえ plus a ば-clause (お金さえあれば), while a verb becomes stem + さえすれば (押しさえすれば). It says nothing else is required.
pitfalls: It marks the sole sufficient condition — 'just this, nothing more' — unlike plain さえ, which only means 'even.'
With verbs, use stem + さえすれば (見さえすれば), not the dictionary form.

examples.ja: お金さえあれば、何でも買えるというわけではない。
examples.en: It's not as if you can buy anything just as long as you have money.
examples.f: お｜金[かね]さえあれば、｜何[なに]でも｜買[か]えるというわけではない。

examples.ja: このボタンを押しさえすれば、機械が動きます。
examples.en: As long as you just press this button, the machine will run.
examples.f: このボタンを｜押[お]しさえすれば、｜機械[きかい]が｜動[うご]きます。

related.note: ば states a general condition; さえ〜ば narrows it to the single sufficient one.
だけで means 'just with / just by' doing something; さえ〜ば frames that one thing as the only condition needed.
Plain さえ highlights an extreme example ('even'); さえ〜ば turns さえ into a sole-condition pattern.

title: させてもらう
meaning: to be allowed to do; to take the liberty of doing (humble)
summary: させてもらう combines the causative with もらう to mean 'receive the favor of being let do X.' You are the one acting, but you frame it as permission granted, which sounds polite and considerate. The extra-polite keigo version is させていただく.
pitfalls: Use the causative て-form: 帰らせてもらう ('be allowed to go home'), not 帰ってもらう ('have someone go home').
For humble, formal situations, raise it to させていただく.

examples.ja: 体調が悪かったので、今日は早く帰らせてもらった。
examples.en: I wasn't feeling well, so I was allowed to leave early today.
examples.f: ｜体調[たいちょう]が｜悪[わる]かったので、｜今日[きょう]は｜早[はや]く｜帰[かえ]らせてもらった。

examples.ja: すみません、少し休ませてもらってもいいですか。
examples.en: Excuse me, would it be all right if I took a short break?
examples.f: すみません、｜少[すこ]し｜休[やす]ませてもらってもいいですか。

synonyms.note: させてください directly asks 'please let me do'; させてもらう describes receiving that permission.

related.note: てもらう has someone else do something for you; させてもらう has them let you do it yourself.
せる・させる is the plain causative 'make/let do'; させてもらう adds もらう to frame it as permission granted to you.

title: さて
meaning: well then; now then; so (shifting to a new topic or action)
summary: さて is a conjunction used to shift gears — to wrap up what came before and move on to a new topic or the next thing you're about to do. It's roughly "well then," "now then," or "so." It usually opens a sentence and signals that the speaker is proceeding to a fresh step.
pitfalls: さて moves the talk forward to a new topic or action; it doesn't state a result — for "and so / and then (as a consequence)" use それで／すると.

examples.ja: さて、そろそろ会議を始めましょう。
examples.en: Well then, let's get the meeting started.
examples.f: さて、そろそろ｜会議[かいぎ]を｜始[はじ]めましょう。

examples.ja: 食事も終わった。さて、片付けを始めよう。
examples.en: The meal's done. Now then, let's start cleaning up.
examples.f: ｜食事[しょくじ]も｜終[お]わった。さて、｜片付[かたづ]けを｜始[はじ]めよう。

related.note: ところで abruptly changes to an unrelated topic ("by the way"); さて moves forward to the next step of the same flow.
それで carries on to a result or consequence; さて just signals a fresh start.
そして adds the next item in sequence; さて marks a shift to a new topic or action.

title: さらに
meaning: furthermore; in addition; even more
summary: さらに adds more on top of what's already there. It has two uses: introducing an additional point ("furthermore, in addition") and raising a degree ("even more so"). さらに大きい = even bigger; 雨が降り、さらに風も出た = it rained, and on top of that the wind came up too.
pitfalls: Two senses share one word: adding another item ("furthermore") and intensifying a degree ("even more") — the surrounding words tell them apart.
さらに is somewhat formal; in casual speech もっと (even more) and それに (besides) are more everyday.

examples.ja: 今日は雨で、さらに風も強くなってきた。
examples.en: Today it's raining, and on top of that the wind has picked up too.
examples.f: ｜今日[きょう]は｜雨[あめ]で、さらに｜風[かぜ]も｜強[つよ]くなってきた。

examples.ja: この店のケーキは、去年よりさらにおいしくなった。
examples.en: This shop's cake has become even more delicious than last year.
examples.f: この｜店[みせ]のケーキは、｜去年[きょねん]よりさらにおいしくなった。

synonyms.note: その上 also means "on top of that," but only adds a further item; さらに can also intensify a degree.

related.note: それに tacks on an extra point in casual speech; さらに is more formal and also does "even more."
〜に加えて adds "in addition to (a specific noun)"; さらに adds another clause on its own.

title: しかない
meaning: have no choice but to (do)
summary: しかない after a dictionary-form verb means there's no option left but to do that action — "have no choice but to." Literally "there is nothing except doing X." It usually carries a note of reluctant acceptance: this is the only path available, so you take it.
pitfalls: Attach it to the dictionary form: 行くしかない, not 行ったしかない.
Don't confuse it with the しか〜ない that wraps a noun to mean "only" (水しかない = there's only water). Here しかない follows a verb and means "no choice but to."

examples.ja: 終電がもうないから、歩いて帰るしかない。
examples.en: The last train's already gone, so I have no choice but to walk home.
examples.f: ｜終電[しゅうでん]がもうないから、｜歩[ある]いて｜帰[かえ]るしかない。

examples.ja: こうなったら、最後までやるしかないね。
examples.en: Now that it's come to this, we've just got to see it through to the end.
examples.f: こうなったら、｜最後[さいご]までやるしかないね。

synonyms.note: 〜よりほかない means the same "nothing for it but to," in a stiffer, more written tone.
〜よりしかたがない also means "no way but to," stressing there's no other method.

related.note: 〜ざるを得ない is a formal "be forced to," stressing outside pressure; しかない is the plainer "no choice but to."
The noun-attaching しか〜ない means "only"; this verb-attaching しかない means "no choice but to."

title: 次第
meaning: as soon as ~; depending on ~
summary: 次第 has two jobs. After a verb stem it means "as soon as ~; the moment ~ is done" (連絡がつき次第 = as soon as I get in touch), and the following clause looks to the future — a plan or request. After a noun it means "depends on ~" (天気次第 = depends on the weather). It's a formal expression common in business and announcements.
pitfalls: With the "as soon as" use, what follows is a plan or request that hasn't happened yet — don't put a past-tense result after it.
It's formal; for casual "as soon as" in everyday speech, 〜たらすぐに is more natural.

examples.ja: 準備ができ次第、出発します。
examples.en: We'll set off as soon as the preparations are ready.
examples.f: ｜準備[じゅんび]ができ｜次第[しだい]、｜出発[しゅっぱつ]します。

examples.ja: 参加するかどうかは、あなた次第です。
examples.en: Whether or not to take part is up to you.
examples.f: ｜参加[さんか]するかどうかは、あなた｜次第[しだい]です。

related.note: 〜次第で extends the noun use to "depending on ~, the outcome varies."
次第に uses the same kanji but means "gradually" — a different point entirely.
〜たとたん is a spontaneous, often surprising past event; 次第 looks ahead to a planned action.

title: しばらく
meaning: for a while; for a moment; for the time being
summary: しばらく is an adverb for an unspecified stretch of time — "for a while," "for a moment," or "for the time being." How long it actually means depends entirely on context: しばらくお待ちください is a short wait, while しばらく会っていない can mean many months.
pitfalls: The length is vague and context-decided — it can mean a few minutes or several months, so lean on the situation to judge.

examples.ja: しばらくお待ちください。すぐに戻ります。
examples.en: Please wait a moment. I'll be right back.
examples.f: しばらくお｜待[ま]ちください。すぐに｜戻[もど]ります。

examples.ja: 引っ越してから、しばらく友達に会っていない。
examples.en: Since I moved, I haven't seen my friends for a while.
examples.f: ｜引っ越[ひっこ]してから、しばらく｜友達[ともだち]に｜会[あ]っていない。

title: 助詞＋の
meaning: a particle kept before の to modify a following noun (からの, での, との…)
summary: When a phrase marked by a particle like から, で, と, or へ needs to modify a noun, you keep that particle and add の — 母からの手紙 = "a letter from mother," 東京での生活 = "life in Tokyo." The particle keeps its normal meaning (from / at / with…) and の links the whole phrase to the noun.
structure: Noun ＋ 助詞（から／で／と／へ／まで…）＋ の ＋ Noun
pitfalls: This is for meaning-particles like から・で・と・へ・まで; を and が don't stack with の this way — they drop or convert instead.
Don't drop the particle: 友達からのメール (a message from a friend) is not the same as 友達のメール (a friend's message).

examples.ja: 友達からのメールを読んで、うれしくなった。
examples.en: I read the message from my friend and it cheered me up.
examples.f: ｜友達[ともだち]からのメールを｜読[よ]んで、うれしくなった。

examples.ja: これは母との約束だから、必ず守ります。
examples.en: This is a promise with my mother, so I'll definitely keep it.
examples.f: これは｜母[はは]との｜約束[やくそく]だから、｜必[かなら]ず｜守[まも]ります。

related.note: Plain の joins two nouns directly (私の本); 助詞＋の keeps a meaning-particle in front of the の.

title: 〜(の)姿
meaning: figure; the visible sight of someone (doing something)
summary: 姿 is a noun for a person's figure or appearance — the way they look, often caught in a particular moment. 〜(の)姿 lets you point to "the sight of someone doing ~": 走る姿 = the sight of them running, 着物姿 = a figure in a kimono. It highlights the visible form of a person.
pitfalls: 姿 is about a person's visible figure or form; for the general look or state of things in the abstract, 様子 or 見た目 usually fit better.

examples.ja: 子どもたちが元気に遊ぶ姿を見ると、うれしくなる。
examples.en: Seeing the children playing happily makes me glad.
examples.f: ｜子[こ]どもたちが｜元気[げんき]に｜遊[あそ]ぶ｜姿[すがた]を｜見[み]ると、うれしくなる。

examples.ja: 彼女の着物姿はとてもきれいだった。
examples.en: She looked beautiful in her kimono.
examples.f: ｜彼女[かのじょ]の｜着物[きもの]｜姿[すがた]はとてもきれいだった。

related.note: 〜ように見える is your impression that something seems a certain way; 姿 names the visible figure itself.

title: ずつ
meaning: each; apiece; at a time; in steady increments
summary: ずつ follows a quantity to mean "that much each" or "that much at a time" — 一つずつ = one apiece, 少しずつ = little by little, 三個ずつ = three each. It spreads an amount evenly across people or occasions, or marks steady, equal increments.
pitfalls: ずつ needs a quantity word in front of it (一つ, 少し, 千円); it doesn't attach straight onto a plain noun.

examples.ja: 子どもたちにお菓子を二つずつ配った。
examples.en: I handed out two sweets to each of the children.
examples.f: ｜子[こ]どもたちにお｜菓子[かし]を｜二[ふた]つずつ｜配[くば]った。

examples.ja: 毎日少しずつ漢字を覚えています。
examples.en: I learn a few kanji at a time every day.
examples.f: ｜毎日[まいにち]｜少[すこ]しずつ｜漢字[かんじ]を｜覚[おぼ]えています。

related.note: 〜ごとに marks "every unit" (一日ごとに = every day); ずつ marks "this much each / at a time."

title: ずっと
meaning: by far; way (more); far and away — in comparisons
summary: In a comparison, ずっと intensifies the gap — "by far," "way more," "far and away." AよりずっとB stresses that B beats A by a wide margin, not just barely. Note this is a separate sense from the ずっと that means "the whole time / continuously."
pitfalls: This comparative ずっと emphasizes a big difference; the same word also means "continuously / the whole time," so let the context tell them apart.

examples.ja: 新しいパソコンは前のよりずっと速い。
examples.en: The new computer is way faster than the old one.
examples.f: ｜新[あたら]しいパソコンは｜前[まえ]のよりずっと｜速[はや]い。

examples.ja: 電車で行くより、歩いたほうがずっと気持ちいい。
examples.en: Walking is far more pleasant than going by train.
examples.f: ｜電車[でんしゃ]で｜行[い]くより、｜歩[ある]いたほうがずっと｜気持[きも]ちいい。

related.note: より marks the thing compared against; ずっと intensifies how wide the gap is.
一番 picks the top of a whole group (superlative); ずっと stresses the margin between just two things.

title: すでに
meaning: already; previously (something is already done or the case)
summary: すでに says an action or state is "already" done or in place by a given point — 会議はすでに始まっていた = the meeting had already started. It's the more formal, written cousin of もう, and unlike もう it isn't used for "soon" or "not anymore."
structure: すでに ＋ Verb（already done / already the case）
pitfalls: すでに is fairly formal and written; in everyday speech もう is the natural choice.
Unlike もう, すでに only means "already" — it isn't used for "(not) any longer" or "soon."

examples.ja: 私が着いたとき、彼らはすでに帰っていた。
examples.en: By the time I arrived, they had already left.
examples.f: ｜私[わたし]が｜着[つ]いたとき、｜彼[かれ]らはすでに｜帰[かえ]っていた。

examples.ja: そのニュースはすでに知っていました。
examples.en: I already knew that news.
examples.f: そのニュースはすでに｜知[し]っていました。

synonyms.note: もう is the everyday spoken word for "already"; すでに is its formal, written equivalent.

related.note: とっくに stresses "already, and long ago"; すでに just states that it's already so.

title: すなわち
meaning: namely; that is to say; in other words
summary: すなわち restates what came just before, more precisely — "namely," "that is," "in other words." It equates two things, where the second is a clearer or more exact version of the first. It's formal and common in writing, explanations, and definitions.
pitfalls: すなわち is formal and equates terms precisely; for a casual "in other words / basically," use つまり.

examples.ja: 彼は父の兄、すなわち私のおじです。
examples.en: He is my father's older brother — that is, my uncle.
examples.f: ｜彼[かれ]は｜父[ちち]の｜兄[あに]、すなわち｜私[わたし]のおじです。

examples.ja: 締め切りは明後日、すなわち水曜日です。
examples.en: The deadline is the day after tomorrow — namely, Wednesday.
examples.f: ｜締め切[しめき]りは｜明後日[みょうごにち]、すなわち｜水曜日[すいようび]です。

synonyms.note: つまり sums up or rephrases in a casual tone; すなわち equates the two precisely and more formally.

related.note: 要するに boils a long point down to its gist; すなわち restates one thing as an equivalent.

title: ずに
meaning: without doing ~
summary: ずに attaches to a verb's negative base to mean "without doing ~" — 朝ご飯を食べずに家を出た = went out without eating breakfast. It's the more formal, written equivalent of ないで. The one irregular form is する → せずに.
pitfalls: する becomes せずに, not しずに.
ずに is more formal and written; ないで is the everyday spoken choice.

examples.ja: 傘を持たずに家を出て、雨に降られてしまった。
examples.en: I left home without taking an umbrella and got caught in the rain.
examples.f: ｜傘[かさ]を｜持[も]たずに｜家[いえ]を｜出[で]て、｜雨[あめ]に｜降[ふ]られてしまった。

examples.ja: よく考えずに返事をして、あとで困った。
examples.en: I answered without thinking it through, and had trouble later.
examples.f: よく｜考[かんが]えずに｜返事[へんじ]をして、あとで｜困[こま]った。

synonyms.note: ないで is the everyday spoken "without doing ~"; ずに is the same meaning in a formal, written register.

related.note: 〜ことなく is a formal "without ever ~ing"; ずに is the plainer "without doing (this time)."
〜ずに済む builds on ずに to mean "get by without having to ~."

title: ずにはいられない
meaning: can't help but do; can't keep oneself from doing
summary: ずにはいられない says you can't stop yourself from doing something — the urge or feeling is too strong to hold back. 笑わずにはいられない = can't help laughing. It's the formal, written partner of ないではいられない, and する becomes せずにはいられない.
structure: Verb［ない-form stem］＋ ずにはいられない
する → せずにはいられない
pitfalls: する becomes せずにはいられない, not しずにはいられない.
It describes a feeling or urge you can't suppress — usually your own; it's not for an outside obligation like "must, because the rules say so."

examples.ja: あの映画の最後は、泣かずにはいられなかった。
examples.en: At the end of that movie, I couldn't help crying.
examples.f: あの｜映画[えいが]の｜最後[さいご]は、｜泣[な]かずにはいられなかった。

examples.ja: 困っている人を見ると、助けずにはいられない。
examples.en: When I see someone in trouble, I can't help but help them.
examples.f: ｜困[こま]っている｜人[ひと]を｜見[み]ると、｜助[たす]けずにはいられない。

synonyms.note: ないではいられない means exactly the same; ずにはいられない is its more formal, written form.

related.note: 〜ざるを得ない is being forced to act by circumstances; ずにはいられない is an inner urge you can't hold back.
〜てたまらない is an unbearably strong feeling; ずにはいられない is an action you can't stop yourself from taking because of one.

title: すると
meaning: and just then; thereupon; whereupon
summary: すると links two events: right after the first, the second happened — often something the speaker observed, sometimes unexpected. ドアを開けた。すると、猫が飛び出してきた = I opened the door, whereupon a cat jumped out. It can also mean "if that's so, then…" in reaction to what was just said.
structure: Sentence。＋ すると、＋ Sentence（and just then / thereupon）
pitfalls: The second clause is usually something that happened on its own, often unexpected — not an action the speaker then chose to take.
Keep it apart from そうすると, which means "if you do it that way / in that case."

examples.ja: ボタンを押した。すると、電気が消えた。
examples.en: I pressed the button, and just then the light went out.
examples.f: ボタンを｜押[お]した。すると、｜電気[でんき]が｜消[き]えた。

examples.ja: 窓を開けた。すると、冷たい風が入ってきた。
examples.en: I opened the window, and in came a cold wind.
examples.f: ｜窓[まど]を｜開[あ]けた。すると、｜冷[つめ]たい｜風[かぜ]が｜入[はい]ってきた。

related.note: そうすると supposes doing "that" and gives the result; すると reports what actually followed.
The conditional と states a general "whenever A, then B"; すると connects two specific past events.
そこで is "and so" leading to a chosen next action; すると is "and just then" for what happened on its own.

title: せいぜい
meaning: at most; at best; no more than
summary: せいぜい caps an amount — "at most," "at best," no more than that — often hinting that it's less than you might expect. 集まってもせいぜい十人だろう = at most about ten people. It can also mean "as much as one can" (せいぜい頑張って), which sometimes sounds faintly sarcastic.
structure: せいぜい ＋ Verb（as much as one can）
