pitfalls: せいぜい usually carries a nuance that the amount is smaller or less impressive than one might expect.
The "do your best" せいぜい〜 can come across as sarcastic depending on tone.

examples.ja: この仕事は、急いでもせいぜい一週間で終わるだろう。
examples.en: Even in a hurry, this job will take at most a week.
examples.f: この｜仕事[しごと]は、｜急[いそ]いでもせいぜい｜一[いち]｜週間[しゅうかん]で｜終[お]わるだろう。

examples.ja: 夏休みに旅行できても、せいぜい二、三回くらいだ。
examples.en: Even if I get to travel over summer break, it'll be two or three times at most.
examples.f: ｜夏休[なつやす]みに｜旅行[りょこう]できても、せいぜい｜二[に]、｜三[さん]｜回[かい]くらいだ。

antonyms.note: 少なくとも sets a lower limit ("at least this much"); せいぜい sets an upper limit ("at most this much").

related.note: せめて is the minimum you'd wish for ("at least"); せいぜい is the maximum you can expect ("at most").
たったの stresses "only, as few as"; せいぜい caps the count as an upper limit.

title: せいで
meaning: because of; due to (blaming an unwanted result on a cause)
summary: せいで pins a bad outcome on a cause — "because of ~, (something unwanted happened)." 電車が遅れたせいで、遅刻した = I was late because the train was delayed. The result is undesirable, and せいで often assigns fault. Its positive-outcome counterpart is おかげで.
pitfalls: せいで is for unwanted results and often assigns blame; for a welcome result, use おかげで.
At the end of a sentence it becomes 〜のせいだ ("it's the fault of ~").

examples.ja: 昨日夜ふかしをしたせいで、今朝は頭が痛い。
examples.en: Because I stayed up late last night, my head hurts this morning.
examples.f: ｜昨日[きのう]｜夜[よ]ふかしをしたせいで、｜今朝[けさ]は｜頭[あたま]が｜痛[いた]い。

examples.ja: 大雨のせいで、電車が止まってしまった。
examples.en: Because of the heavy rain, the trains stopped.
examples.f: ｜大雨[おおあめ]のせいで、｜電車[でんしゃ]が｜止[と]まってしまった。

antonyms.note: おかげで credits a good result to its cause ("thanks to"); せいで blames a bad one on it.

related.note: ので is a neutral "because" with no blame; せいで adds fault for an unwanted outcome.
〜ために gives a neutral cause (or a purpose); せいで specifically pins down blame for a bad result.

title: せっかく
meaning: with much effort; a precious/long-awaited chance (so it'd be a shame to waste it)
summary: せっかく marks something as the fruit of special effort or a rare opportunity, so it would be a shame to let it go to waste. It often pairs with のに (regret that the effort or chance was wasted) or だから (so let's make the most of it): せっかく作ったのに = I went to all that trouble to make it, yet…
structure: せっかく ＋ Verb／Noun（… のに／… だから）
pitfalls: Two common patterns: せっかく〜のに (regret the effort or chance was wasted) and せっかく〜だから (so let's take advantage of it).
せっかく frames the value of an effort or chance; it isn't just a plain "with effort" adverb like 一生懸命 (which describes doing something hard).

examples.ja: せっかく京都まで来たのだから、お寺を見て回ろう。
examples.en: Since we've come all the way to Kyoto, let's go around and see some temples.
examples.f: せっかく｜京都[きょうと]まで｜来[き]たのだから、お｜寺[てら]を｜見[み]て｜回[まわ]ろう。

examples.ja: せっかくの休みなのに、ずっと雨だった。
examples.en: It was a precious day off, and yet it rained all day.
examples.f: せっかくの｜休[やす]みなのに、ずっと｜雨[あめ]だった。

related.note: わざわざ stresses going out of one's way to do something deliberately; せっかく stresses that the effort or chance shouldn't be wasted.
せっかく often leads into のに to voice regret that the effort came to nothing.

title: 前者は・後者は
kana: ぜんしゃは・こうしゃは
meaning: the former ~ ; the latter ~
summary: 前者 means "the former" (the first of two things mentioned) and 後者 means "the latter" (the second). Used together, they let you refer back to two items without repeating them: 前者は安く、後者は速い = the former is cheap, the latter is fast. It's a formal pairing, common in writing and comparisons.
pitfalls: 前者／後者 work only when exactly two things have been named; for three or more, refer to them by name instead.
後者 is read こうしゃ; don't read this pair as the time words 前 (before) / 後 (after).

examples.ja: 犬と猫なら、前者のほうが世話が楽だと思う。
examples.en: Between a dog and a cat, I think the former is easier to take care of.
examples.f: ｜犬[いぬ]と｜猫[ねこ]なら、｜前者[ぜんしゃ]のほうが｜世話[せわ]が｜楽[らく]だと｜思[おも]う。

examples.ja: 電車とバスを比べると、後者のほうが安いことが多い。
examples.en: Comparing trains and buses, the latter is often the cheaper one.
examples.f: ｜電車[でんしゃ]とバスを｜比[くら]べると、｜後者[こうしゃ]のほうが｜安[やす]いことが｜多[おお]い。

related.note: 一方で contrasts two sides of a situation; 前者／後者 point back to two specific items already named.

title: そうすると
meaning: if you do that; if that's done; in that case
summary: そうすると takes the previous action or statement as a condition and gives what follows from it — "if you do that, then…" or "in that case." 右に曲がってください。そうすると、駅が見えます = Turn right; if you do that, you'll see the station. It's more explicit than plain すると about supposing "that (action/situation)."
pitfalls: そうすると supposes doing or accepting "that" and states the outcome; plain すると just reports what happened right after an event.

examples.ja: 毎日運動してください。そうすると、体が丈夫になります。
examples.en: Please exercise every day. If you do that, your body will grow stronger.
examples.f: ｜毎日[まいにち]｜運動[うんどう]してください。そうすると、｜体[からだ]が｜丈夫[じょうぶ]になります。

examples.ja: ここでお金を入れます。そうすると、切符が出てきます。
examples.en: You put money in here. Then a ticket comes out.
examples.f: ここでお｜金[かね]を｜入[い]れます。そうすると、｜切符[きっぷ]が｜出[で]てきます。

related.note: すると narrates what actually happened next; そうすると sets up "do that → this results."
そこで leads to the speaker's next chosen action; そうすると gives the result of supposing "that."

title: そうもない・そうにない
kana: そうもない・そうにない
romaji: sou mo nai / sou ni nai
meaning: very unlikely to; showing no sign of (happening)
summary: This is the negative of the "looks like / seems" そう. Added to a verb stem, そうもない・そうにない says something shows no sign of happening — it looks very unlikely. 雨がやみそうにない = the rain doesn't look like it'll stop. It's your read of how things look, not a flat statement of fact.
structure: Verb［stem］＋ そうもない／そうにない
pitfalls: Built on the appearance そう, so it attaches to the verb stem: 終わりそうにない, not 終わるそうにない.
Don't mix it up with the hearsay そうだ ("I hear that ~"); this form is about how things look, in the "unlikely" negative sense.

examples.ja: 仕事が多くて、今日じゅうに終わりそうにない。
examples.en: There's so much work that it doesn't look like it'll get finished today.
examples.f: ｜仕事[しごと]が｜多[おお]くて、｜今日[きょう]じゅうに｜終[お]わりそうにない。

examples.ja: 約束の時間になっても、彼は来そうもない。
examples.en: Even though it's past the time we agreed on, he shows no sign of coming.
examples.f: ｜約束[やくそく]の｜時間[じかん]になっても、｜彼[かれ]は｜来[き]そうもない。

antonyms.note: そうだ (appearance) says something looks likely to happen; そうにない is its "looks unlikely" negative.

related.note: そうな／そうに modifies with a "looks like ~" impression; そうにない is the negative "looks like it won't."
〜かねない warns something bad might well happen; そうもない says something looks very unlikely to.

title: そこで
meaning: and so; that being the case, I (deliberately) did ...
summary: As a conjunction, そこで describes a situation and then introduces the action the speaker purposely took in response — roughly "and so" or "that's why I ...". The key point is that what follows is a deliberate step taken because of the circumstances, not an outcome that simply happened by itself.
pitfalls: そこで introduces an action taken on purpose in response to a situation; when the second part is an automatic result, その結果 or それで fits better.
Don't confuse this connector with the phrase そこで meaning 'there, at that place' — as a conjunction it opens a new sentence.

examples.ja: 部屋が暗くなってきた。そこで、電気をつけた。
examples.en: The room was getting dark, so I turned on the light.
examples.f: ｜部屋[へや]が｜暗[くら]くなってきた。そこで、｜電気[でんき]をつけた。

examples.ja: 資料が足りなくなった。そこで、部長に相談することにした。
examples.en: We ran short of materials, so I decided to consult the manager.
examples.f: ｜資料[しりょう]が｜足[た]りなくなった。そこで、｜部長[ぶちょう]に｜相談[そうだん]することにした。

related.note: その結果 states an outcome that follows on its own; そこで introduces an action the speaker deliberately takes.
そのため(に) gives the reason for what follows; そこで frames the action prompted by that situation.

title: その結果
meaning: as a result (of that)
summary: その結果 opens a sentence to present the outcome that the previous sentence led to — "as a result." It frames what happened as the natural consequence of what came before, and is common in explanations and reports.
pitfalls: Keep the conjunction その結果 (which starts a new sentence) apart from the plain noun 結果 ('a result') used inside a sentence.

examples.ja: 毎日走る練習を続けた。その結果、大会で優勝できた。
examples.en: I kept up running practice every day. As a result, I won the tournament.
examples.f: ｜毎日[まいにち]｜走[はし]る｜練習[れんしゅう]を｜続[つづ]けた。その｜結果[けっか]、｜大会[たいかい]で｜優勝[ゆうしょう]できた。

examples.ja: 値段を下げた。その結果、売り上げが二倍になった。
examples.en: They lowered the price. As a result, sales doubled.
examples.f: ｜値段[ねだん]を｜下[さ]げた。その｜結果[けっか]、｜売り上[うりあ]げが｜二[に]｜倍[ばい]になった。

related.note: 結果 is the noun 'result' used within a clause; その結果 is the fixed connector 'as a result' that opens a sentence.
そこで introduces a deliberate response; その結果 introduces an outcome that followed automatically.
そのため(に) points to a cause; その結果 points to the effect that came out of it.

title: そのため(に)
meaning: because of that; for that reason (also: to that end)
summary: そのため(に) refers back to something just stated and presents it as the reason for what follows — "because of that; for that reason." The に is optional. Depending on context it can also mean "to that end / for that purpose."
pitfalls: It has two readings: after a cause it means 'for that reason'; after a stated goal it means 'to that end.' Context decides which.

examples.ja: 昨日は大雪だった。そのため、電車が止まった。
examples.en: Yesterday there was heavy snow. Because of that, the trains stopped.
examples.f: ｜昨日[きのう]は｜大雪[おおゆき]だった。そのため、｜電車[でんしゃ]が｜止[と]まった。

examples.ja: 医者になりたい。そのために、毎日遅くまで勉強している。
examples.en: I want to become a doctor. To that end, I study late every day.
examples.f: ｜医者[いしゃ]になりたい。そのために、｜毎日[まいにち]｜遅[おそ]くまで｜勉強[べんきょう]している。

related.note: その結果 highlights the effect that followed; そのため(に) highlights the cause behind what follows.
そこで presents a deliberate action taken; そのため(に) presents the reason for the next statement.
ために is the general 'because of / in order to' pattern; そのため(に) packages a whole prior sentence as 'that.'

title: それとも
meaning: or; or else (offering a choice in a question)
summary: それとも sits between two questions or options and asks the listener to choose — "or (is it) ...?" It belongs in questions where you lay out alternatives, not in plain statements.
structure: Noun ＋ それとも ＋ Noun（within a question）
pitfalls: それとも offers a choice inside a question; to join nouns in a statement ('A or B'), use または or か, not それとも.

examples.ja: コーヒーにしますか。それとも、紅茶にしますか。
examples.en: Will you have coffee? Or would you rather have tea?
examples.f: コーヒーにしますか。それとも、｜紅茶[こうちゃ]にしますか。

examples.ja: 今日行くの?それとも明日にするの?
examples.en: Are you going today? Or are you making it tomorrow?
examples.f: ｜今日[きょう]｜行[い]くの?それとも｜明日[あした]にするの?

related.note: または joins nouns in a statement ('A or B'); それとも offers a choice between questions.
あるいは is a more formal 'or' used in statements; それとも is for spoken either/or questions.
か〜か lists the options inside one clause; それとも links two separate questions.

title: 第一
meaning: first of all; above all; the most important thing
summary: 第一(に) singles something out as the top priority or the first in a sequence — "first of all; above all." As 第一に it opens a list ('firstly'); as 第一(だ) it stresses what matters most of all.
pitfalls: As a set adverb, 第一 marks priority or order; keep it separate from counter uses like 第一課 ('Lesson 1').

examples.ja: 旅行では、第一に安全を考えるべきだ。
examples.en: When traveling, you should think of safety first of all.
examples.f: ｜旅行[りょこう]では、｜第[だい]｜一[いち]に｜安全[あんぜん]を｜考[かんが]えるべきだ。

examples.ja: 何よりも健康が第一だ。
examples.en: More than anything, health comes first.
examples.f: ｜何[なに]よりも｜健康[けんこう]が｜第[だい]｜一[いち]だ。

title: だけしか
meaning: only; nothing but (emphatic)
summary: だけしか stacks だけ onto しか to drive home "only / nothing but," and like plain しか it must be followed by a negative verb. The doubling makes the limitation sound stronger, and often more regretful, than だけ on its own.
structure: Noun ＋ だけしか ＋ Verb［ない form］
Number＋Counter ＋ だけしか ＋ Verb［ない form］
pitfalls: Because of しか, the predicate must be negative: 百円だけしかない, not 百円だけしかある.
It stresses scarcity; plain だけ (which takes a positive verb) is neutral by comparison.

examples.ja: 財布には百円だけしか残っていない。
examples.en: I've got nothing but a hundred yen left in my wallet.
examples.f: ｜財布[さいふ]には｜百[ひゃく]｜円[えん]だけしか｜残[のこ]っていない。

examples.ja: この店には古い服だけしか置いていなかった。
examples.en: That shop had nothing but old clothes.
examples.f: この｜店[みせ]には｜古[ふる]い｜服[ふく]だけしか｜置[お]いていなかった。

synonyms.note: しか〜ない is the base 'only ... not' pattern; だけしか adds だけ for extra emphasis on the limit.

related.note: だけ takes a positive verb and is neutral; だけしか demands a negative and stresses how little there is.
のみ is a formal, written 'only'; だけしか is emphatic and colloquial with a regretful tone.

title: だけでなく(て)〜も
meaning: not only ~ but also ~
summary: だけでなく(て)〜も adds a second, often bigger item onto the first — "not only X but also Y." The も marks the added item. The なくて form is a touch more conversational than the plain なく.
structure: Noun ＋ だけでなく（て）、＋ Noun ＋ も
Sentence［plain form］＋ だけでなく（て）、〜も
pitfalls: Mark the added second item with も: 英語だけでなく中国語も, not just 英語だけでなく中国語.

examples.ja: 彼は英語だけでなく、中国語も話せる。
examples.en: He can speak not only English but also Chinese.
examples.f: ｜彼[かれ]は｜英語[えいご]だけでなく、｜中国[ちゅうごく]｜語[ご]も｜話[はな]せる。

examples.ja: この町は景色がきれいなだけでなく、食べ物もおいしい。
examples.en: This town not only has beautiful scenery but also great food.
examples.f: この｜町[まち]は｜景色[けしき]がきれいなだけでなく、｜食べ物[たべもの]もおいしい。

synonyms.note: だけでなく is the same 'not only' idea; だけでなく(て)〜も foregrounds the paired も on the added item.

related.note: 〜ばかりでなく is a near-equal 'not only'; the だけでなく version is the more everyday phrasing.

title: 確かに
meaning: certainly; it's true that ... (often conceding a point)
summary: 確かに expresses that something is certainly true — "surely; certainly." Very often it concedes a point before a pushback: 確かに〜が means "it's true that ..., but ...". On its own it simply confirms that you're sure of something.
structure: 確かに ＋ Sentence ＋ が／けれど、＋ Sentence
pitfalls: Don't mix up the adverb 確かに ('certainly') with the な-adjective 確か ('sure, reliable') or 確か used to mean 'if I remember right.'

examples.ja: 確かに、彼の言うことにも一理ある。
examples.en: Certainly, there's something to what he says too.
examples.f: ｜確[たし]かに、｜彼[かれ]の｜言[い]うことにも｜一理[いちり]ある。

examples.ja: 確かにこの店は高いが、味は本物だ。
examples.en: It's true this restaurant is pricey, but the flavor is the real thing.
examples.f: ｜確[たし]かにこの｜店[みせ]は｜高[たか]いが、｜味[あじ]は｜本物[ほんもの]だ。

title: 直ちに
meaning: immediately; at once (formal)
summary: 直ちに means "immediately; at once," with a formal, often official tone — you meet it in announcements, instructions, and written notices rather than casual talk. It stresses that no time passes before the action.
pitfalls: 直ちに is stiff and formal; in everyday speech, すぐに is the natural choice.

examples.ja: 地震が起きたら、直ちに火を消してください。
examples.en: If an earthquake strikes, put out any flames immediately.
examples.f: ｜地震[じしん]が｜起[お]きたら、｜直[ただ]ちに｜火[ひ]を｜消[け]してください。

examples.ja: 準備ができ次第、会議は直ちに始まります。
examples.en: As soon as preparations are ready, the meeting will begin at once.
examples.f: ｜準備[じゅんび]ができ｜次第[しだい]、｜会議[かいぎ]は｜直[ただ]ちに｜始[はじ]まります。

title: たって
meaning: even if; even though (casual)
summary: たって is the casual, spoken version of ても — "even if; even though." You hear it in conversation where ても would sound a bit stiff. It attaches differently to each word type, and for nouns and な-adjectives it surfaces as だって.
pitfalls: たって is colloquial; in writing or polite speech, use ても instead: 急いでも rather than 急いだって.
For nouns and な-adjectives the form becomes だって (子供だって, 静かだって), not たって.

examples.ja: 今から走ったって、もう間に合わないよ。
examples.en: Even if you run now, you won't make it in time.
examples.f: ｜今[いま]から｜走[はし]ったって、もう｜間に合[まにあ]わないよ。

examples.ja: どんなに高くたって、これはどうしても欲しい。
examples.en: No matter how expensive it is, I really want this.
examples.f: どんなに｜高[たか]くたって、これはどうしても｜欲[ほ]しい。

synonyms.note: ても is the standard 'even if'; たって is its casual, spoken counterpart.

related.note: たとえ〜ても spells out the hypothesis up front and is more emphatic; たって is a plain casual 'even if.'
だって is the form たって takes after a noun or な-adjective (子供だって = even a child).

title: だって
meaning: but; because (excuse); also 'even; too'
summary: だって has a few everyday jobs. At the start of a reply it pushes back or gives an excuse — "but; because." After a noun it means "even; too" (子供だって = even a child). Its tone is casual throughout.
pitfalls: Sentence-initial だって ('but, because') is casual and can sound childish or defensive; in polite explanations use から or ので.
Noun＋だって ('even') overlaps with も and でも; だって is the most conversational of the three.

examples.ja: 「どうして食べないの?」「だって、お腹が痛いんだもん。」
examples.en: "Why aren't you eating?" "Because my stomach hurts."
examples.f: 「どうして｜食[た]べないの?」「だって、お｜腹[なか]が｜痛[いた]いんだもん。」

examples.ja: そんなこと、子供だって知っているよ。
examples.en: Even a child knows something like that.
examples.f: そんなこと、｜子供[こども]だって｜知[し]っているよ。

related.note: さえ is an emphatic, more formal 'even'; the 'even' sense of だって is the casual, spoken option.
でも/ても cover 'even/even if' neutrally; だって is the conversational, sometimes defensive cousin.
たって is the matching form after verbs and い-adjectives; だって follows nouns and な-adjectives.

title: たて
meaning: freshly done; just done (and still fresh)
summary: たて attaches to a verb stem to say the action was done just moments ago and the result is still fresh — 焼きたてのパン = freshly baked bread, できたて = just made. It forms a noun-like word and pairs with a limited set of verbs, especially about food and freshness.
pitfalls: たて works with only a handful of verbs (焼く, できる, 炊く, 塗る …); it isn't a free 'just did' marker — for that, use 〜たばかり.
Before a noun it links with の: 焼きたてのパン, not 焼きたてパン.

examples.ja: 焼きたてのパンはとてもいい匂いがする。
examples.en: Freshly baked bread smells wonderful.
examples.f: ｜焼[や]きたてのパンはとてもいい｜匂[にお]いがする。

examples.ja: このお米は炊きたてだから、本当においしい。
examples.en: This rice was just cooked, so it's really delicious.
examples.f: このお｜米[こめ]は｜炊[た]きたてだから、｜本当[ほんとう]においしい。

related.note: 〜たばかり works with any verb to say an action just happened; たて emphasizes the still-fresh result and forms a noun.

title: たとえ〜ても
meaning: even if (hypothetically) ...
summary: たとえ〜ても sets up a hypothetical and says the result holds no matter what — "even if." The たとえ at the front signals early that a supposition is coming, and it pairs with a following ても. It stresses that the outcome won't change.
structure: たとえ ＋ Verb［て form］＋ も
pitfalls: たとえ needs a matching ても／でも later in the sentence; don't leave it hanging.
たとえ ('even if') is a different word from 例えば ('for example') — don't swap them.

examples.ja: たとえ雨が降っても、試合は行われます。
examples.en: Even if it rains, the match will be held.
examples.f: たとえ｜雨[あめ]が｜降[ふ]っても、｜試合[しあい]は｜行[おこな]われます。

examples.ja: たとえ失敗しても、挑戦したことに意味がある。
examples.en: Even if I fail, there's meaning in having taken on the challenge.
examples.f: たとえ｜失敗[しっぱい]しても、｜挑戦[ちょうせん]したことに｜意味[いみ]がある。

synonyms.note: ても alone can mean 'even if'; たとえ〜ても adds an explicit, emphatic 'suppose that ...' at the front.

related.note: たって is a casual spoken 'even if'; たとえ〜ても is the standard, emphatic hypothetical.

title: たとたん(に)
meaning: the moment ...; just as ...; as soon as ...
summary: たとたん(に) marks the instant one thing happened and something else immediately followed — "the moment ...; as soon as ...". The second event is usually unexpected or beyond the speaker's control, and both clauses are in the past. The に is optional.
structure: Verb［た form］＋ とたん（に）、＋ Sentence
pitfalls: The second clause reports something that just happened, not a plan or request: no volitional, command, or invitation after とたん.
Both events are past and sudden; for a habitual 'every time,' use たびに instead.

examples.ja: 家を出たとたん、雨が降り出した。
examples.en: The moment I left the house, it started to rain.
examples.f: ｜家[いえ]を｜出[で]たとたん、｜雨[あめ]が｜降り出[ふりだ]した。

examples.ja: 立ち上がったとたんに、めまいがした。
examples.en: The instant I stood up, I felt dizzy.
examples.f: ｜立ち上[たちあ]がったとたんに、めまいがした。

related.note: たら is a broad trigger 'when/if'; とたん pins down one sudden, unexpected instant that just passed.
たびに is a repeated 'every time'; とたん is a single sudden moment.

title: たびに
meaning: every time; whenever
summary: たびに says that each time one thing happens, another regularly follows — "every time; whenever." It attaches to a dictionary-form verb or to a noun with の, and points to something that repeats on each occasion.
pitfalls: Use the dictionary form, not the past: 会うたびに, not 会ったたびに.
たびに is about repeated occasions; for one sudden moment ('as soon as'), use とたん.

examples.ja: 彼女は会うたびに、新しい話を聞かせてくれる。
examples.en: Every time I see her, she tells me a new story.
examples.f: ｜彼女[かのじょ]は｜会[あ]うたびに、｜新[あたら]しい｜話[はなし]を｜聞[き]かせてくれる。

examples.ja: 旅行のたびに、その土地の名物を買って帰る。
examples.en: Every time I travel, I buy the local specialty to bring home.
examples.f: ｜旅行[りょこう]のたびに、その｜土地[とち]の｜名物[めいぶつ]を｜買[か]って｜帰[かえ]る。

synonyms.note: 毎〜のように means 'nearly every time'; たびに means literally each and every time, without exception.

related.note: とたん marks one sudden instant; たびに marks a recurring pattern across many occasions.

title: ために
meaning: because of; as a result of (cause)
summary: In this use ために gives the reason or cause for what follows — "because of; as a result of." It often introduces a circumstance that led to a notable or unwanted outcome. It attaches to a plain-form clause, or to a noun with の.
pitfalls: This 'because of' ために tends to explain a notable or negative result and is more formal than から／ので.
The same shape ために also means 'in order to' (purpose); tell them apart by whether the second clause is a goal or an outcome.

examples.ja: 大雨のために、川の水が増えた。
examples.en: Because of the heavy rain, the river's water rose.
examples.f: ｜大雨[おおあめ]のために、｜川[かわ]の｜水[みず]が｜増[ふ]えた。

examples.ja: 事故があったために、道路が渋滞している。
examples.en: Because there was an accident, the road is jammed.
examples.f: ｜事故[じこ]があったために、｜道路[どうろ]が｜渋滞[じゅうたい]している。

synonyms.note: ので states a cause neutrally in everyday speech; ために sounds more formal and often flags a significant result.
から gives the speaker's reasoning; ために more often reports an objective cause and effect.

related.note: Same shape, other sense: ため(に) as 'in order to' states a goal; this ために states a cause.
そのため(に) packages a whole prior sentence as 'that reason'; ために attaches directly to the cause clause.

title: ため(に)
meaning: in order to; for the sake of (purpose)
summary: In this use ため(に) states the goal you act toward — "in order to; for the sake of." With a dictionary-form verb it gives the purpose of a deliberate action; with a noun and の it means "for the benefit of." The subject controls the action aimed at the goal.
pitfalls: The goal ために takes a controllable, volitional verb and usually the same subject in both clauses; for aims you can't directly control (できる, 分かる, なる), use ように.
Say 合格するために ('in order to pass'), not 合格できるために — potential and uncontrollable verbs go with ように.

examples.ja: 日本語を上手に話すために、毎日練習している。
examples.en: I practice every day in order to speak Japanese well.
examples.f: ｜日本語[にほんご]を｜上手[じょうず]に｜話[はな]すために、｜毎日[まいにち]｜練習[れんしゅう]している。

examples.ja: 家族のために、一生懸命働いている。
examples.en: I work hard for the sake of my family.
examples.f: ｜家族[かぞく]のために、｜一生懸命[いっしょうけんめい]｜働[はたら]いている。

synonyms.note: ように states a goal reached through change or ability you can't fully control; ため(に) is for a deliberate, controllable aim.

related.note: Same shape, other sense: this ため(に) is 'in order to' (purpose); the cause ために means 'because of.'

title: たものだ
meaning: used to do; would often do (nostalgic)
summary: たものだ looks back fondly on something you used to do again and again — "used to ...; would often ...". It carries a nostalgic, reminiscing tone about a past habit, not a one-time event. It attaches to the た form.
structure: Verb［た form］＋ ものだった
pitfalls: It describes a repeated past habit with a nostalgic feel; for a single past action, just use the plain past.
Keep it apart from other ものだ uses (general truths, strong feeling); the nostalgic 'used to' sense needs the た form.

examples.ja: 子供の頃、この川でよく泳いだものだ。
examples.en: As a child, I used to swim in this river a lot.
examples.f: ｜子供[こども]の｜頃[ころ]、この｜川[かわ]でよく｜泳[およ]いだものだ。

examples.ja: 学生時代は、朝まで友達と語り合ったものだ。
examples.en: Back in my student days, we'd often talk with friends until morning.
examples.f: ｜学生[がくせい]｜時代[じだい]は、｜朝[あさ]まで｜友達[ともだち]と｜語り合[かたりあ]ったものだ。

related.note: ものだ covers general truths and strong feeling; the た-form たものだ is specifically the nostalgic 'used to.'

title: だらけ
meaning: covered in; full of (usually something unwelcome)
summary: だらけ attaches to a noun to say something is covered in or full of that thing — usually something unwelcome, like 泥だらけ (covered in mud) or 間違いだらけ (full of mistakes). It gives a strong impression of an unpleasant excess.
structure: Noun ＋ だらけ ＋ の ＋ Noun
pitfalls: だらけ almost always describes something negative or messy; for a neutral 'full of,' use でいっぱい.
Before a noun it needs の: 傷だらけの車, not 傷だらけ車.

examples.ja: 子供たちは泥だらけになって遊んでいた。
examples.en: The kids were playing, covered head to toe in mud.
examples.f: ｜子供[こども]たちは｜泥[どろ]だらけになって｜遊[あそ]んでいた。

examples.ja: 彼のレポートは間違いだらけだった。
examples.en: His report was full of mistakes.
examples.f: ｜彼[かれ]のレポートは｜間違[まちが]いだらけだった。

synonyms.note: 〜まみれ is very close but stays physical — smeared or coated with a substance; だらけ also covers non-physical excess like mistakes.

related.note: ばかり ('nothing but') can be neutral; だらけ specifically stresses an unpleasant, messy excess.

title: 中
meaning: during; throughout; within (by the end of)
summary: 中 after a noun means "during / throughout," but the reading shifts the sense. ちゅう marks an ongoing action or a deadline (電話中 = mid-call, 今日中に = by the end of today); じゅう marks a whole span of time or space (一日中 = all day long, 世界中 = all over the world).
structure: Time／period ＋ 中に（ちゅうに）、＋ Sentence
pitfalls: The reading carries meaning: ちゅう = in the middle of / by the end of; じゅう = all through. The split isn't fully regular (今日中 = きょうじゅう, but 午前中 = ごぜんちゅう), so learn set words.
ちゅう〜に often sets a deadline ('by the end of'); for a continuous 'the whole time,' it's じゅう.

examples.ja: 午前中に宿題を終わらせます。
examples.en: I will finish my homework during the morning.
examples.f: ｜午前[ごぜん]｜中[ちゅう]に｜宿題[しゅくだい]を｜終[お]わらせます。

examples.ja: 弟は一日じゅうゲームをしている。
examples.en: My little brother plays games all day long.
examples.f: ｜弟[おとうと]は｜一[いち]｜日[にち]じゅうゲームをしている。

related.note: 間 marks a continuous span 'while / during'; 中 (じゅう) stresses 'the whole extent of' that span.
うちに means 'while / before it ends'; 中(ちゅう)に sets a plain deadline 'by the end of.'
までに gives a specific cutoff time; 中(ちゅう)に gives a looser 'within this period.'

title: つい
meaning: without meaning to; end up doing despite oneself
summary: つい marks doing something you didn't really mean to do — you slip and do it despite knowing better, often out of habit or weak willpower. It very frequently pairs with 〜てしまう, which underlines the unintended result. Typical of everyday confessions like eating sweets or staying up too late.
pitfalls: つい is about slipping into an unintended action; don't confuse it with ついに (finally, at last).
It commonly teams up with 〜てしまう to stress that the result was unintended: つい食べてしまった.

examples.ja: ダイエット中なのに、つい甘いものを食べてしまった。
examples.en: Even though I'm on a diet, I ended up eating something sweet without meaning to.
examples.f: ダイエット｜中[ちゅう]なのに、つい｜甘[あま]いものを｜食[た]べてしまった。

examples.ja: 面白くて、つい夜遅くまで本を読んでしまった。
examples.en: It was so interesting that I ended up reading late into the night before I knew it.
examples.f: ｜面白[おもしろ]くて、つい｜夜[よる]｜遅[おそ]くまで｜本[ほん]を｜読[よ]んでしまった。

related.note: Sounds close but ついに means 'finally, at last'; つい means 'without meaning to.'

title: ついでに
meaning: while you're at it; on the same occasion; on the way
summary: ついでに marks doing a second thing while you're already doing the first — you take advantage of one occasion to get another errand done at little extra effort. It attaches to a verb (dictionary or た form) or to a noun with の. The main action comes first; the ついでに action is the bonus.
structure: Verb［dictionary form］／［た form］＋ ついでに
pitfalls: The primary action is stated first; the ついでに part is the extra, secondary thing done 'while you're at it.'
Attach it to a noun with の: 散歩のついでに, not 散歩ついでに.

examples.ja: 買い物に行くついでに、郵便局にも寄ってきます。
examples.en: While I'm out shopping, I'll stop by the post office too.
examples.f: ｜買い物[かいもの]に｜行[い]くついでに、｜郵便[ゆうびん]｜局[きょく]にも｜寄[よ]ってきます。

examples.ja: 散歩のついでに、パンを買って帰った。
examples.en: On my walk, I bought some bread on the way back.
examples.f: ｜散歩[さんぽ]のついでに、パンを｜買[か]って｜帰[かえ]った。

related.note: ながら is doing two actions at the same moment; ついでに is one occasion used to also handle a secondary errand.

title: ついに
meaning: finally; at last; in the end
summary: ついに marks the arrival of something long awaited or long building — after much time or effort, it finally comes to pass. With a negative it means something never happened in the end (ついに来なかった = never showed up in the end). It often carries a note of emotion or significance.
pitfalls: Don't confuse it with the similar-looking つい (without meaning to): ついに = finally, つい = accidentally.
With a negative it means 'never ~ in the end': ついに分からなかった = in the end I never figured it out.

examples.ja: ずっと頑張って、ついに試験に合格した。
examples.en: After working hard all along, I finally passed the exam.
examples.f: ずっと｜頑張[がんば]って、ついに｜試験[しけん]に｜合格[ごうかく]した。

examples.ja: 待っていた新しいゲームが、ついに発売された。
examples.en: The new game I'd been waiting for has finally gone on sale.
examples.f: ｜待[ま]っていた｜新[あたら]しいゲームが、ついに｜発売[はつばい]された。

related.note: Sounds close but つい means 'without meaning to'; ついに means 'finally, at last.'

title: っけ
meaning: what was it again? (casual ending to confirm a half-remembered thing)
summary: っけ is a casual sentence-final particle you tack on when you're trying to recall or double-check something you've half-forgotten — 'what was it again?' It usually follows the plain past (〜たっけ) or だ→だっけ. It belongs to relaxed, friendly speech among close people.
pitfalls: It's casual; in polite situations people say 〜でしたっけ / 〜ましたっけ instead.
With nouns and な-adjectives it becomes だっけ: 今日は何曜日だっけ.

examples.ja: あれ、鍵はどこに置いたっけ。
examples.en: Huh, where did I put the keys again?
examples.f: あれ、｜鍵[かぎ]はどこに｜置[お]いたっけ。

examples.ja: 明日の会議は何時からだっけ。
examples.en: What time was tomorrow's meeting again?
examples.f: ｜明日[あした]の｜会議[かいぎ]は｜何[なん]｜時[じ]からだっけ。

title: っぱなし
meaning: leaving something in a state (often through neglect); leaving it on/open/as-is
summary: っぱなし attaches to the ます-stem and means leaving the result of an action in place — the light left on (つけっぱなし), the door left open (開けっぱなし). It usually carries a hint of carelessness: you did something and neglected to undo it. It can also describe an action that just keeps going without a break.
pitfalls: Attach it to the stem: つけっぱなし, not つけるっぱなし.
It usually implies something was left the way it shouldn't be (negligence), unlike the neutral まま.

examples.ja: 電気をつけっぱなしにして出かけてしまった。
examples.en: I went out and left the lights on.
examples.f: ｜電気[でんき]をつけっぱなしにして｜出[で]かけてしまった。

examples.ja: 窓を開けっぱなしにしていたら、部屋が寒くなった。
examples.en: I'd left the window open, and the room got cold.
examples.f: ｜窓[まど]を｜開[あ]けっぱなしにしていたら、｜部屋[へや]が｜寒[さむ]くなった。

related.note: まま neutrally states a state left unchanged; っぱなし adds the nuance that leaving it that way was careless.

title: っぽい
meaning: -ish; -like; has the quality of; tends to
summary: っぽい tacks onto a noun, adjective stem, or verb stem to say something has the quality or tendency of that word — 子供っぽい = childish, 忘れっぽい = forgetful, 安っぽい = cheap-looking. The whole compound behaves like an い-adjective. It's colloquial and often carries a mildly critical tone.
pitfalls: With a verb stem it means 'tends to / easily does' (怒りっぽい = quick to anger), not 'looks like.'
It's casual and can sound negative: 安っぽい means 'cheap-looking,' not simply 'inexpensive.'

examples.ja: 彼は忘れっぽくて、よく約束を忘れる。
examples.en: He's forgetful and often forgets his promises.
examples.f: ｜彼[かれ]は｜忘[わす]れっぽくて、よく｜約束[やくそく]を｜忘[わす]れる。

examples.ja: その色は少し子供っぽいと思う。
examples.en: I think that color is a little childish.
examples.f: その｜色[いろ]は｜少[すこ]し｜子供[こども]っぽいと｜思[おも]う。

synonyms.note: みたいだ says something resembles or looks like another thing; っぽい says it has that quality or tendency, more casually.

related.note: がち is about how often an event tends to happen; っぽい 'tends to' describes a lasting quality or trait.
らしい means 'befitting / typical of'; っぽい often means the opposite — merely -ish, or not quite befitting.

title: つまり
meaning: in other words; that is to say; in short
summary: つまり introduces a restatement or summary of what was just said — you rephrase it more simply or boil it down to its point. 'In other words / that is to say / in short.' It links a fuller explanation to a tighter conclusion drawn from it.
pitfalls: つまり restates or sums up the same content; it doesn't introduce a new result the way だから or それで does.

examples.ja: 父の姉、つまり私のおばが遊びに来た。
examples.en: My father's older sister — in other words, my aunt — came to visit.
examples.f: ｜父[ちち]の｜姉[あね]、つまり｜私[わたし]のおばが｜遊[あそ]びに｜来[き]た。

examples.ja: 彼は返事をくれなかった。つまり、興味がないということだ。
examples.en: He didn't reply. In other words, he isn't interested.
examples.f: ｜彼[かれ]は｜返事[へんじ]をくれなかった。つまり、｜興味[きょうみ]がないということだ。

synonyms.note: すなわち is a more formal, precise 'namely'; つまり is the everyday 'in other words.'

related.note: ということだ often closes a つまり restatement, summing up 'it means that ~.'

title: つもりだった
meaning: had intended to (but didn't); thought I had done
summary: つもりだった is つもり (intention) in the past — you had meant to do something, usually with the implication that it didn't turn out that way. In the 〜たつもりだった pattern it means you were under the impression you'd already done something when in fact you hadn't.
structure: Verb［dictionary form］＋ つもりだった
Verb［た form］＋ つもりだった
pitfalls: It often implies the intention went unfulfilled: 早く帰るつもりだった = I meant to leave early (but didn't).
〜たつもりだった = 'I thought I had done it' — a mistaken belief: 送ったつもりだった = I was sure I'd sent it.

examples.ja: 今日は早く寝るつもりだったのに、遅くなってしまった。
examples.en: I'd meant to go to bed early today, but I ended up staying up late.
examples.f: ｜今日[きょう]は｜早[はや]く｜寝[ね]るつもりだったのに、｜遅[おそ]くなってしまった。

examples.ja: メールを送ったつもりだったが、下書きに残っていた。
examples.en: I thought I'd sent the email, but it was still sitting in my drafts.
examples.f: メールを｜送[おく]ったつもりだったが、｜下書[したが]きに｜残[のこ]っていた。

related.note: つもりだ states a present intention; つもりだった puts it in the past, often hinting it fell through.
はずだ is an expectation based on reasoning; つもりだった is your own past intention or belief.

title: つもりで
meaning: with the intention of; with the mindset that; as if
summary: つもりで sets the mindset or assumption you act under — you carry out the main action 'with the intention of' or 'as if' something were the case. 手伝うつもりで来た = I came intending to help; 死んだつもりで頑張る = give it your all as if your life depended on it. It leads into a following action rather than ending the sentence.
structure: Verb［dictionary form］／［た form］＋ つもりで
pitfalls: つもりで colors the attitude behind the next action; it isn't a sentence-ender like つもりだ.
With 〜たつもりで it means 'acting as if you had ~': 貯金したつもりで = as though you'd saved that money.

examples.ja: 新しい気持ちで、一年生になったつもりで頑張ります。
examples.en: I'll do my best with a fresh attitude, as if I were a first-year all over again.
examples.f: ｜新[あたら]しい｜気持[きも]ちで、｜一[いち]｜年生[ねんせい]になったつもりで｜頑張[がんば]ります。

examples.ja: 手伝うつもりで来たので、何でも言ってください。
examples.en: I came intending to help, so tell me whatever you need.
examples.f: ｜手伝[てつだ]うつもりで｜来[き]たので、｜何[なに]でも｜言[い]ってください。

related.note: つもりだ ends a sentence stating an intention; つもりで leads into the action done under that intention.
つもりだった is a past intention, often unfulfilled; つもりで is the mindset you act under right now.

title: である
meaning: to be (formal, written-style copula)
summary: である is a formal, written-style copula that stands in for だ — you meet it in essays, reports, news, and academic writing rather than conversation. It states 'X is Y' with an objective, authoritative tone. Its negative is ではない and its past is であった.
pitfalls: である belongs to written or formal register; in everyday speech use だ or です instead.
Don't stack だ onto it: say 学生である, not 学生であるだ.

examples.ja: 言語は文化の一部である。
examples.en: Language is a part of culture.
examples.f: ｜言語[げんご]は｜文化[ぶんか]の｜一部[いちぶ]である。

examples.ja: この問題は非常に重要である。
examples.en: This issue is extremely important.
examples.f: この｜問題[もんだい]は｜非常[ひじょう]に｜重要[じゅうよう]である。

synonyms.note: だ・です are the plain and polite copulas of speech; である is the formal written-style equivalent.

title: で言うと
meaning: in terms of; speaking in terms of; if we go by
summary: で言うと frames a matter through a chosen measure or category — 'speaking in terms of ~,' 'if we put it in ~ terms.' 値段で言うと = in terms of price; 東京で言うと = if we compare it to Tokyo. You pick a yardstick and express the thing through it.
pitfalls: It takes a noun naming the frame of reference: 年齢で言うと = in terms of age.
Close to 〜と言えば as a topic-opener, but で言うと specifically casts things into a chosen unit or standard.

examples.ja: この町の大きさは、東京で言うと渋谷ぐらいです。
examples.en: In terms of size, this town is about like Shibuya if you compare it to Tokyo.
examples.f: この｜町[まち]の｜大[おお]きさは、｜東京[とうきょう]で｜言[い]うと｜渋谷[しぶや]ぐらいです。

examples.ja: 値段で言うと、こちらのほうが少し高いです。
examples.en: In terms of price, this one is a little more expensive.
examples.f: ｜値段[ねだん]で｜言[い]うと、こちらのほうが｜少[すこ]し｜高[たか]いです。

title: ている場合じゃない
kana: ているばあいじゃない
meaning: this is no time to be doing (something)
summary: 〜ている場合じゃない says the situation is too urgent or serious to be doing something — 'this is no time to be ~.' You point out that the current activity is inappropriate given more pressing matters. 笑っている場合じゃない = this is no time to be laughing.
structure: Verb［て form］＋ いる場合じゃない／ではない
pitfalls: 場合 here means 'situation,' so the phrase judges that the ongoing action doesn't fit the circumstances.
The fuller, more polite form is 〜ている場合ではない; 〜じゃない is the casual version.

examples.ja: 明日試験なのに、テレビを見ている場合じゃない。
examples.en: There's an exam tomorrow — this is no time to be watching TV.
examples.f: ｜明日[あした]｜試験[しけん]なのに、テレビを｜見[み]ている｜場合[ばあい]じゃない。

examples.ja: のんびりしている場合じゃない。早く準備しよう。
examples.en: This is no time to be taking it easy. Let's get ready quickly.
examples.f: のんびりしている｜場合[ばあい]じゃない。｜早[はや]く｜準備[じゅんび]しよう。

title: てからでないと
meaning: not until you first do; can't unless you do first
summary: 〜てからでないと sets a required first step — nothing further can happen until it's done. It's usually followed by a negative outcome: 予約してからでないと入れない = you can't get in unless you book first. Literally 'if it isn't after doing ~.'
structure: Verb［て form］＋ からでないと／からでなければ ＋ （negative）
pitfalls: The second clause is normally negative (〜ない／〜できない): 確認してからでないと答えられない.
It stresses order — X must come first before Y is possible; plain てから just says 'after,' without the 'can't otherwise' nuance.

examples.ja: 手を洗ってからでないと、食べてはいけません。
examples.en: You mustn't eat until you've washed your hands first.
examples.f: ｜手[て]を｜洗[あら]ってからでないと、｜食[た]べてはいけません。

examples.ja: 上司に確認してからでないと、返事ができません。
examples.en: I can't give an answer until I've checked with my boss first.
examples.f: ｜上司[じょうし]に｜確認[かくにん]してからでないと、｜返事[へんじ]ができません。

related.note: てから simply means 'after doing'; てからでないと adds that nothing else is possible until then.
なければならない states that an action is necessary; てからでないと makes that action a prerequisite for something else.

title: 的
meaning: -al; -ic; relating to; turns a noun into a な-adjective or adverb
summary: 的 attaches to a noun to make an adjective-like word meaning 'relating to / -al / -ic' — 一般的 = general, 科学的 = scientific, 積極的 = proactive. Add な before a noun (的な考え) and に to use it adverbially (的に説明する). It's extremely common in both writing and speech.
pitfalls: Use 的な before a noun and 的に as an adverb: 具体的な例, 具体的に説明する.
It attaches mainly to kanji compound nouns (社会的, 経済的), not usually to everyday native words.

examples.ja: もっと具体的に説明してください。
examples.en: Please explain it more concretely.
examples.f: もっと｜具体[ぐたい]｜的[てき]に｜説明[せつめい]してください。

examples.ja: 彼は積極的な性格で、すぐ友達を作る。
examples.en: He has a proactive personality and makes friends quickly.
examples.f: ｜彼[かれ]は｜積極[せっきょく]｜的[てき]な｜性格[せいかく]で、すぐ｜友達[ともだち]を｜作[つく]る。

related.note: っぽい is a casual '-ish' added to everyday words; 的 forms categorical '-al/-ic' adjectives from kanji compounds.

title: できれば・できたら
meaning: if possible; if you can
summary: できれば and できたら both mean 'if possible / if you can' — they soften a request or state a preference without insisting. できれば手伝ってほしい = I'd like your help if possible. They are the ば and たら conditional forms of できる (to be able).
structure: できれば／できたら ＋ request or wish
pitfalls: The two are largely interchangeable here; できれば leans a touch more formal, できたら a touch more casual.
It presents the request as desirable but optional, not as a demand.

examples.ja: できれば、明日までにお返事をいただきたいです。
examples.en: If possible, I'd like to have your reply by tomorrow.
examples.f: できれば、｜明日[あした]までにお｜返事[へんじ]をいただきたいです。

examples.ja: できたら、少し早めに来てくれると助かります。
examples.en: If you can, it would help if you came a little early.
examples.f: できたら、｜少[すこ]し｜早[はや]めに｜来[き]てくれると｜助[たす]かります。

related.note: たら is the general 'if/when' conditional; できたら is that form of できる, fixed as 'if possible.'
ば is the general conditional; できれば is that form of できる, meaning 'if it can be managed.'

title: てごらん
meaning: go on, try doing; (please) look
summary: 〜てごらん is a soft, encouraging way to tell someone to try doing something — warmer than a plain command, and typically used by adults toward children or by a senior toward a junior. It comes from ご覧なさい (look/see). 食べてごらん = go on, try eating it.
pitfalls: It's used downward — to children, students, or close juniors — not toward superiors.
It's gentler than なさい but still a command; for a polite request to equals or superiors use 〜てみてください.

examples.ja: 難しくないから、自分でやってごらん。
examples.en: It's not hard, so try doing it yourself.
examples.f: ｜難[むずか]しくないから、｜自分[じぶん]でやってごらん。

examples.ja: あそこを見てごらん。虹が出ているよ。
examples.en: Look over there — there's a rainbow.
examples.f: あそこを｜見[み]てごらん。｜虹[にじ]が｜出[で]ているよ。

synonyms.note: てみる is the neutral 'try doing'; てごらん turns it into a gentle 'go ahead and try' command.

related.note: なさい is a firm command; てごらん is softer and more encouraging.
てください is a polite request usable with anyone; てごらん is casual and aimed at juniors or children.

title: てしょうがない・てしかたがない
kana: てしょうがない・てしかたがない
romaji: te shou ga nai / te shikata ga nai
meaning: can't help feeling; unbearably; extremely
summary: 〜てしょうがない (and its twin 〜てしかたがない) says a feeling or sensation is so strong you can't do anything about it — you're overwhelmed by it. 眠くてしょうがない = unbearably sleepy; 気になってしょうがない = I can't stop worrying about it. It's mostly used about one's own feelings.
structure: Verb［て form］／い-adjective［て form］＋ しょうがない／しかたがない
な-adjective ＋ で ＋ しょうがない／しかたがない
pitfalls: しょうがない and しかたがない are interchangeable here; しょうがない is a bit more casual.
It's for spontaneous feelings and sensations (sleepy, hungry, worried), not for deliberate actions.

examples.ja: 朝から何も食べていないので、お腹がすいてしょうがない。
examples.en: I haven't eaten since morning, so I'm unbearably hungry.
examples.f: ｜朝[あさ]から｜何[なに]も｜食[た]べていないので、お｜腹[なか]がすいてしょうがない。

examples.ja: 試験の結果が気になってしかたがない。
examples.en: I can't stop worrying about the exam results.
examples.f: ｜試験[しけん]の｜結果[けっか]が｜気[き]になってしかたがない。

synonyms.note: てたまらない is a very close 'unbearably ~'; てしょうがない is slightly softer and more everyday.
てならない carries the same 'can't help feeling,' but sounds more written or literary.

title: て済む
meaning: can get by with just; be settled by (only)
summary: 〜て済む means a situation can be settled or gotten through with only that much — often less trouble than you'd feared. 電話で済む = it can be handled with just a phone call. 済む means 'to be finished / settled,' so the pattern says 'doing that much is all it takes.'
structure: Verb［て form］／い-adjective［て form］＋ 済む
pitfalls: It often implies 'that's all it takes / you get off with just ~,' a lighter outcome than expected.
Distinct from 〜ずに済む / 〜ないで済む, which mean 'get by without having to do ~.'

examples.ja: 軽いけがで、消毒するだけで済んだ。
examples.en: It was a light injury, and just disinfecting it was all it took.
examples.f: ｜軽[かる]いけがで、｜消毒[しょうどく]するだけで｜済[す]んだ。

examples.ja: 今日は電話で済む用事だけだった。
examples.en: Today I only had errands that could be handled by phone.
examples.f: ｜今日[きょう]は｜電話[でんわ]で｜済[す]む｜用事[ようじ]だけだった。

related.note: ずに済む means getting by WITHOUT doing something; て済む means getting by with just doing that much.

title: では・それでは・じゃあ
kana: では・それでは・じゃあ
romaji: de wa / sore de wa / jaa
meaning: well then; in that case; all right then
summary: では, それでは, and the casual じゃあ open a new move in a conversation — wrapping something up, starting off, or drawing a conclusion from what came before. 'Well then / in that case / all right then.' では is more formal; じゃあ (and じゃ) is casual.
structure: では／それでは／じゃあ ＋ Sentence
pitfalls: では and それでは are neutral-to-formal; じゃあ is casual, spoken language.
Here it's a discourse connector ('well then'); don't confuse it with the では inside 〜てはいけない or contrastive では.

examples.ja: では、今日の会議を始めましょう。
examples.en: Well then, let's begin today's meeting.
examples.f: では、｜今日[きょう]の｜会議[かいぎ]を｜始[はじ]めましょう。

examples.ja: じゃあ、また明日ね。
examples.en: All right then, see you tomorrow.
examples.f: じゃあ、また｜明日[あした]ね。

related.note: それで means 'and so, because of that,' giving a result; それでは means 'well then,' shifting to the next move.
なら attaches to a clause as 'if that's the case'; それでは stands alone as 'well then, in that case.'

title: てはいけないから
meaning: because you mustn't ~ (so...); so as not to
summary: 〜てはいけないから gives a prohibition itself as a reason — 'because you mustn't ~, ...' You state that some action is forbidden or undesirable, and that's why you take (or avoid) another action. 遅れてはいけないから、早く出た = I left early because I mustn't be late.
structure: Verb［て form］＋ はいけないから ＋ Sentence
pitfalls: It's simply 〜てはいけない (must not) plus から (because); the から-clause gives the reason for the main clause.
The main clause is usually a precaution taken to avoid the forbidden outcome.

examples.ja: 風邪をうつしてはいけないから、今日はマスクをしている。
examples.en: I mustn't pass on my cold, so I'm wearing a mask today.
examples.f: ｜風邪[かぜ]をうつしてはいけないから、｜今日[きょう]はマスクをしている。

examples.ja: 忘れてはいけないから、手帳にメモしておいた。
examples.en: I mustn't forget, so I jotted it down in my planner.
examples.f: ｜忘[わす]れてはいけないから、｜手帳[てちょう]にメモしておいた。

related.note: てはいけない states the prohibition itself; てはいけないから uses that prohibition as the reason for another action.
ように expresses 'so that (a bad thing) won't happen'; てはいけないから frames the same idea as 'because it mustn't happen.'

title: てばかりいる
meaning: to do nothing but ~; to always be ~ing (often critical)
summary: 〜てばかりいる attaches to the て form and says someone does one action over and over and little else — 遊んでばかりいる = does nothing but play around. It usually carries a critical or exasperated tone, painting the behavior as excessive and unbalanced. The いる can conjugate (ばかりいた, ばかりいて).
structure: Verb［て form］＋ ばかりいる
pitfalls: It usually sounds critical — that the person does this to the exclusion of what they should be doing.
Attach ばかり after the て form here: 泣いてばかりいる, not 泣くばかりいる.
Keep it apart from Verb［た form］＋ばかり ('just did'); てばかりいる is a repeated habit, not a one-off that just happened.

examples.ja: 弟は遊んでばかりいて、宿題を全然やらない。
examples.en: My little brother does nothing but play around and never does his homework.
examples.f: ｜弟[おとうと]は｜遊[あそ]んでばかりいて、｜宿題[しゅくだい]を｜全然[ぜんぜん]やらない。

examples.ja: 最近、姉はスマホを見てばかりいる。
examples.en: Lately my older sister does nothing but look at her phone.
examples.f: ｜最近[さいきん]、｜姉[あね]はスマホを｜見[み]てばかりいる。

synonyms.note: ばかり is the base 'only' particle; 〜てばかりいる is its ongoing-habit form with a verb and a critical edge.

related.note: だけ neutrally limits to 'only'; 〜てばかりいる adds the sense of an excessive, unbalanced habit.

title: て初めて
meaning: not until ~; only after doing ~ (did I realize/come to)
summary: 〜てはじめて joins the て form to say that only after experiencing X does something Y become true — usually a realization. ひとりで暮らしてはじめて = only after living alone (did I understand...). The 初めて here means 'only at that point', not literally 'for the first time counting occasions'.
pitfalls: 初めて here means 'not until then / only at that point', so it is often followed by realization verbs like 分かる, 気づく.
The X part is a real experience that triggers the realization, not a hypothetical.

examples.ja: ひとりで暮らしてはじめて、親のありがたさが分かった。
examples.en: It was only after living on my own that I understood how much I owe my parents.
examples.f: ひとりで｜暮[く]らしてはじめて、｜親[おや]のありがたさが｜分[わ]かった。

examples.ja: 病気になってはじめて、健康の大切さに気づいた。
examples.en: Not until I got sick did I realize how important health is.
examples.f: ｜病気[びょうき]になってはじめて、｜健康[けんこう]の｜大切[たいせつ]さに｜気[き]づいた。

related.note: からこそ stresses 'precisely because'; てはじめて stresses that the realization came only after the experience.

title: ではなくて・じゃなくて
kana: ではなくて・じゃなくて
meaning: not A but B; it isn't A, (it's B)
summary: 〜ではなくて (casual じゃなくて) negates one noun and connects on to the correct one — これは私のではなくて、姉のです = this isn't mine, it's my sister's. It is the connective (て) form of ではない, used to swap out a wrong choice for the right one.
structure: Noun／な-adjective ＋ ではなくて／じゃなくて（＋ B）
pitfalls: で is copula-based, so this frame is for nouns and な-adjectives; for verbs and い-adjectives use the plain negative + くて (安くなくて) or 〜のではなくて.
じゃなくて is just the casual contraction of ではなくて — same meaning, softer register.

examples.ja: テストは明日じゃなくて、あさってですよ。
examples.en: The test isn't tomorrow, it's the day after.
examples.f: テストは｜明日[あした]じゃなくて、あさってですよ。

examples.ja: これは私のではなくて、姉のかばんです。
examples.en: This isn't mine; it's my older sister's bag.
examples.f: これは｜私[わたし]のではなくて、｜姉[あね]のかばんです。

related.note: というより corrects a description ('more like B than A'); ではなくて flatly rejects A and states B instead.

title: ても〜なくても
meaning: whether ~ or not (the result is the same)
summary: Pairing a positive 〜ても with the matching negative 〜なくても for the same word says the outcome holds either way — 降っても降らなくても = whether it rains or not. You state the two opposite cases and then a result that does not depend on which one is true.
structure: Verb［て form］＋ も ＋ Verb［ない form → なくて］＋ も
pitfalls: Both halves use the same predicate in opposite polarity: 行っても行かなくても, not two unrelated verbs.
For nouns and な-adjectives the pattern becomes 〜でも〜でなくても.

examples.ja: 雨が降っても降らなくても、試合は行われます。
examples.en: Whether it rains or not, the match will be held.
examples.f: ｜雨[あめ]が｜降[ふ]っても｜降[ふ]らなくても、｜試合[しあい]は｜行[おこな]われます。

examples.ja: 参加してもしなくても、料金は変わりません。
examples.en: Whether you take part or not, the fee doesn't change.
examples.f: ｜参加[さんか]してもしなくても、｜料金[りょうきん]は｜変[か]わりません。

related.note: ても covers a single 'even if' case; 〜ても〜なくても lines up both cases to say it makes no difference.
てもかまわない grants permission for one case; 〜ても〜なくても says the result is fixed across both cases.

title: でもある
meaning: is also ~; is at the same time ~
summary: 〜でもある adds a second identity or quality on top of one already established — 彼は歌手であり、俳優でもある = he's a singer and also an actor. It is で + も + ある, so it layers an extra 'is also' onto a noun.
pitfalls: It typically comes after another clause that sets up the first role, then でもある adds the second.
To present two qualities together in one breath, the frame 〜であり、〜でもある is common.

examples.ja: 彼は歌手であり、俳優でもある。
examples.en: He is a singer, and also an actor.
examples.f: ｜彼[かれ]は｜歌手[かしゅ]であり、｜俳優[はいゆう]でもある。

examples.ja: この本は辞書でもあるので、とても便利です。
examples.en: This book doubles as a dictionary, so it's very handy.
examples.f: この｜本[ほん]は｜辞書[じしょ]でもあるので、とても｜便利[べんり]です。

related.note: だけでなく adds 'not only ~ but also' across a whole clause; でもある simply tacks a second identity onto a noun.

title: ても構わない
meaning: it's fine even if ~; I don't mind if ~
summary: 〜てもかまわない says that even if X happens, it doesn't bother the speaker — so it grants permission or shows willingness. 高くてもかまわない = I don't mind if it's expensive. 構わない literally means 'don't mind', giving it a softer feel than the blunter てもいい.
structure: Verb［て form］＋ もかまわない
pitfalls: 構わない means 'don't mind', so it reads as gentle permission; てもいい is a more direct 'may / it's okay to'.
The negative なくてもかまわない means 'it's fine even if you don't'.

examples.ja: 少し高くてもかまわないので、質のいいものが欲しい。
examples.en: I don't mind if it's a little pricey; I want something of good quality.
examples.f: ｜少[すこ]し｜高[たか]くてもかまわないので、｜質[しつ]のいいものが｜欲[ほ]しい。

examples.ja: ここで写真を撮ってもかまいませんか。
examples.en: Is it all right if I take photos here?
examples.f: ここで｜写真[しゃしん]を｜撮[と]ってもかまいませんか。

synonyms.note: てもいい is a plainer 'may / it's okay to'; てもかまわない softens it to 'I don't mind if'.

antonyms.note: てはいけない forbids the action; てもかまわない allows it.

related.note: ても is the bare 'even if'; てもかまわない adds the judgment that the case is acceptable.

title: てもしょうがない・てもしかたがない
kana: てもしょうがない・てもしかたがない
romaji: temo shou ga nai / temo shikata ga nai
meaning: there's no use ~ing; no point even if you ~
summary: 〜てもしょうがない (also てもしかたがない) says that even if you do X, it won't help — expressing resignation or futility. 悔やんでもしょうがない = there's no use regretting it. The も is essential: it frames X as a pointless action.
structure: Verb［て form］＋ もしょうがない／もしかたがない
pitfalls: Don't drop the も: てしょうがない (no も) means 'can't help feeling; unbearably', a completely different point.
しょうがない and しかたがない are interchangeable here; しょうがない is the more casual spelling.

examples.ja: 終わったことを悔やんでもしょうがない。
examples.en: There's no use regretting something that's already over.
examples.f: ｜終[お]わったことを｜悔[く]やんでもしょうがない。

examples.ja: 今から急いでもしかたがないよ。電車はもう出た。
examples.en: There's no point rushing now; the train has already left.
examples.f: ｜今[いま]から｜急[いそ]いでもしかたがないよ。｜電車[でんしゃ]はもう｜出[で]た。

synonyms.note: ても始まらない stresses that the action produces no progress; てもしょうがない stresses that it simply can't be helped.

related.note: Without も, てしょうがない means 'can't help feeling / extremely', not futility — an easy pair to confuse.

title: ても始まらない
meaning: it's no use even if you ~; nothing will come of ~ing
summary: 〜ても始まらない says that even if you do X, nothing will change or come of it, so there's no point. ひとりで悩んでも始まらない = it won't get you anywhere to worry alone. 始まらない is idiomatic here — 'nothing will get started', i.e. no progress.
structure: Verb［て form］＋ も始まらない
pitfalls: 始まらない is figurative ('nothing will come of it'), not literally about something starting.
It is often used to talk someone out of pointless worry, complaint, or hesitation.

examples.ja: ひとりで悩んでも始まらないから、先生に相談しよう。
examples.en: Worrying about it alone won't get you anywhere, so let's talk to the teacher.
examples.f: ひとりで｜悩[なや]んでも｜始[はじ]まらないから、｜先生[せんせい]に｜相談[そうだん]しよう。

examples.ja: 過ぎたことを気にしても始まらない。
examples.en: There's no use fretting over what's already past.
examples.f: ｜過[す]ぎたことを｜気[き]にしても｜始[はじ]まらない。

synonyms.note: てもしょうがない frames the action as simply useless; ても始まらない frames it as producing no progress.

related.note: ても is the plain 'even if'; ても始まらない fixes the outcome as 'and it changes nothing'.

title: でよければ
meaning: if [X] is okay (with you); if you don't mind it being ~
summary: 〜でよければ offers something modest and checks that it's acceptable — 私でよければ = if I'll do / if you don't mind it being me. It combines で ('being/as') with よければ ('if it's good'), a humble way to offer help or a plain item while acknowledging it may not be ideal.
pitfalls: で marks the offered thing as possibly not good enough, giving a humble, tentative tone.
Compare plain なら: でよければ specifically asks 'if this much is good enough for you'.

examples.ja: 私でよければ、相談に乗りますよ。
examples.en: If you don't mind it being me, I'm happy to talk it over with you.
examples.f: ｜私[わたし]でよければ、｜相談[そうだん]に｜乗[の]りますよ。

examples.ja: 簡単な料理でよければ、作りますよ。
examples.en: If simple cooking is okay with you, I'll make something.
examples.f: ｜簡単[かんたん]な｜料理[りょうり]でよければ、｜作[つく]りますよ。

related.note: ばいい is a general 'it'd be good if / you should'; でよければ specifically offers a modest thing and checks it's acceptable.

title: 〜点
meaning: in terms of ~; the respect/point that ~
summary: 〜点 uses 点 as an abstract 'point/respect' to name the angle from which something is judged — usually as 〜という点で ('in the respect that') or 〜点で(は) ('in terms of'). 値段が安いという点で = in terms of being cheap. It pins down which aspect you're evaluating.
structure: Sentence［plain form］＋ という点で(は)
pitfalls: Common frames: 〜という点で ('in the respect that ~') and 〜点では ('in terms of ~').
Here 点 is an abstract aspect or respect, not a physical dot or a numeric test score.

examples.ja: このスマホは、値段が安いという点では魅力的だ。
examples.en: In terms of being cheap, this smartphone is appealing.
examples.f: このスマホは、｜値段[ねだん]が｜安[やす]いという｜点[てん]では｜魅力[みりょく]｜的[てき]だ。

examples.ja: 経験が豊富だという点で、彼は適任だと思う。
examples.en: In the respect that he has plenty of experience, I think he's the right person.
examples.f: ｜経験[けいけん]が｜豊富[ほうふ]だという｜点[てん]で、｜彼[かれ]は｜適任[てきにん]だと｜思[おも]う。

related.note: という labels or names a clause; 〜という点で uses it to single out the specific aspect under discussion.

title: ということだ
meaning: it means that ~; I hear that ~; in other words
summary: 〜ということだ has two everyday uses: reporting hearsay ('I hear that ~') and drawing or restating a conclusion ('which means that ~'). つまり〜ということだ sums something up; 部長は来ないということだ passes on news. Context tells the two apart.
structure: Sentence［plain form］＋ ということだ
pitfalls: The hearsay use relays information from a source; the conclusion use rephrases or infers, often after つまり.
Don't confuse it with というものだ, which asserts what something truly is.

examples.ja: 部長はあした来られないということだ。
examples.en: I hear the manager can't come tomorrow.
examples.f: ｜部長[ぶちょう]はあした｜来[こ]られないということだ。

examples.ja: 返事がないということは、興味がないということだ。
examples.en: No reply means they're not interested.
examples.f: ｜返事[へんじ]がないということは、｜興味[きょうみ]がないということだ。

synonyms.note: そうだ only reports hearsay; ということだ also draws or restates conclusions.

related.note: というわけだ presents a conclusion that follows naturally from what was said; ということだ can also just relay hearsay.
というものだ asserts the true nature of something; ということだ reports or restates.

title: と言うと
meaning: speaking of ~; when you say ~ (do you mean...)
summary: 〜というと picks up a word or topic just mentioned and either expands on the association it brings to mind ('speaking of ~') or asks the other person to confirm what they meant ('when you say ~, do you mean...?'). 京都というと、古いお寺 = speaking of Kyoto, old temples come to mind.
pitfalls: It overlaps with と言えば, but というと leans toward an automatic association or a request to clarify.
The 言う here is idiomatic ('when it comes to ~'), not a literal 'say'.

examples.ja: 京都というと、古いお寺を思い出す。
examples.en: Speaking of Kyoto, old temples come to mind.
examples.f: ｜京都[きょうと]というと、｜古[ふる]いお｜寺[てら]を｜思い出[おもいだ]す。

examples.ja: 「あの人」というと、田中さんのことですか。
examples.en: When you say 'that person', do you mean Tanaka?
examples.f: 「あの｜人[ひと]」というと、｜田中[たなか]さんのことですか。

synonyms.note: といえば is nearly the same; というと leans toward an automatic link or asking the speaker to clarify.

related.note: というのは stops to define or explain the topic; というと reacts to it or seeks confirmation.
そういえば means 'come to think of it', a looser reminder; というと ties to a topic just named.

title: というのは
meaning: the thing called ~ is; that is to say; the reason is that ~
summary: 〜というのは raises a topic to explain it — either defining it ('~ is (defined as)...') or giving the reason behind it ('the reason is that...'). 「敷金」というのは…お金のことです defines a word; 疲れているというのは、忙しいからです explains a cause, often ending in からだ.
pitfalls: In the definition use it often ends with 〜ことです／意味です.
In the explanatory use it usually ends with 〜からだ ('the reason is that...').

examples.ja: 「敷金」というのは、部屋を借りるときに払うお金のことです。
examples.en: 'Shikikin' refers to money you pay when renting a room.
examples.f: 「｜敷金[しききん]」というのは、｜部屋[へや]を｜借[か]りるときに｜払[はら]うお｜金[かね]のことです。

examples.ja: 最近疲れているというのは、仕事が忙しいからです。
examples.en: The reason I've been tired lately is that work is busy.
examples.f: ｜最近[さいきん]｜疲[つか]れているというのは、｜仕事[しごと]が｜忙[いそが]しいからです。

synonyms.note: というと reacts to a topic or asks for clarification; というのは stops to define or explain it.

related.note: という names or labels a word; というのは takes that named word as the topic to explain.
ということだ restates a conclusion or relays hearsay; というのは sets up a definition or reason.

title: というのは事実だ
romaji: to iu no wa jijitsu da
meaning: it is a fact that ~; there's no denying that ~
summary: 〜というのは事実だ affirms that a stated thing — sometimes surprising or contested — really is true. 努力したというのは事実だ = it's a fact that he made an effort. It often concedes a point before a 'but', acknowledging the truth of X on the way to a qualification.
structure: Sentence［plain form］＋ というのは事実だ
pitfalls: It commonly sets up a concession: 'it's a fact that X, but...'.
事実 asserts something as factually true, not as mere hearsay or opinion.

examples.ja: 彼が努力したというのは事実だ。ただ、結果は出なかった。
examples.en: It's a fact that he worked hard. It's just that the results didn't follow.
examples.f: ｜彼[かれ]が｜努力[どりょく]したというのは｜事実[じじつ]だ。ただ、｜結果[けっか]は｜出[で]なかった。

examples.ja: 物価が上がっているというのは事実だ。
examples.en: It is a fact that prices are rising.
examples.f: ｜物価[ぶっか]が｜上[あ]がっているというのは｜事実[じじつ]だ。

related.note: というのは opens a topic to define or explain; というのは事実だ closes by affirming that topic as true.
ということだ restates or relays; というのは事実だ asserts the stated matter is factual.

title: というより
meaning: rather than ~; more like B than A
summary: 〜というより refines how you describe one thing, saying B is a more accurate label than A — 優しいというより気が弱い = not so much kind as timid. It compares two descriptions of the same thing and is often followed by むしろ ('rather').
pitfalls: It weighs two descriptions of one thing, not two separate options — that latter job belongs to plain より.
It's often reinforced by むしろ in the second half.

examples.ja: 彼は優しいというより、ただ気が弱いだけだ。
examples.en: He's not so much kind as just timid.
examples.f: ｜彼[かれ]は｜優[やさ]しいというより、ただ｜気[き]が｜弱[よわ]いだけだ。

examples.ja: これは趣味というより、もう仕事だね。
examples.en: At this point this is more like work than a hobby.
examples.f: これは｜趣味[しゅみ]というより、もう｜仕事[しごと]だね。

synonyms.note: ではなくて flatly rejects A for B; というより softens it to 'B is the more fitting way to put it'.

related.note: より alone compares two separate things; というより compares two labels for the same thing.

title: という理由で
meaning: for the reason that ~; on the grounds that ~
summary: 〜という理由で presents the stated matter as the given or official reason for something — 体調が悪いという理由で欠席した = missed it on the grounds of feeling unwell. It's more explicit and formal than plain から, and can hint that the reason is merely the stated pretext.
structure: Sentence［plain form］／Noun ＋ という理由で
pitfalls: It's more formal and explicit than から, naming the reason as 'the grounds'.
Depending on context it can carry a 'under the pretext of ~' undertone.

examples.ja: 体調が悪いという理由で、彼は会議を欠席した。
examples.en: He missed the meeting on the grounds that he wasn't feeling well.
examples.f: ｜体調[たいちょう]が｜悪[わる]いという｜理由[りゆう]で、｜彼[かれ]は｜会議[かいぎ]を｜欠席[けっせき]した。

examples.ja: 危険だという理由で、その道は通行止めになった。
examples.en: That road was closed off for the reason that it's dangerous.
examples.f: ｜危険[きけん]だという｜理由[りゆう]で、その｜道[みち]は｜通行止[つうこうど]めになった。

related.note: からといって rejects a reason as insufficient ('just because ~ doesn't mean...'); という理由で presents the reason straight.
によって marks a cause or means broadly; という理由で names a specific stated reason or grounds.

title: と言えば
meaning: speaking of ~; if you mention ~
summary: 〜といえば takes up a word or topic just raised and offers the association or comment it evokes — 夏といえば花火 = speaking of summer, fireworks. It's the go-to way to say 'now that you mention ~' and bring up a representative example or a related remark.
pitfalls: Very close to というと; といえば slightly emphasizes the speaker's own strong association or a typical example.
Keep it apart from から言えば ('from the standpoint of ~'), a different frame.

examples.ja: 夏といえば、やっぱり花火だ。
examples.en: Speaking of summer, it's got to be fireworks.
examples.f: ｜夏[なつ]といえば、やっぱり｜花火[はなび]だ。

examples.ja: 田中さんといえば、最近見かけないね。
examples.en: Speaking of Tanaka, I haven't seen him around lately.
examples.f: ｜田中[たなか]さんといえば、｜最近[さいきん]｜見[み]かけないね。

synonyms.note: というと leans toward asking for clarification; といえば leans toward volunteering an association or example.

related.note: そういえば means 'come to think of it' with no set topic word; といえば hooks onto a specific word just said.

title: と言える
meaning: you can say that ~; it can be said that ~
summary: 〜と言える presents a conclusion as something reasonably assertible — 成功したと言える = you could say it succeeded. It marks a measured, justified judgment rather than a whim, and is common in analysis. The negative 〜とは言えない means 'you can't really say that'.
pitfalls: It frames a reasoned, defensible conclusion, so it fits essays and analysis, not casual venting.
The negative 〜とは言えない ('you can't really say that') is a very common counterpart.

examples.ja: 努力すれば必ず成功するとは言えない。
examples.en: You can't necessarily say that effort always leads to success.
examples.f: ｜努力[どりょく]すれば｜必[かなら]ず｜成功[せいこう]するとは｜言[い]えない。

examples.ja: この結果を見ると、計画は成功したと言えるだろう。
examples.en: Looking at these results, you could say the plan succeeded.
examples.f: この｜結果[けっか]を｜見[み]ると、｜計画[けいかく]は｜成功[せいこう]したと｜言[い]えるだろう。

synonyms.note: と言ってもいい permits a slightly bold way of putting it ('you could even say'); と言える states a straightforwardly justified conclusion.

related.note: と考えられる frames it as 'is thought/considered'; と言える frames it as 'can be stated'.

title: と言っても
meaning: although I say ~; even though you'd say ~ (it's actually more modest)
summary: 〜と言っても concedes a statement and then immediately scales it back — 料理ができると言っても、卵を焼くくらいだ = although I say I can cook, it's only frying an egg. It heads off an overblown reading of the first part by admitting the reality is more modest.
pitfalls: The follow-up tones down whatever expectation the first part raised.
Don't confuse it with fixed phrases like 何といっても ('by all means / after all').

examples.ja: 料理ができると言っても、卵を焼くくらいだ。
examples.en: Although I say I can cook, it's really only about frying an egg.
examples.f: ｜料理[りょうり]ができると｜言[い]っても、｜卵[たまご]を｜焼[や]くくらいだ。

examples.ja: 近いと言っても、歩いて三十分はかかる。
examples.en: Even though I call it close, it still takes a good thirty minutes on foot.
examples.f: ｜近[ちか]いと｜言[い]っても、｜歩[ある]いて｜三[さん]｜十[じゅう]｜分[ふん]はかかる。

related.note: からといって rejects a reason ('just because ~ doesn't mean...'); と言っても walks back a claim you just made.
何といっても is a fixed 'after all, above all'; plain と言っても concedes and then qualifies.

title: 〜同士
meaning: fellow ~; between/among each other (of like parties)
summary: 〜同士 attaches to a noun — usually people — to mean 'those of the same kind, among themselves': 友達同士 = among friends, 隣同士 = next-door to each other. It marks a mutual relationship between parties of the same type.
pitfalls: Attach it straight to the noun with no の: 女同士, not 女の同士.
It's for like parties interacting with each other; don't confuse it with the homophone 同志 ('comrades in a cause').

examples.ja: 子ども同士でけんかしても、すぐに仲直りする。
examples.en: Even when the kids fight among themselves, they make up right away.
examples.f: ｜子[こ]ども｜同士[どうし]でけんかしても、すぐに｜仲直[なかなお]りする。

examples.ja: 隣同士なので、よく話します。
examples.en: We're next-door neighbors to each other, so we talk a lot.
examples.f: ｜隣[となり]｜同士[どうし]なので、よく｜話[はな]します。

title: どうしても
meaning: no matter what; at any cost; (with a negative) just cannot, however hard one tries
summary: どうしても is an adverb with two related sides. With a wish or a will (〜たい, 〜なければ) it means 'no matter what, at any cost' — どうしても行きたい = I want to go no matter what. With a negative, usually a potential negative, it means 'however hard I try, I just can't' — どうしても思い出せない = I just can't remember it. Both share the feeling of an unmovable situation.
structure: どうしても ＋ ［expression of will or desire (〜たい／〜なければ)］
どうしても ＋ ［negative potential (〜られない)］
pitfalls: Watch which side you mean: with a wish it is 'by all means', but with a negative potential it flips to 'simply cannot' — the English changes completely.
For the 'cannot' sense the predicate is normally a potential negative (思い出せない, 開けられない), not a plain negative.

examples.ja: どうしてもこの大学に入りたいんです。
examples.en: I want to get into this university no matter what.
examples.f: どうしてもこの｜大学[だいがく]に｜入[はい]りたいんです。

examples.ja: 名前は聞いたのに、どうしても思い出せない。
examples.en: I did hear the name, but however hard I try I just can't remember it.
examples.f: ｜名前[なまえ]は｜聞[き]いたのに、どうしても｜思い出[おもいだ]せない。

related.note: どんなに〜ても sets up 'no matter how much A'; どうしても is a single adverb for a fixed will or an absolute inability.
なかなか〜ない is 'just won't easily happen'; どうしても〜ない is a flat 'cannot, however hard I try'.

title: 通す
meaning: to do (an action) all the way through to the end; to carry on doing without stopping
summary: As an auxiliary, Verb［stem］＋ 通す says you carry an action right through to the finish, often sticking with it despite difficulty — やり通す = see it through, 言い通す = keep insisting to the end. It conjugates like a normal う-verb (通した, 通して). The nuance is persistence: you hold to the action from start to finish.
pitfalls: Attach it to the stem: 守り通す, not 守る通す.
〜通す stresses keeping something up all the way through, often against resistance; 〜切る simply means finishing a set amount off (食べ切る = eat it all up).

examples.ja: 苦しかったが、最後まで走り通した。
examples.en: It was tough, but I ran the whole way through to the end.
examples.f: ｜苦[くる]しかったが、｜最後[さいご]まで｜走[はし]り｜通[とお]した。

examples.ja: 彼は自分がやっていないと言い通した。
examples.en: He kept insisting all along that he hadn't done it.
examples.f: ｜彼[かれ]は｜自分[じぶん]がやっていないと｜言[い]い｜通[とお]した。

synonyms.note: 〜抜く also means carrying through to the end, but highlights getting there despite hardship; 〜通す highlights staying consistent the whole way.

related.note: 〜切る is finishing a quantity off completely; 〜通す is keeping one action going right to the end.
〜続ける just keeps an action going; 〜通す adds the sense of sticking with it all the way to completion.

title: と同じくらい
meaning: about the same as; roughly as ... as
summary: Noun ＋ と同じくらい compares two things and says they are about equal in some quality or amount — 弟は父と同じくらい背が高い = my brother is about as tall as my father. くらい (＝ぐらい) softens it to 'roughly, about the same', not exactly equal. An adjective or amount usually follows to say what they match in.
structure: Noun ＋ と同じくらい ＋ ［い-adjective／な-adjective／quantity］
pitfalls: It means 'about the same', not 'exactly the same'; for a strict equality use と同じ without くらい.
The thing you compare against takes と, not より: 父と同じくらい, not 父より同じくらい.

examples.ja: この店のケーキは、有名な店のと同じくらいおいしい。
examples.en: The cake at this shop is about as good as the ones from famous shops.
examples.f: この｜店[みせ]のケーキは、｜有名[ゆうめい]な｜店[みせ]のと｜同[おな]じくらいおいしい。

examples.ja: 妹は私と同じくらいの背の高さになった。
examples.en: My little sister has grown to be about the same height as me.
examples.f: ｜妹[いもうと]は｜私[わたし]と｜同[おな]じくらいの｜背[せ]の｜高[たか]さになった。

synonyms.note: と並んで ranks two things as being on the same level or reputation; と同じくらい measures them as roughly equal in a stated quality.

related.note: AほどBない compares by saying B falls short of A; と同じくらい says two things land at about the same point.
に比べて sets up a contrast between two things; と同じくらい stresses that they come out about even.

title: と同じで・と違って
kana: とおなじで・とちがって
meaning: like, the same as (と同じで); unlike, different from (と違って)
summary: This pair sets up a comparison as the background to a statement. Noun ＋ と同じで means 'just like ~, (so) ...' — 兄と同じで、私も甘いものが好きだ = like my brother, I love sweets too. Noun ＋ と違って means 'unlike ~, ...' — 去年と違って、今年は涼しい = unlike last year, this year is cool. The first half names what you compare with; the main point comes after.
pitfalls: The compared thing takes と: 兄と違って, not 兄に違って.
と同じで introduces a similarity that leads into your point; when you just want to state 'A and B are the same', use と同じだ at the end instead.

examples.ja: 兄と同じで、私も朝が苦手です。
examples.en: Like my older brother, I'm not a morning person either.
examples.f: ｜兄[あに]と｜同[おな]じで、｜私[わたし]も｜朝[あさ]が｜苦手[にがて]です。

examples.ja: 去年と違って、今年の夏はとても涼しい。
examples.en: Unlike last year, this summer is very cool.
examples.f: ｜去年[きょねん]と｜違[ちが]って、｜今年[ことし]の｜夏[なつ]はとても｜涼[すず]しい。

synonyms.note: と同じくらい measures two things as roughly equal in degree; と同じで just flags a likeness to lead into a point.

related.note: に比べて frames an explicit contrast of amounts; と違って simply says 'not like ~' as a setup for the main clause.

title: とおり(に)
meaning: in the same way as; just as; exactly as
summary: とおり(に) says an action happens exactly the way something else describes or predicts. After a verb it uses the plain form — 私が言ったとおりになった = it turned out just as I said; 書いてあるとおりに作る = make it just as it is written. After a noun, join with の — 地図のとおりに行く = go exactly as the map shows. The に is often dropped with no change in meaning.
pitfalls: After a noun you need の: 地図のとおり, not 地図とおり.
Use the た form for something already done or said you are matching (言ったとおり), and the dictionary form for an instruction to follow now (言うとおり).

examples.ja: 説明書に書いてあるとおりに、組み立ててください。
examples.en: Please assemble it exactly as written in the instructions.
examples.f: ｜説明[せつめい]｜書[しょ]に｜書[か]いてあるとおりに、｜組み立[くみた]ててください。

examples.ja: 彼が予想したとおりに、試合は接戦になった。
examples.en: Just as he predicted, the match turned into a close contest.
examples.f: ｜彼[かれ]が｜予想[よそう]したとおりに、｜試合[しあい]は｜接戦[せっせん]になった。

related.note: まま keeps a state unchanged while you do something else; とおり(に) matches an action to a model or instruction.

title: ところが
meaning: however; even so; but (contrary to what was expected)
summary: ところが begins a new sentence to introduce a result that runs against what you expected. You set up an expectation, then ところが flips it: 楽しみにしていた。ところが、当日は雨で中止になった = I'd been looking forward to it. But then it rained that day and it got cancelled. The surprise is a fact that happened, not something you planned.
pitfalls: What follows ところが is an unexpected fact, not your will or a request: you can't say ところが、行きましょう.
It marks a genuine reversal of expectation; for a plain neutral 'but' between clauses, しかし or が is enough.

examples.ja: 簡単だと思っていた。ところが、やってみると本当に難しかった。
examples.en: I'd thought it would be easy. But when I tried it, it was really hard.
examples.f: ｜簡単[かんたん]だと｜思[おも]っていた。ところが、やってみると｜本当[ほんとう]に｜難[むずか]しかった。

examples.ja: 彼は来ると約束した。ところが、当日は連絡さえなかった。
examples.en: He promised he'd come. And yet on the day there wasn't even a word from him.
examples.f: ｜彼[かれ]は｜来[く]ると｜約束[やくそく]した。ところが、｜当日[とうじつ]は｜連絡[れんらく]さえなかった。

synonyms.note: しかし is a neutral 'however'; ところが specifically marks a result that reverses what you expected.

related.note: けれども contrasts two clauses within a sentence; ところが starts a fresh sentence with a surprising turn.
Easy to confuse: ところで changes the topic ('by the way'); ところが marks an unexpected reversal ('however').

title: どころか
meaning: far from; let alone; not to mention; on the contrary
summary: どころか denies one idea and replaces it with something further off. In one use, reality is the opposite of what was suggested — 謝るどころか、もっと怒り出した = far from apologizing, he got even angrier. In the other, it rules out a smaller thing to stress a bigger one — 漢字どころか、ひらがなも読めない = he can't read hiragana, let alone kanji. Either way, what comes after is more extreme.
structure: な-adjective［plain form］／い-adjective／Verb［plain form］＋ どころか
pitfalls: The second half must go beyond or reverse the first; it's not a neutral 'and also' — for plain addition use だけでなく.
In the 'let alone' pattern the easier or smaller item comes first, and the more surprising one follows with も.

examples.ja: 彼は漢字どころか、ひらがなも読めない。
examples.en: He can't even read hiragana, let alone kanji.
examples.f: ｜彼[かれ]は｜漢字[かんじ]どころか、ひらがなも｜読[よ]めない。

examples.ja: 薬を飲んだのに、よくなるどころか熱が上がった。
examples.en: I took the medicine, but far from getting better my fever went up.
examples.f: ｜薬[くすり]を｜飲[の]んだのに、よくなるどころか｜熱[ねつ]が｜上[あ]がった。

synonyms.note: ばかりか adds a further, heavier point ('not only ... but even'); どころか can also flatly reverse the expectation.

related.note: むしろ says 'rather, if anything'; どころか denies the first idea outright and pushes to the opposite or beyond.

title: ところだった
meaning: almost; nearly; was about to (but it didn't actually happen)
summary: Verb［dictionary form］＋ ところだった describes something that very nearly happened but in the end did not — もう少しで転ぶところだった = I almost fell over. It often comes with もう少しで or 危うく ('nearly, narrowly'). The key point is that the event was avoided; you are relieved or startled that it didn't come to pass.
structure: Verb［dictionary form］＋ ところだった
もう少しで／危うく ＋ Verb［dictionary form］＋ ところだった
pitfalls: The action did not actually happen — it was a near miss, not a real event.
Use the dictionary form for 'was about to' (乗り遅れるところだった); the た form + ところ (乗り遅れたところ) means 'had just done it', which is the opposite outcome.

examples.ja: もう少しで電車に乗り遅れるところだった。
examples.en: I very nearly missed the train.
examples.f: もう｜少[すこ]しで｜電車[でんしゃ]に｜乗り遅[のりおく]れるところだった。

examples.ja: 危うく大事な約束を忘れるところだった。
examples.en: I almost forgot an important appointment.
examples.f: ｜危[あや]うく｜大事[だいじ]な｜約束[やくそく]を｜忘[わす]れるところだった。

related.note: 〜かける is an action started but left half-done; ところだった is one that nearly started but never actually happened.

title: ところで
meaning: by the way; now then (changing the topic)
summary: ところで begins a sentence to switch to a new, often unrelated topic — a spoken 'by the way'. It frequently leads into a question: そうですか。ところで、ご家族はお元気ですか = I see. By the way, is your family well? Use it to move the conversation somewhere new after finishing, or setting aside, the current subject.
pitfalls: Don't mix it up with ところが: ところで changes the topic, ところが marks an unexpected result.
It introduces a break from the current topic, so it's usually followed by a fresh remark or a question, not a continuation of the same thread.

examples.ja: 今日は本当に暑いね。ところで、明日の予定は決まった。
examples.en: It's really hot today. By the way, have you decided on tomorrow's plans?
examples.f: ｜今日[きょう]は｜本当[ほんとう]に｜暑[あつ]いね。ところで、｜明日[あした]の｜予定[よてい]は｜決[き]まった。

examples.ja: 報告は以上です。ところで、来週の会議は何時からでしょうか。
examples.en: That's the end of my report. By the way, what time does next week's meeting start?
examples.f: ｜報告[ほうこく]は｜以上[いじょう]です。ところで、｜来週[らいしゅう]の｜会議[かいぎ]は｜何[なん]｜時[じ]からでしょうか。

synonyms.note: さて shifts to the next stage of the same flow ('now then'); ところで jumps to a new, often unrelated topic.

related.note: Look-alike: ところが means 'however' and reverses an expectation; ところで just changes the subject.

title: として
meaning: as; in the role of; in the capacity of
summary: Noun ＋ として names the role, position, or capacity in which someone or something acts — 医者として働く = work as a doctor; お礼として渡す = give it as a token of thanks. It labels the standpoint from which the action is done, so the noun before it is a role, status, or purpose rather than a person's viewpoint.
pitfalls: として marks the role something serves in (代表として = as a representative); にとって marks whose viewpoint you judge from (私にとって = for me) — don't swap them.
For 'as a rule / in principle' senses, として combines into set phrases like 原則として; the core idea is still 'in the capacity of'.

examples.ja: 彼女は通訳として、その会議に参加した。
examples.en: She took part in that meeting as an interpreter.
examples.f: ｜彼女[かのじょ]は｜通訳[つうやく]として、その｜会議[かいぎ]に｜参加[さんか]した。

examples.ja: この部屋は、今は物置として使っています。
examples.en: We're using this room as a storage space for now.
examples.f: この｜部屋[へや]は、｜今[いま]は｜物置[ものおき]として｜使[つか]っています。

related.note: にとって gives the standpoint from which you evaluate ('for ~'); として gives the role in which one acts ('as ~').

title: とすれば・としたら・とすると
kana: とすれば・としたら・とすると
romaji: to sureba / to shitara / to suruto
meaning: assuming that; supposing; if A (is the case), then B
