summary: These three attach to a plain-form clause to set up a supposition and draw a logical consequence — 彼の話が本当だとしたら、大変だ = supposing his story is true, that's a serious matter. You assume A for the sake of argument, then state what would follow. とすれば, としたら, and とすると are largely interchangeable; the second clause is usually a judgement, guess, or conclusion.
structure: Sentence［plain form］＋ とすれば／としたら／とすると
pitfalls: This is a hypothesis for reasoning, so the second clause is typically a judgement or inference, not a request or command.
Don't confuse it with plain たら for 'when': ついたら電話して is temporal, but 本当だとしたら大変だ is 'supposing it's true'.

examples.ja: 今から出発するとすれば、着くのは夜になるだろう。
examples.en: Assuming we leave now, we probably won't arrive until night.
examples.f: ｜今[いま]から｜出発[しゅっぱつ]するとすれば、｜着[つ]くのは｜夜[よる]になるだろう。

examples.ja: この話が事実だとしたら、大きな問題だ。
examples.en: If this story is true, then it's a serious problem.
examples.f: この｜話[はなし]が｜事実[じじつ]だとしたら、｜大[おお]きな｜問題[もんだい]だ。

synonyms.note: なら also picks up a supposition to comment on; とすれば・としたら leans more toward reasoning out a logical consequence.

related.note: たら often means 'when/after' in time; としたら is purely 'supposing that', for hypothetical reasoning.
と言えば picks up a word to talk about it ('speaking of'); としたら assumes something is so and reasons from it.

title: 途中で・途中に
kana: とちゅうで・とちゅうに
meaning: on the way; partway; in the middle of (doing something)
summary: 途中で marks a point partway through a movement or an action, often where something interrupts it — 家に帰る途中で友達に会った = I met a friend on the way home; 会議の途中で電話が鳴った = the phone rang in the middle of the meeting. After a verb use the dictionary form; after a noun join with の. で is the usual particle, marking where the mid-point event occurs.
pitfalls: After a noun you need の: 会議の途中で, not 会議途中で.
途中で points at a specific mid-point where something happens; うちに and あいだに frame a whole span of time during which you do something.

examples.ja: 駅に行く途中で、財布を落としてしまった。
examples.en: I dropped my wallet on the way to the station.
examples.f: ｜駅[えき]に｜行[い]く｜途中[とちゅう]で、｜財布[さいふ]を｜落[お]としてしまった。

examples.ja: 映画の途中で、彼は寝てしまった。
examples.en: He fell asleep partway through the movie.
examples.f: ｜映画[えいが]の｜途中[とちゅう]で、｜彼[かれ]は｜寝[ね]てしまった。

related.note: あいだに frames a whole stretch of time in which you do something; 途中で pinpoints a single moment partway through.
うちに is 'while a state still holds'; 途中で is 'at a point midway through an action or trip'.

title: とても〜ない
meaning: cannot possibly; by no means; there's no way (one could)
summary: When とても is followed by a negative — usually a potential negative — it stops meaning 'very' and instead means 'cannot possibly'. この量は一日ではとても終わらない = there's no way this amount finishes in a day; そんな高い車はとても買えない = I couldn't possibly buy such an expensive car. It stresses that something is far beyond one's ability or reach.
structure: とても ＋ Verb［ない form］［usually a potential negative］
pitfalls: Here とても means '(not) possibly', the opposite of its everyday 'very'; the clue is the negative predicate that follows.
It needs a negative ending — usually a potential negative like 買えない, 終わらない — not an affirmative one.

examples.ja: そんな高い車は、とても買えない。
examples.en: There's no way I could buy such an expensive car.
examples.f: そんな｜高[たか]い｜車[くるま]は、とても｜買[か]えない。

examples.ja: こんなにたくさんの宿題は、とても終わらない。
examples.en: There's no way this much homework will get finished.
examples.f: こんなにたくさんの｜宿題[しゅくだい]は、とても｜終[お]わらない。

synonyms.note: なかなか〜ない is 'just won't happen easily'; とても〜ない is a flat 'cannot possibly, it's out of reach'.

related.note: どうしても〜ない is 'can't, however hard I try'; とても〜ない is 'can't possibly, it's beyond reach'.

title: と同時に
meaning: at the same time as; the moment that; while also being
summary: と同時に joins two things that happen or hold at the same time. With events it means 'the instant one happens, so does the other' — ベルが鳴ると同時に、みんな立ち上がった = the moment the bell rang, everyone stood up. With states it means 'while also being' — 彼は歌手であると同時に俳優でもある = he is a singer and at the same time an actor. It is fairly formal and common in writing.
structure: Noun ＋ である ＋ と同時に
pitfalls: It ties two things to the very same moment or holds two qualities at once; it is not a casual 'while' for background action — for that use ながら.
With a noun, insert である: 教師であると同時に, not 教師と同時に.

examples.ja: ベルが鳴ると同時に、生徒たちは教室を出た。
examples.en: The moment the bell rang, the students left the classroom.
examples.f: ベルが｜鳴[な]ると｜同時[どうじ]に、｜生徒[せいと]たちは｜教室[きょうしつ]を｜出[で]た。

examples.ja: この仕事は大変であると同時に、とてもやりがいがある。
examples.en: This job is demanding and at the same time very rewarding.
examples.f: この｜仕事[しごと]は｜大変[たいへん]であると｜同時[どうじ]に、とてもやりがいがある。

synonyms.note: と共に can mean 'together with' as well as 'at the same time'; と同時に focuses squarely on simultaneity.

related.note: ながら is one person doing two things at once as background and foreground; と同時に ties two separate events or states to the same instant.

title: と共に
meaning: together with; along with; at the same time as
summary: と共に has two related uses. With a noun it means 'together with' — 家族と共に新年を迎えた = I welcomed the new year together with my family. With a verb of change it means 'as ~ happens, so does ...' — 年を取ると共に体力が落ちる = as you age, your stamina declines. It is a formal, written-flavoured equivalent of 〜と一緒に and 〜につれて.
pitfalls: It is stiff and written; in casual speech 〜と一緒に is more natural for 'together with'.
The 'as ~ changes' use needs a verb of change or development (増える, 進む), where two things shift in parallel.

examples.ja: 卒業生たちは、家族と共に喜びを分かち合った。
examples.en: The graduates shared their joy together with their families.
examples.f: ｜卒業生[そつぎょうせい]たちは、｜家族[かぞく]と｜共[とも]に｜喜[よろこ]びを｜分[わ]かち｜合[あ]った。

examples.ja: 技術が進むと共に、私たちの生活も変わってきた。
examples.en: As technology has advanced, our lives have changed along with it.
examples.f: ｜技術[ぎじゅつ]が｜進[すす]むと｜共[とも]に、｜私[わたし]たちの｜生活[せいかつ]も｜変[か]わってきた。

related.note: と同時に pins two things to the same instant; と共に can be broader 'together with' or a gradual parallel change.
につれて is 'as A gradually changes, B changes too'; と共に covers that plus plain 'together with'.
にしたがって also means 'as ~ proceeds'; と共に adds the separate sense of accompaniment ('together with').

title: と並んで
meaning: along with; on a par with; ranking alongside; as ... as
summary: Literally 'standing in a row with', Noun ＋ と並んで is mostly used figuratively to rank two things at the same level — この寺は京都と並んで有名だ = this temple is famous, on a par with Kyoto. It presents the two as comparable in standing or reputation. It has a formal, evaluative tone, common when praising or ranking things.
pitfalls: Figuratively it ranks two items as equals in level or fame, not just 'next to' in space.
The thing you rank alongside takes と: 京都と並んで, not 京都に並んで.

examples.ja: この温泉は、有名な観光地と並んで人気がある。
examples.en: This hot spring is popular, on a par with the famous sightseeing spots.
examples.f: この｜温泉[おんせん]は、｜有名[ゆうめい]な｜観光[かんこう]｜地[ち]と｜並[なら]んで｜人気[にんき]がある。

examples.ja: 彼は、その時代を代表する画家と並んで高く評価されている。
examples.en: He is held in high regard, ranking alongside the leading painters of that era.
examples.f: ｜彼[かれ]は、その｜時代[じだい]を｜代表[だいひょう]する｜画家[がか]と｜並[なら]んで｜高[たか]く｜評価[ひょうか]されている。

synonyms.note: と同じくらい measures two things as roughly equal in a stated degree; と並んで ranks them at the same level of standing.

related.note: と共に is 'together with / at the same time'; と並んで places two things side by side as equals in rank.

title: とは限らない
meaning: not necessarily; it isn't always the case that ~
summary: Sentence［plain form］＋ とは限らない pushes back on a general assumption, saying it doesn't always hold — 高いものが必ずいいとは限らない = expensive things aren't necessarily good. It admits the idea is often true while denying that it's always true. It pairs naturally with 必ずしも ('not always') earlier in the sentence.
structure: Sentence［plain form］＋ とは限らない
pitfalls: It means 'not always', not 'never': it allows exceptions rather than denying the idea outright.
It often teams up with 必ずしも for emphasis: 必ずしも〜とは限らない.

examples.ja: 高いものが、必ずしもいいとは限らない。
examples.en: Expensive things aren't necessarily good.
examples.f: ｜高[たか]いものが、｜必[かなら]ずしもいいとは｜限[かぎ]らない。

examples.ja: たくさん練習したからといって、試合に勝てるとは限らない。
examples.en: Practicing a lot doesn't necessarily mean you'll win the match.
examples.f: たくさん｜練習[れんしゅう]したからといって、｜試合[しあい]に｜勝[か]てるとは｜限[かぎ]らない。

related.note: 必ずしも is the adverb 'not always' that often sets up this pattern; とは限らない is the ending that denies a blanket rule.
わけではない denies a conclusion drawn from the situation; とは限らない denies that a general rule always holds.

title: どんなに〜ても
meaning: no matter how (much); however much ~
summary: どんなに sets up a degree and the 〜ても at the end says the result holds regardless — どんなに疲れていても、日記だけは書く = no matter how tired I am, I still write my diary. With verbs use the て form + も; with い-adjectives use 〜くても. The point is that even at an extreme degree, the outcome doesn't change.
structure: どんなに ＋ Verb［て form］＋ も
どんなに ＋ い-adjective［stem］＋ くても
pitfalls: どんなに wants the 〜ても ending to complete it; don't leave it as a plain 〜ば or 〜たら.
It stresses 'regardless of degree', so the main clause states a result that stays fixed however far things go.

examples.ja: どんなに練習しても、なかなか上手にならない。
examples.en: No matter how much I practice, I just don't get any better.
examples.f: どんなに｜練習[れんしゅう]しても、なかなか｜上手[じょうず]にならない。

examples.ja: どんなに忙しくても、朝ごはんは必ず食べる。
examples.en: However busy I am, I always eat breakfast.
examples.f: どんなに｜忙[いそが]しくても、｜朝[あさ]ごはんは｜必[かなら]ず｜食[た]べる。

related.note: ても is the basic 'even if'; どんなに〜ても adds 'no matter how far/much', emphasizing degree.
どうしても is a single adverb ('no matter what'); どんなに〜ても frames a whole clause about however much A.

title: ないうちに
meaning: before ~ happens; while ~ has not yet occurred
summary: Verb［ない form］＋ うちに means 'do something before an (often unwelcome) change sets in' — 暗くならないうちに帰ろう = let's head home before it gets dark; 忘れないうちにメモする = jot it down before I forget. You act during the window while the change has not yet happened, usually to get ahead of it.
pitfalls: Use the plain ない form, not the past: 忘れないうちに, not 忘れなかったうちに.
It usually means acting before an unwanted change; plain 〜うちに (雨のうちに) means 'while a state still lasts' instead.

examples.ja: 暗くならないうちに、家に帰りましょう。
examples.en: Let's get home before it gets dark.
examples.f: ｜暗[くら]くならないうちに、｜家[いえ]に｜帰[かえ]りましょう。

examples.ja: 忘れないうちに、必要なものをメモしておこう。
examples.en: Let me note down what I need before I forget.
examples.f: ｜忘[わす]れないうちに、｜必要[ひつよう]なものをメモしておこう。

related.note: plain うちに is 'while a state still holds'; ないうちに is 'before that state changes / before it happens'.
前に simply marks 'before' an event; ないうちに adds the sense of a limited window before an unwanted change.

title: ないことはない
meaning: it's not that one can't; it is possible (though with reservation); not impossible
summary: This double negative softly affirms that something is possible after all — 急げば間に合わないことはない = it's not impossible to make it if we hurry. It admits the possibility while holding back full enthusiasm, so it often carries a reluctant or hedged tone. Attach ことはない to a verb's ない form, or to 〜くない for adjectives.
structure: Verb［ない form］＋ ことはない
い-adjective［stem］＋ くないことはない
pitfalls: It's a soft, hedged 'yes, it's possible', weaker than a plain affirmative — often with unspoken reluctance.
Don't confuse it with ことはない meaning 'there's no need to' (謝ることはない = no need to apologize), which has no first ない.

examples.ja: からいものも食べないことはないが、あまり好きではない。
examples.en: It's not that I can't eat spicy food, but I don't really like it.
examples.f: からいものも｜食[た]べないことはないが、あまり｜好[す]きではない。

examples.ja: 急げば、終電に間に合わないことはない。
examples.en: If we hurry, it's not impossible to catch the last train.
examples.f: ｜急[いそ]げば、｜終電[しゅうでん]に｜間に合[まにあ]わないことはない。

related.note: わけではない denies a conclusion ('it doesn't mean that'); ないことはない softly admits a possibility exists.
ことはない (no first ない) means 'there's no need to'; ないことはない is a double negative meaning 'it's not impossible'.

title: なかなか
meaning: quite; considerably; (with a negative) just won't ~
summary: なかなか has two everyday jobs. Before an affirmative word it means 'quite / considerably', often with a touch of surprise that something beats your expectations — なかなかおいしい = surprisingly tasty. Before a negative verb (なかなか〜ない) it means the action is slow or hard to happen — 'just won't ~' — as in バスがなかなか来ない ('the bus just won't come'). Read the polarity of the sentence to tell the two uses apart.
structure: なかなか ＋ Verb［ない form］
pitfalls: With a negative, なかなか〜ない means something is slow or hard to happen ('just won't ~'), not merely 'not very'.
In the affirmative 'quite' sense it carries mild admiration or surprise that something exceeds what you expected, so it suits praise more than plain measurement.

examples.ja: この店のラーメンはなかなかおいしい。
examples.en: The ramen at this shop is quite good.
examples.f: この｜店[みせ]のラーメンはなかなかおいしい。

examples.ja: バスがなかなか来なくて、遅刻しそうだ。
examples.en: The bus just won't come, and it looks like I'll be late.
examples.f: バスがなかなか｜来[こ]なくて、｜遅刻[ちこく]しそうだ。

synonyms.note: けっこう also means 'quite / fairly' but is plainer, without なかなか's note of pleasant surprise.

related.note: The dedicated negative pattern なかなか〜ない ('just won't ~'); here it is the affirmative 'quite' use.

title: ながらも
meaning: although; even though; despite ~
summary: ながらも is a concessive connector: it links two clauses that clash, meaning 'although / despite'. It attaches to a verb ます-stem, an い-adjective, a な-adjective, or a noun — 忙しいと言いながらも ('although he says he's busy'), 狭いながらも ('cramped though it is'). The も makes the contrast explicit, so what follows goes against what the first part leads you to expect.
pitfalls: This is the concessive ながら ('although'), not the ながら of two simultaneous actions ('while doing'); the added も signals the contrast.
The two clauses must clash — the second goes against what you would expect from the first.

examples.ja: 彼は忙しいと言いながらも、いつも手伝ってくれる。
examples.en: Even though he says he's busy, he always helps me out.
examples.f: ｜彼[かれ]は｜忙[いそが]しいと｜言[い]いながらも、いつも｜手伝[てつだ]ってくれる。

examples.ja: 狭いながらも、自分の部屋を持てて嬉しい。
examples.en: Cramped though it is, I'm happy to have my own room.
examples.f: ｜狭[せま]いながらも、｜自分[じぶん]の｜部屋[へや]を｜持[も]てて｜嬉[うれ]しい。

synonyms.note: Plain concessive ながら carries the same 'although'; ながらも just states the contrast more firmly.
ものの also means 'although' but is more written; ながらも attaches tightly to a stem or adjective.

related.note: のに often adds complaint or dissatisfaction; ながらも is a neutral concessive.

title: なぜなら〜から
meaning: the reason is; this is because ~
summary: なぜなら opens a sentence that gives the reason for something you just said. It typically pairs with から or のだ at the end — 'The reason is that ~'. You state a claim first, then a fresh sentence beginning なぜなら explains why. It belongs to writing and formal speech.
structure: Sentence1。なぜなら（ば）、Sentence2 ＋ から（だ）／のだ。
pitfalls: なぜなら explains something already stated, so it starts the second sentence and usually closes with から or のだ.
It sounds formal or written; in casual talk people just use から or だって.

examples.ja: 今日は早く帰ります。なぜなら、母の誕生日だからです。
examples.en: I'm going home early today. The reason is that it's my mother's birthday.
examples.f: ｜今日[きょう]は｜早[はや]く｜帰[かえ]ります。なぜなら、｜母[はは]の｜誕生[たんじょう]｜日[び]だからです。

examples.ja: その計画には反対だ。なぜなら、費用がかかりすぎるからだ。
examples.en: I'm against that plan, because it costs far too much.
examples.f: その｜計画[けいかく]には｜反対[はんたい]だ。なぜなら、｜費用[ひよう]がかかりすぎるからだ。

synonyms.note: から states a reason within one sentence; なぜなら〜から spreads it across two for emphasis.

related.note: だって is the casual spoken 'because'; なぜなら is its formal, written counterpart.
ものだから gives a reason as an excuse or explanation; なぜなら plainly labels the reason.

title: なんか・なんて
meaning: things like ~; such as ~ (often dismissive or emphatic)
summary: なんか and なんて are casual, emotional versions of など. After a noun they mean 'things like ~ / such as ~', usually with a dismissive or belittling tone — スポーツなんか興味がない ('no interest in stuff like sports'). なんて can also follow a whole clause to show surprise or disbelief — 負けるなんて ('to think you'd lose!'). The feeling behind them is what sets them apart from plain など.
pitfalls: なんか・なんて often sound dismissive or belittling, so avoid them for things you mean to treat with respect.
They are the casual, feeling-laden cousins of など, which is the neutral 'and so on / such as'.

examples.ja: スポーツなんか全然興味がない。
examples.en: I have no interest at all in things like sports.
examples.f: スポーツなんか｜全然[ぜんぜん]｜興味[きょうみ]がない。

examples.ja: 君が負けるなんて、信じられない。
examples.en: You, losing? I can't believe it.
examples.f: ｜君[きみ]が｜負[ま]けるなんて、｜信[しん]じられない。

synonyms.note: など is the neutral 'such as / and so on'; なんか・なんて add a casual, often dismissive feeling.

title: に当たる
meaning: to correspond to; amount to; be equivalent to
summary: に当たる links a noun to what it corresponds to or equals — a value, a relationship, or a position. 百円は約一ドルに当たる ('100 yen amounts to about one dollar'); 母の兄に当たる人 ('the person who is my mother's older brother'). Use it to line one thing up against its equivalent.
pitfalls: Do not confuse this with にあたって／に当たり (N2, 'on the occasion of ~'); に当たる here means 'corresponds to / equals'.

examples.ja: 一ドルは今、約百五十円に当たります。
examples.en: One dollar currently amounts to about 150 yen.
examples.f: ｜一[いち]ドルは｜今[いま]、｜約[やく]｜百[ひゃく]｜五[ご]｜十[じゅう]｜円[えん]に｜当[あ]たります。

examples.ja: 彼は私の母の兄に当たる人です。
examples.en: He is the person who is my mother's older brother.
examples.f: ｜彼[かれ]は｜私[わたし]の｜母[はは]の｜兄[あに]に｜当[あ]たる｜人[ひと]です。

related.note: にあたって means 'on the occasion of / when about to'; に当たる means 'corresponds to'.

title: に合わせて・に合った
kana: にあわせて・にあった
meaning: in accordance with; matching; to suit ~
summary: に合わせて means you adjust something to match a standard, a partner, or the situation — 相手に合わせて話す ('speak in a way that matches the listener'), 音楽に合わせて踊る ('dance in time with the music'). Before a noun, use に合った to describe something that suits or fits — 季節に合った服 ('clothes suited to the season').
pitfalls: に合わせて is 'adjust to match'; use に合った before a noun to describe something that already suits or fits it.

examples.ja: 相手のレベルに合わせて、話し方を変えます。
examples.en: I change the way I speak to match the level of the person I'm talking with.
examples.f: ｜相手[あいて]のレベルに｜合[あ]わせて、｜話し方[はなしかた]を｜変[か]えます。

examples.ja: 音楽に合わせて体を動かしてください。
examples.en: Please move your body in time with the music.
examples.f: ｜音楽[おんがく]に｜合[あ]わせて｜体[からだ]を｜動[うご]かしてください。

synonyms.note: に応じて means 'in response to / depending on'; に合わせて stresses actively matching a target.

related.note: に沿って means 'along / in line with (a plan or guideline)'; に合わせて is tuning to fit.
に基づいて means 'based on (a foundation)'; に合わせて is adjusting to match.

title: において・における
meaning: in; at; on (place, time, or field); regarding ~ (formal)
summary: において marks where, when, or in what field something happens — a formal, written stand-in for the particle で. 会議は本社において開かれる ('the meeting is held at the head office'); 現代社会において ('in modern society'). Before a noun, use における — 教育における問題 ('problems in education').
pitfalls: において is a formal, written substitute for で; in everyday conversation で sounds far more natural.
Use における before a noun (会社における教育) and において before a verb.

examples.ja: 現代社会において、インターネットは欠かせないものだ。
examples.en: In modern society, the internet is indispensable.
examples.f: ｜現代[げんだい]｜社会[しゃかい]において、インターネットは｜欠[か]かせないものだ。

examples.ja: この分野における研究は、まだ始まったばかりだ。
examples.en: Research in this field has only just begun.
examples.f: この｜分野[ぶんや]における｜研究[けんきゅう]は、まだ｜始[はじ]まったばかりだ。

synonyms.note: The particle で marks place or setting in ordinary speech; において is its formal equivalent.

related.note: に関して means 'on the topic of'; において marks a place, time, or field.

title: に限る
meaning: nothing beats ~; ~ is the best
summary: に限る states the speaker's opinion that nothing is better than the thing named — 'you can't beat ~ / ~ is best'. It follows a noun or a plain verb: 疲れた時は寝るに限る ('when you're tired, nothing beats sleeping'), 夏はビールに限る ('in summer you can't beat a beer'). It is a warm, personal recommendation.
structure: Noun／Verb［dictionary form］／Verb［ない form］＋ に限る
pitfalls: This に限る means 'is the best choice' and voices the speaker's opinion; keep it apart from に限らず ('not limited to') and に限って ('of all ~').

examples.ja: 疲れた時は、寝るに限る。
examples.en: When you're tired, there's nothing like sleeping.
examples.f: ｜疲[つか]れた｜時[とき]は、｜寝[ね]るに｜限[かぎ]る。

examples.ja: 夏はやっぱり冷たいビールに限るね。
examples.en: In summer, you really can't beat a cold beer.
examples.f: ｜夏[なつ]はやっぱり｜冷[つめ]たいビールに｜限[かぎ]るね。

synonyms.note: 〜ほうがいい advises one option over another; に限る declares one thing simply the best.

related.note: に限らず means 'not just ~ (but also)'; に限る means '~ is the best'.
に限って means 'of all ~ (and no other)'; に限る means 'nothing beats ~'.

title: にかけて
meaning: over (a span of time or space); from ... through ~
summary: にかけて marks a rough, continuous span, usually paired with から: 〜から〜にかけて ('from ~ through ~'). 今夜から明日にかけて ('from tonight through tomorrow'); 北から南にかけて ('from the north down to the south'). The endpoints are vague, unlike the clear-cut 〜から〜まで.
structure: Noun ＋ から ＋ Noun ＋ にかけて
pitfalls: から〜にかけて marks a loose, continuous stretch; when you need clear-cut endpoints, use から〜まで instead.

examples.ja: 今夜から明日の朝にかけて、雪が降るでしょう。
examples.en: It will probably snow from tonight through tomorrow morning.
examples.f: ｜今夜[こんや]から｜明日[あした]の｜朝[あさ]にかけて、｜雪[ゆき]が｜降[ふ]るでしょう。

examples.ja: 北から南にかけて、桜が咲き始めた。
examples.en: The cherry blossoms have begun to bloom from the north down to the south.
examples.f: ｜北[きた]から｜南[みなみ]にかけて、｜桜[さくら]が｜咲[さ]き｜始[はじ]めた。

synonyms.note: The same から〜にかけて 'from ~ through ~' pattern; にかけて is its second half.

related.note: まで marks a clear endpoint 'up to'; にかけて leaves the span vague.
にわたって stresses the whole extent covered; にかけて marks a from-to range.

title: に代わって・に代わり
kana: にかわって・にかわり
meaning: instead of; in place of; on behalf of ~
summary: に代わって marks doing something in place of, or on behalf of, a specific person or thing — 社長に代わって挨拶する ('give the greeting on behalf of the president'), 現金に代わって電子マネーを使う ('use electronic money instead of cash'). に代わり is the same in a slightly more formal style.
structure: Noun ＋ に代わって／に代わり
pitfalls: に代わって replaces a specific person or thing ('in place of A'); 代わりに can do that too but also means 'in exchange / to make up for'.

examples.ja: 社長に代わって、私がご挨拶いたします。
examples.en: In place of the company president, I will give the greeting.
examples.f: ｜社長[しゃちょう]に｜代[か]わって、｜私[わたし]がご｜挨拶[あいさつ]いたします。

examples.ja: 最近は現金に代わって、電子マネーを使う人が増えた。
examples.en: Recently the number of people using electronic money instead of cash has grown.
examples.f: ｜最近[さいきん]は｜現金[げんきん]に｜代[か]わって、｜電子[でんし]マネーを｜使[つか]う｜人[ひと]が｜増[ふ]えた。

synonyms.note: 代わりに also means 'instead of', but it can additionally mean 'in exchange / to make up for'.

title: に関する・に関して
kana: にかんする・にかんして
meaning: regarding; concerning; about ~ (formal)
summary: に関して marks the topic something concerns — 'regarding / about ~' — in a formal or written register. その事件に関して調べる ('investigate regarding that incident'). Before a noun, use に関する — 環境に関する本 ('a book about the environment').
pitfalls: Use に関する (not に関して) directly before a noun: 経済に関する記事, not 経済に関して記事.
に関して is more formal than について; the two are otherwise close in meaning.

examples.ja: その事件に関して、警察が調べている。
examples.en: The police are investigating that incident.
examples.f: その｜事件[じけん]に｜関[かん]して、｜警察[けいさつ]が｜調[しら]べている。

examples.ja: 環境問題に関する本を読んでいます。
examples.en: I'm reading a book concerning environmental problems.
examples.f: ｜環境[かんきょう]｜問題[もんだい]に｜関[かん]する｜本[ほん]を｜読[よ]んでいます。

synonyms.note: について is the everyday 'about ~'; に関して is the more formal equivalent.

related.note: に対して aims an action or feeling at a target ('toward'); に関して marks the topic.

title: に比べて
meaning: compared to; in comparison with ~
summary: に比べて sets a baseline you measure something against — 'compared to ~'. 去年に比べて雨が多い ('there's more rain compared to last year'), 都会に比べて田舎は安い ('the countryside is cheaper compared to the city'). The noun before に比べて is the reference point; the new information comes in the main clause. に比べ is the same, a touch more formal.
pitfalls: The thing after に比べて is the baseline you measure against; the point you want to make comes in the main clause.

examples.ja: 去年に比べて、今年は雨が多い。
examples.en: Compared to last year, there's a lot of rain this year.
examples.f: ｜去年[きょねん]に｜比[くら]べて、｜今年[ことし]は｜雨[あめ]が｜多[おお]い。

examples.ja: 都会に比べて、田舎は物価が安い。
examples.en: Compared to the city, prices are cheaper in the countryside.
examples.f: ｜都会[とかい]に｜比[くら]べて、｜田舎[いなか]は｜物価[ぶっか]が｜安[やす]い。

synonyms.note: より marks the standard in a plain comparison ('than'); に比べて frames a broader 'compared with'.

related.note: に対して sets two things in direct contrast; に比べて weighs one against a baseline.
わりに means 'considering / for (what you'd expect)'; に比べて is a straight comparison.

title: にしたがって
meaning: as (one thing changes, another does); in accordance with ~
summary: にしたがって has two related senses. As a proportional link it means 'as one thing changes, another changes with it' — 山を登るにしたがって空気が薄くなる ('as you climb, the air thins'). As 'in accordance with' it means following rules or instructions — 指示にしたがって動く ('act according to the instructions'). Context tells the two apart.
structure: Verb［dictionary form］／Noun ＋ にしたがって
pitfalls: One form, two senses: 'as one thing changes, another follows' (proportional) and 'obeying / following (rules, instructions)'; context decides which.

examples.ja: 山を登るにしたがって、空気が薄くなってきた。
examples.en: As we climbed the mountain, the air gradually grew thinner.
examples.f: ｜山[やま]を｜登[のぼ]るにしたがって、｜空気[くうき]が｜薄[うす]くなってきた。

examples.ja: 係員の指示にしたがって、避難してください。
examples.en: Please evacuate in accordance with the staff's instructions.
examples.f: ｜係員[かかりいん]の｜指示[しじ]にしたがって、｜避難[ひなん]してください。

synonyms.note: につれて covers only the proportional 'as ~ changes' sense; にしたがって also means 'following (rules)'.

related.note: に伴って marks a change that accompanies another; にしたがって stresses the two moving together in step.
したがって at the head of a sentence means 'therefore'; にしたがって attaches to a noun or verb.

title: にしては
meaning: for; considering it's ~ (the result is unexpected)
summary: にしては judges a result against a clear yardstick and notes it doesn't fit — 'for ~ / considering it's ~'. 初心者にしては上手 ('good for a beginner'), 冬にしては暖かい ('warm for winter'). The outcome is usually a mild surprise given the standard you'd expect.
pitfalls: にしては measures a result against a definite reference point (a beginner, winter …) and finds it doesn't match; the outcome tends to be surprising.
わりに(は) is close, but its standard can be looser; にしては needs a clear reference point.

examples.ja: 彼は初心者にしては、上手にピアノを弾く。
examples.en: For a beginner, he plays the piano well.
examples.f: ｜彼[かれ]は｜初心者[しょしんしゃ]にしては、｜上手[じょうず]にピアノを｜弾[ひ]く。

examples.ja: 今日は冬にしては暖かいね。
examples.en: It's warm for winter today, isn't it?
examples.f: ｜今日[きょう]は｜冬[ふゆ]にしては｜暖[あたた]かいね。

synonyms.note: わりに means 'considering / for', with a looser standard; にしては needs a definite reference point.

related.note: くせに adds blame or criticism to the contrast; にしては simply notes an unexpected result.
にしても means 'even if / even supposing'; にしては judges a result against a standard.

title: にしても
meaning: even if; even though; even supposing ~
summary: にしても grants a point and then pushes back against it — 'even if ~ / even supposing ~'. 行くにしても準備に時間がかかる ('even if we go, prep takes time'), 冗談にしてもひどい ('even as a joke, that's awful'). You accept the situation for the sake of argument, then state something that still holds.
pitfalls: にしても grants a point ('even supposing X') and then counters it; don't mix it up with にしては ('for / considering', which judges a result against a standard).

examples.ja: 行くにしても、準備には時間がかかる。
examples.en: Even if we go, the preparations will take time.
examples.f: ｜行[い]くにしても、｜準備[じゅんび]には｜時間[じかん]がかかる。

examples.ja: 冗談にしても、その言い方はひどいよ。
examples.en: Even as a joke, that way of putting it is awful.
examples.f: ｜冗談[じょうだん]にしても、その｜言い方[いいかた]はひどいよ。

related.note: にしろ〜にしろ pairs two cases 'whether A or B'; にしても concedes a single point.
いずれにしても means 'in any case, whichever it is'; にしても concedes one specific supposition.
にしては judges a result against a standard ('for ~'); にしても concedes 'even if ~'.

title: に対して
meaning: toward (a target); in contrast to ~
summary: に対して has two jobs. It aims an action or feeling at a target — お客様に対して丁寧に話す ('speak politely toward customers'). It also sets two things in contrast — 兄が明るいのに対して弟は静かだ ('in contrast to the cheerful older brother, the younger one is quiet'). Before a noun, use に対する.
pitfalls: Two jobs: aiming an action or feeling at someone ('toward'), and setting two things against each other ('in contrast to').
に対して directs something at a target; keep it apart from に関して／について, which mean 'on the topic of'.

examples.ja: お客様に対して、丁寧な言葉を使いましょう。
examples.en: Let's use polite language toward customers.
examples.f: お｜客様[きゃくさま]に｜対[たい]して、｜丁寧[ていねい]な｜言葉[ことば]を｜使[つか]いましょう。

examples.ja: 兄が明るいのに対して、弟は静かだ。
examples.en: In contrast to the cheerful older brother, the younger one is quiet.
examples.f: ｜兄[あに]が｜明[あか]るいのに｜対[たい]して、｜弟[おとうと]は｜静[しず]かだ。

related.note: に比べて weighs one thing against a baseline; に対して sets two things side by side in contrast.
に反して means 'contrary to (what was expected)'; に対して's contrast sense is a neutral 'whereas'.
に向かって is aiming at a physical direction; に対して aims an action or attitude at a target.

title: に違いない
meaning: must be; surely; no doubt that ~
summary: に違いない states a firm guess based on evidence — 'it must be ~ / surely ~'. 電気が消えているから、もう寝たに違いない ('the lights are off, so he must have gone to bed'). It is stronger than かもしれない but is still an inference, not a confirmed fact. It follows a noun, adjective, or plain verb.
structure: Noun／な-adjective／い-adjective／Verb［plain form］＋ に違いない
pitfalls: に違いない voices a confident guess from evidence — stronger than かもしれない, but still a guess, not a known fact.

examples.ja: 電気が消えているから、彼はもう寝たに違いない。
examples.en: The lights are off, so he must have already gone to bed.
examples.f: ｜電気[でんき]が｜消[き]えているから、｜彼[かれ]はもう｜寝[ね]たに｜違[ちが]いない。

examples.ja: この宝石は本物に違いない。
examples.en: This jewel must be genuine.
examples.f: この｜宝石[ほうせき]は｜本物[ほんもの]に｜違[ちが]いない。

synonyms.note: はずだ is a logical expectation from known facts; に違いない is a strong personal conviction.
に決まっている is an even more emphatic, casual 'bound to be'; に違いない is confident but a bit more measured.

related.note: かもしれない is a weak 'might be'; に違いない is a strong 'must be'.

title: について
meaning: about; concerning; regarding ~
summary: について marks the topic you speak, write, or think about — 'about / concerning ~'. この町の歴史について調べる ('research about this town's history'). Before a noun, add の — その問題についての意見 ('an opinion about that problem'). It is the everyday way to name a subject.
pitfalls: Add の to modify a noun: 事故についての説明, not 事故について説明.
について marks the topic you speak or think about; に対して aims an action at a target — don't swap them.

examples.ja: この町の歴史について、調べています。
examples.en: I'm researching the history of this town.
examples.f: この｜町[まち]の｜歴史[れきし]について、｜調[しら]べています。

examples.ja: その問題についての意見を聞かせてください。
examples.en: Please let me hear your opinion about that problem.
examples.f: その｜問題[もんだい]についての｜意見[いけん]を｜聞[き]かせてください。

synonyms.note: に関して is the more formal 'regarding'; について is the everyday equivalent.

related.note: に対して aims an action or feeling at a target ('toward'); について names the topic.
において marks a place, time, or field; について marks the topic under discussion.

title: につれて
meaning: as (one thing changes, another follows); in proportion as ~
summary: につれて links two gradual changes: as one thing progresses, another shifts along with it — 時間がたつにつれて痛みが消える ('as time passes, the pain fades'), 年をとるにつれて体力が落ちる ('as you age, your stamina drops'). Both sides must move gradually and together.
pitfalls: につれて needs a gradual, linked change on both sides; it doesn't fit a one-time or sudden event.

examples.ja: 時間がたつにつれて、痛みは少しずつ消えていった。
examples.en: As time passed, the pain gradually faded away.
examples.f: ｜時間[じかん]がたつにつれて、｜痛[いた]みは｜少[すこ]しずつ｜消[き]えていった。

examples.ja: 年をとるにつれて、体力が落ちてきた。
examples.en: As I've grown older, my stamina has declined.
examples.f: ｜年[とし]をとるにつれて、｜体力[たいりょく]が｜落[お]ちてきた。

synonyms.note: にしたがって covers this same proportional 'as ~ changes', and also 'following (rules)'.
に伴って marks a change accompanying another; につれて stresses the two moving together step by step.

related.note: 〜ば〜ほど means 'the more ~, the more ~'; につれて tracks two changes progressing together over time.

title: にとって
meaning: to; for; from the standpoint of ~
summary: にとって attaches to a noun — usually a person, group, or organization — and weighs something from that party's standpoint: how it looks, matters, or feels to them. 私にとって = for me / as far as I'm concerned. It is almost always followed by an evaluation (大切だ, 難しい, 幸せだ). Use it to say who something is significant, hard, or valuable for.
pitfalls: にとって marks whose viewpoint you are judging from; it is not the 'for whose benefit' に of あげる/くれる. For 'I bought it for my mother', use のために, not にとって.
Follow it with an evaluation or judgment (大切, 必要, つらい…), not an ordinary action — にとって does not mark the doer of a plain verb.

examples.ja: 私にとって、家族が一番大切です。
examples.en: For me, family is the most important thing.
examples.f: ｜私[わたし]にとって、｜家族[かぞく]が｜一番[いちばん]｜大切[たいせつ]です。

examples.ja: この問題は子供にとって難しすぎます。
examples.en: This problem is too difficult for children.
examples.f: この｜問題[もんだい]は｜子供[こども]にとって｜難[むずか]しすぎます。

related.note: として states the role or capacity someone acts in; にとって states whose viewpoint something is weighed from.
に対して directs an action or attitude toward a target; にとって gives the standpoint from which something is judged.

title: に慣れる
meaning: to get used to; to grow accustomed to ~
summary: に慣れる means you have grown accustomed to something through repeated experience, so it no longer feels new or hard. The thing you get used to is marked with に — 新しい仕事に慣れる = get used to a new job. To make an action the target, nominalize it first with の: 早く起きるのに慣れる. The form 慣れている describes the settled state of already being used to something.
pitfalls: The thing you get used to takes に, not を: 生活に慣れる, not 生活を慣れる.
To get used to doing an action, nominalize the verb with の first: 使うのに慣れる, not 使う慣れる.

examples.ja: この町の生活にだんだん慣れてきました。
examples.en: I've gradually gotten used to life in this town.
examples.f: この｜町[まち]の｜生活[せいかつ]にだんだん｜慣[な]れてきました。

examples.ja: 新しいパソコンを使うのに、まだ慣れていません。
examples.en: I'm still not used to using my new computer.
examples.f: ｜新[あたら]しいパソコンを｜使[つか]うのに、まだ｜慣[な]れていません。

related.note: ようになる marks reaching a new ability or habit; に慣れる marks that something no longer feels unfamiliar.

title: には
meaning: in order to ~; for the purpose of (what it takes) ~
summary: A dictionary-form verb plus には sets up a goal and then tells you what is needed, useful, or required to reach it — 痩せるには、運動が一番だ = to lose weight, exercise is best. It frames the rest of the sentence as the means or condition for achieving that aim. This には is simply the goal-marking に joined to the topic marker は.
pitfalls: Use the dictionary form before には: 合格するには, not 合格したには.
This には introduces what is needed to reach a goal; for a plain 'in order to' purpose clause, ために is the more general choice.

examples.ja: 電車に間に合うには、今すぐ出なければならない。
examples.en: To make the train, we have to leave right now.
examples.f: ｜電車[でんしゃ]に｜間に合[まにあ]うには、｜今[いま]すぐ｜出[で]なければならない。

examples.ja: 漢字を覚えるには、何度も書くのがいいです。
examples.en: To memorize kanji, writing them over and over is good.
examples.f: ｜漢字[かんじ]を｜覚[おぼ]えるには、｜何[なん]｜度[ど]も｜書[か]くのがいいです。

related.note: ために is the general 'in order to'; 〜には frames a goal and then states what it takes to reach it.
のに marks 'for doing X', usually before a judgment of cost or suitability; 〜には leads into what is needed to achieve X.

title: に反して
meaning: contrary to; against; in contradiction to ~
summary: に反して attaches to a noun and says the result runs counter to it — often 予想 (prediction), 期待 (expectation), or 意志 (will). 予想に反して = contrary to expectations. It marks a clash between what was anticipated or intended and what actually happened. Before a noun, switch to the form に反する (期待に反する結果).
pitfalls: It pairs with nouns like 予想, 期待, ルール, 意志; it is not attached directly to a plain verb clause.
Before a noun, use に反する: 予想に反する結果, not 予想に反して結果.

examples.ja: 予想に反して、試合は簡単に終わった。
examples.en: Contrary to expectations, the match ended easily.
examples.f: ｜予想[よそう]に｜反[はん]して、｜試合[しあい]は｜簡単[かんたん]に｜終[お]わった。

examples.ja: 両親の希望に反して、彼は大学をやめた。
examples.en: Against his parents' wishes, he quit university.
examples.f: ｜両親[りょうしん]の｜希望[きぼう]に｜反[はん]して、｜彼[かれ]は｜大学[だいがく]をやめた。

related.note: に対して contrasts two things or aims an action at a target; に反して stresses going against an expectation or rule.

title: に基づいて
meaning: based on; on the basis of; in accordance with ~
summary: に基づいて marks the foundation that an action or judgment is built on — データに基づいて = based on the data, 事実に基づいて = based on the facts. What follows is done in line with that basis. Before a noun, use に基づく or に基づいた (事実に基づいた話). It has a somewhat formal, factual tone.
structure: Noun ＋ に基づく／に基づいた ＋ Noun
pitfalls: The basis takes に: 経験に基づいて, not 経験を基づいて.
It fits solid grounds like data, facts, rules, or experience; for 'according to (a source of information)', によると is the natural choice.

examples.ja: アンケートの結果に基づいて、新しい商品を作った。
examples.en: Based on the survey results, we made a new product.
examples.f: アンケートの｜結果[けっか]に｜基[もと]づいて、｜新[あたら]しい｜商品[しょうひん]を｜作[つく]った。

examples.ja: この映画は本当にあった事件に基づいています。
examples.en: This movie is based on a real incident.
examples.f: この｜映画[えいが]は｜本当[ほんとう]にあった｜事件[じけん]に｜基[もと]づいています。

related.note: をもとに means 'using X as material or reference'; に基づいて stresses conforming to X as a firm basis.
によると reports what a source says; に基づいて marks the grounds an action rests on.
にしたがって means following along with a rule or a change; に基づいて grounds a decision on a basis.

title: によって・による
meaning: by means of; due to; by (agent); depending on ~
summary: によって has several linked uses: means or method (話し合いによって解決する = solve through discussion), cause (地震によって = due to the earthquake), the agent in a passive sentence (学生によって作られた = made by a student), and variation (人によって違う = differs from person to person). The prenominal form is による (事故による遅れ). Context tells you which sense is meant.
pitfalls: In a passive sentence with a clear doer — especially create/discover verbs — the agent takes によって: この寺は昔の人々によって建てられた.
'X によって違う／変わる' means something varies depending on X; do not read that as 'caused by X'.
Before a noun, use による, not によって: 雨による中止.

examples.ja: 国によって、習慣が違います。
examples.en: Customs differ from country to country.
examples.f: ｜国[くに]によって、｜習慣[しゅうかん]が｜違[ちが]います。

examples.ja: この寺は昔の人々によって建てられました。
examples.en: This temple was built by people long ago.
examples.f: この｜寺[てら]は｜昔[むかし]の｜人々[ひとびと]によって｜建[た]てられました。

related.note: によると marks the source of reported information ('according to'); によって marks means, cause, or the agent of an action.
に基づいて grounds something on a basis; によって marks the means or agent by which it happens.

title: によると・によれば
meaning: according to (a source) ~
summary: によると (or によれば) names the source of information you are passing on — 天気予報によると = according to the weather forecast. The sentence it introduces is reported speech, so it usually ends in a hearsay marker like そうだ, らしい, or だろう. Use it to make clear you got the information from somewhere else rather than from your own direct knowledge.
structure: Noun ＋ によると／によれば ＋ Sentence ＋ そうだ／らしい
pitfalls: It reports information, so end the sentence with a hearsay marker like そうだ or らしい rather than stating it as your own fact.
Use it for a source of information (news, a person, a report), not for 'by means of' — that sense is によって.

examples.ja: ニュースによると、明日は大雪になるそうです。
examples.en: According to the news, it's going to snow heavily tomorrow.
examples.f: ニュースによると、｜明日[あした]は｜大雪[おおゆき]になるそうです。

examples.ja: 友達によれば、あの店のケーキはとてもおいしいらしい。
examples.en: According to my friend, the cake at that shop is apparently delicious.
examples.f: ｜友達[ともだち]によれば、あの｜店[みせ]のケーキはとてもおいしいらしい。

related.note: そうだ reports what you heard; によると names the source it came from — the two often appear together.
によって marks means, cause, or agent; によると marks the source of reported information.
って casually quotes or reports something; によると introduces the source more explicitly and politely.

title: の間に
meaning: while; during; in the course of ~
summary: の間に marks a span of time and says something happens at some point within it — 夏休みの間に = at some point during summer vacation. The に signals that the second event fits inside that period, typically a one-time action or change. Without に, 間 alone means the action continues through the whole span. It attaches to a noun; after a clause the form is just 間に.
pitfalls: 間に (with に) marks a point inside the period where something happens; 間 without に means all the way through it: 留守の間に (something happened while I was out) vs 留守の間 (the whole time I was out).
Use it for a bounded stretch of time, not a single instant.

examples.ja: 母が出かけているあいだに、部屋をきれいに掃除した。
examples.en: While my mother was out, I cleaned the room until it was spotless.
examples.f: ｜母[はは]が｜出[で]かけているあいだに、｜部屋[へや]をきれいに｜掃除[そうじ]した。

examples.ja: 夏休みのあいだに、本をたくさん読みたい。
examples.en: I want to read a lot of books during the summer break.
examples.f: ｜夏休[なつやす]みのあいだに、｜本[ほん]をたくさん｜読[よ]みたい。

related.note: 間に after a plain clause works the same way; の間に is the version that attaches to a noun.
うちに stresses doing something before a state changes or ends; の間に simply locates an event inside a period.
とき points to the general time 'when'; の間に marks a point within an ongoing stretch of time.

title: のでしょうか
meaning: I wonder if ~; could it be that ~? (soft, polite question)
summary: のでしょうか softens a question by combining explanatory の with the tentative でしょう and question か. It makes you sound less blunt and more considerate — as if wondering aloud or gently seeking an explanation. どうして遅れたのでしょうか is a softer, more polite 'why were you late?' than 遅れたんですか. It is common when asking about reasons or circumstances.
structure: Sentence［plain form］＋ のでしょうか
な-adjective／Noun ＋ なのでしょうか
pitfalls: Attach の to plain forms; with nouns and な-adjectives insert な: 大丈夫なのでしょうか, not 大丈夫のでしょうか.
It adds softness and politeness; a plain 〜ですか is a more direct question.

examples.ja: この漢字は、どう読むのでしょうか。
examples.en: I wonder how you read this kanji?
examples.f: この｜漢字[かんじ]は、どう｜読[よ]むのでしょうか。

examples.ja: 会議は何時から始まるのでしょうか。
examples.en: Might I ask what time the meeting starts?
examples.f: ｜会議[かいぎ]は｜何[なん]｜時[じ]から｜始[はじ]まるのでしょうか。

related.note: でしょう alone guesses or seeks agreement; のでしょうか wraps a question in that same softness while asking for an explanation.
だろう is the plain-style guess; のでしょうか is the polite, question-form version used to ask gently.
explanatory の／んだ gives background or reasons; のでしょうか turns that explanatory tone into a soft question.

title: のは〜の方だ
meaning: the one who/that ~ is X (it is X that ~)
summary: This pattern singles out which side something is really true of, out of two possibilities. のは names the situation, and 〜の方だ points to the party or option it actually applies to — 謝るのはあなたの方だ = the one who should apologize is you. It often corrects or clarifies who or which is really the case, against a mistaken assumption.
structure: Verb［plain form］／Sentence ＋ のは ＋ Noun ＋ の方だ
pitfalls: 方 here contrasts one side against another; the pattern works when there are two candidates and you are picking which one it truly applies to.
方 in this pattern reads ほう (the 'side/option' word), not かた ('person/way').

examples.ja: 悪いのは私の方だから、私が謝ります。
examples.en: The one in the wrong is me, so I'll apologize.
examples.f: ｜悪[わる]いのは｜私[わたし]の｜方[ほう]だから、｜私[わたし]が｜謝[あやま]ります。

examples.ja: 忙しいのは母の方で、父は毎日暇そうだ。
examples.en: The one who's busy is my mother; my father seems free every day.
examples.f: ｜忙[いそが]しいのは｜母[はは]の｜方[ほう]で、｜父[ちち]は｜毎日[まいにち]｜暇[ひま]そうだ。

related.note: 〜方がいい recommends one option over another; 〜のは〜の方だ points out which side something is actually true of.
nominalizing の turns a clause into a noun; this cleft uses that の to spotlight which party a statement applies to.

title: は〜くらいです
meaning: about the only ~ is; roughly the extent of it is ~
summary: は〜くらいです presents something as the modest limit of what applies — the most you can say, or the only real example. 運動と言えば、犬の散歩くらいです = as for exercise, dog-walking is about the only one. くらい here downplays the amount or degree, framing it as small or the sole case.
structure: Topic ＋ は ＋ … ＋ くらいです
pitfalls: くらい (also ぐらい) here marks a modest limit or the sole example, not an approximate number like '10 people or so'.
The tone is downplaying — 'it's only about this much'; it does not emphasize a large amount.

examples.ja: 私が作れる料理は、卵焼きくらいです。
examples.en: About the only dish I can make is rolled omelette.
examples.f: ｜私[わたし]が｜作[つく]れる｜料理[りょうり]は、｜卵焼[たまごや]きくらいです。

examples.ja: 日曜日にすることは、家でゆっくり休むくらいです。
examples.en: Roughly all I do on Sundays is rest at home.
examples.f: ｜日曜日[にちようび]にすることは、｜家[いえ]でゆっくり｜休[やす]むくらいです。

related.note: くらい・ぐらい broadly marks approximate amount or degree; は〜くらいです uses it to frame something as the modest limit.
〜しかない flatly limits things to 'nothing but'; は〜くらいです softly presents the modest extent instead.
ほど also scales degree; くらい in this pattern downplays it to 'about the only / that little'.

title: は〜で有名
meaning: X is famous for ~
summary: 〜は〜で有名です says what something is well known for — その町はお茶で有名です = that town is famous for its tea. The で marks the reason or feature it is famous for. To say 'famous for doing something', nominalize the verb with こと first: 早く走ることで有名だ.
structure: Noun ＋ は ＋ Noun ＋ で有名（だ）
Verb［plain form］＋ ことで有名（だ）
pitfalls: With で, the place is famous because of that feature; 〜が有名 instead means that feature itself is the famous thing.
For being famous for an action, turn the verb into a noun with こと: 作ることで有名, not 作るで有名.

examples.ja: この地方はおいしいお茶で有名です。
examples.en: This region is famous for its delicious tea.
examples.f: この｜地方[ちほう]はおいしいお｜茶[ちゃ]で｜有名[ゆうめい]です。

examples.ja: 彼は絵がうまいことで有名です。
examples.en: He's famous for being good at drawing.
examples.f: ｜彼[かれ]は｜絵[え]がうまいことで｜有名[ゆうめい]です。

related.note: 〜として marks the role or capacity something is known in; 〜で有名 marks the feature it is famous for.

title: は〜となっている
meaning: is (formally) set as; has become; stands as ~
summary: 〜となっている presents something as an established, official state — a rule, schedule, or settled result — in a formal, impersonal tone. 受付は10時からとなっております = reception is set from 10. It is like になっている but more formal, and is common in announcements, documents, and signs. The 〜は marks what the arrangement is about.
structure: Topic ＋ は ＋ Noun ＋ となっている
Sentence［plain form］＋ こととなっている
pitfalls: となっている is the more formal, official-sounding version of になっている, common in notices and rules.
It describes a settled state or arrangement, not an action happening right now.

examples.ja: 館内での飲食は禁止となっています。
examples.en: Eating and drinking inside the building is prohibited (by the rules).
examples.f: ｜館内[かんない]での｜飲食[いんしょく]は｜禁止[きんし]となっています。

examples.ja: 会議は来週の月曜日からとなっております。
examples.en: The meeting is set to start from next Monday.
examples.f: ｜会議[かいぎ]は｜来週[らいしゅう]の｜月曜日[げつようび]からとなっております。

related.note: なる marks a change into a new state; 〜となっている presents the resulting state as an established, formal arrangement.
ことになる settles that something has been decided; 〜となっている states the standing arrangement in formal, notice-like language.
〜ている marks an ongoing state; となっている is that state framed formally as an official arrangement.

title: ば〜のに
meaning: if only ~; it would be ... if (regret, wish) ~
summary: The ば〜のに pattern voices a regret or wish about something that is not the case — もっとお金があれば、旅行できるのに = if only I had more money, I could travel. The ば clause sets an unmet condition, and のに adds the disappointed 'but (it isn't so)' feeling. It is how you say 'if only… / it would be nice, but it isn't'.
structure: Verb［ば form］／い-adjective ＋ ければ ＋ … のに
pitfalls: The のに here carries regret or complaint about a situation that did not come true; it is not the plain 'even though' connector between two facts.
It describes something contrary to reality, so the main clause is typically a wish or an unrealized possibility.

examples.ja: もう少し安ければ、買うのに。
examples.en: If only it were a little cheaper, I'd buy it.
examples.f: もう｜少[すこ]し｜安[やす]ければ、｜買[か]うのに。

examples.ja: 天気がよければ、海に行けるのに。
examples.en: If the weather were nice, we could go to the sea (but it isn't).
examples.f: ｜天気[てんき]がよければ、｜海[うみ]に｜行[い]けるのに。

related.note: 〜ばよかった regrets a past action you wish you had taken; ば〜のに regrets a present situation that isn't so.
のに on its own means 'even though' between two real facts; ば〜のに colors an unreal condition with regret.
なら supposes a case and gives advice; ば〜のに laments a condition that is not met.

title: ば〜ほど
meaning: the more ~, the more ~
summary: ば〜ほど links two changes that rise together — 練習すればするほど上手になる = the more you practice, the better you get. You repeat the same word, first in ば-form and then in dictionary/plain form, before ほど. As the first grows, so does the second. It is the standard 'the more…, the more…' pattern.
structure: Verb［ば form］＋ Verb［dictionary form］＋ ほど
い-adjective ＋ ければ ＋ い-adjective ＋ ほど
な-adjective ＋ なら ＋ な-adjective ＋ なほど
pitfalls: Repeat the same word: 見れば見るほど, 高ければ高いほど — the ば-form, then the plain form before ほど.
For な-adjectives, the frame is 〜なら〜なほど (静かなら静かなほど); do not force them into the verb pattern.

examples.ja: この本は、読めば読むほど面白くなる。
examples.en: The more you read this book, the more interesting it gets.
examples.f: この｜本[ほん]は、｜読[よ]めば｜読[よ]むほど｜面白[おもしろ]くなる。

examples.ja: 部屋は、広ければ広いほどいいです。
examples.en: As for rooms, the bigger the better.
examples.f: ｜部屋[へや]は、｜広[ひろ]ければ｜広[ひろ]いほどいいです。

related.note: ほど by itself marks a degree or extent; ば〜ほど pairs two rising degrees into 'the more…, the more…'.

title: ばいい
meaning: should ~; it'd be good if ~; you can just ~
summary: 〜ばいい suggests that doing something is a good idea or the way to solve a problem — 分からなければ、先生に聞けばいい = if you don't understand, you can just ask the teacher. It can give advice ('you should just…'), state a solution, or express a wish (雨が止めばいい = I hope the rain stops). The ば-form carries the 'if you do it' sense and いい adds 'that would be good'.
pitfalls: Depending on context, ばいい ranges from friendly advice ('you can just…') to a slightly blunt 'just do it'; tone matters when suggesting.
〜ばよかった (past) expresses regret about what you should have done; 〜ばいい is present advice or a wish.

examples.ja: 道が分からなければ、駅の人に聞けばいいですよ。
examples.en: If you don't know the way, you can just ask someone at the station.
examples.f: ｜道[みち]が｜分[わ]からなければ、｜駅[えき]の｜人[ひと]に｜聞[き]けばいいですよ。

examples.ja: 迷ったら、地図を見ればいいです。
examples.en: If you get lost, you can just look at the map.
examples.f: ｜迷[まよ]ったら、｜地図[ちず]を｜見[み]ればいいです。

related.note: 〜方がいい compares and recommends one option; 〜ばいい points to doing something as the good move or solution.
the 〜たら conditional can replace ば here (聞いたらいい); both give advice about what to do.
〜ばよかった regrets what you should have done; 〜ばいい advises what is good to do now.

title: は言うまでもない
meaning: it goes without saying that ~; needless to say ~
summary: 〜は言うまでもない states that something is so obvious it need not be said — 健康の大切さは言うまでもない = the importance of health goes without saying. It marks the point as too self-evident to need explaining, often before adding a further point. The connective form 言うまでもなく means 'needless to say', at the head of a sentence.
structure: Noun ＋ は言うまでもない
Sentence［plain form］＋ のは言うまでもない
pitfalls: It presents something as obvious to everyone; do not use it for information that is actually new or surprising to the listener.
言うまでもなく at the head of a clause works as an adverb ('needless to say'); 〜は言うまでもない closes a statement.

examples.ja: 準備が大切なのは言うまでもない。
examples.en: It goes without saying that preparation is important.
examples.f: ｜準備[じゅんび]が｜大切[たいせつ]なのは｜言[い]うまでもない。

examples.ja: この地方の冬の寒さは言うまでもありません。
examples.en: The harshness of winter in this region goes without saying.
examples.f: この｜地方[ちほう]の｜冬[ふゆ]の｜寒[さむ]さは｜言[い]うまでもありません。

related.note: 〜までもない (N1) says an action isn't even worth doing; 言うまでもない is the set phrase 'it goes without saying'.

title: ばかりだ
meaning: keeps only getting ~ (a one-way change, usually for the worse)
summary: A dictionary-form change verb plus ばかりだ says a situation keeps moving in a single direction, with nothing to stop it — 病気は悪くなるばかりだ = the illness just keeps getting worse. It usually carries a negative, worsening tone: things go on changing one way only. The verb is a change verb in dictionary form.
pitfalls: This ばかりだ takes a dictionary-form change verb and means 'keeps heading one way (often worse)'; it differs from 〜たばかり ('just did') and from plain 〜ばかり ('only').
It leans negative — a one-way slide; 〜一方だ is close but ばかりだ stresses that nothing improves.

examples.ja: 物の値段は、上がるばかりだ。
examples.en: Prices just keep on rising.
examples.f: ｜物[もの]の｜値段[ねだん]は、｜上[あ]がるばかりだ。

examples.ja: 練習しないと、下手になるばかりですよ。
examples.en: If you don't practice, you'll only get worse.
examples.f: ｜練習[れんしゅう]しないと、｜下手[へた]になるばかりですよ。

related.note: 〜一方だ also marks a one-way change; 〜ばかりだ adds the sense that nothing stops or improves it.
〜たばかり means 'just did (moments ago)'; 〜ばかりだ with the dictionary form means a situation keeps changing one way.
〜ばかりで lists 'only this, nothing else'; 〜ばかりだ marks a steady one-way change.

title: ばかりで
meaning: only ~ and nothing else (with a negative slant) ~
summary: 〜ばかりで presents a situation as nothing but one thing, usually with a critical or dissatisfied tone about what is missing — 文句を言うばかりで、何もしない = he only complains and doesn't do anything. The ばかり limits it to that single thing, and で leads into the resulting lack or problem.
pitfalls: It carries a complaining nuance ('all it does is…, and that's the problem'); it is not a neutral 'only'.
The clause after で usually points to what is lacking or wrong as a result: 遊んでばかりで、勉強しない.

examples.ja: 弟はゲームをするばかりで、少しも勉強しない。
examples.en: My little brother does nothing but play games and won't study at all.
examples.f: ｜弟[おとうと]はゲームをするばかりで、｜少[すこ]しも｜勉強[べんきょう]しない。

examples.ja: この店は高いばかりで、あまりおいしくない。
examples.en: This restaurant is just expensive and not even that tasty.
examples.f: この｜店[みせ]は｜高[たか]いばかりで、あまりおいしくない。

related.note: 〜ばかりだ marks a one-way change; 〜ばかりで sets up 'only this' before pointing out what's missing.
〜ばかりでなく adds 'not only… but also…'; 〜ばかりで complains that there is only the one thing.
〜だけ neutrally limits things to 'only'; ばかりで adds a critical 'nothing but this' tone.

title: ばかりでなく
meaning: not only ~ but also ~
summary: 〜ばかりでなく means 'not only X but also Y', adding a second, often broader point on top of the first — 彼は英語ばかりでなく、中国語も話せる = he can speak not only English but also Chinese. The second part usually carries も ('also'). It is a slightly more formal way to say 〜だけでなく.
structure: Noun ＋ ばかりでなく ＋ … も
Verb［plain form］／い-adjective ＋ ばかりでなく
な-adjective ＋ な ＋ ばかりでなく
pitfalls: The added part often takes も ('also'): 子供ばかりでなく、大人も楽しめる.
〜だけでなく is the everyday equivalent; 〜ばかりでなく sounds a little more formal or written.

examples.ja: この公園は子供ばかりでなく、大人も楽しめます。
examples.en: This park can be enjoyed not only by children but also by adults.
examples.f: この｜公園[こうえん]は｜子供[こども]ばかりでなく、｜大人[おとな]も｜楽[たの]しめます。

examples.ja: 彼女は歌が上手なばかりでなく、ダンスもできる。
examples.en: She's not only good at singing but can also dance.
examples.f: ｜彼女[かのじょ]は｜歌[うた]が｜上手[じょうず]なばかりでなく、ダンスもできる。

synonyms.note: 〜だけでなく is the more everyday 'not only… but also…'; 〜ばかりでなく is a bit more formal.

related.note: 〜のみならず (N1) is the formal, written version of the same 'not only… but also…'.
〜ばかりで complains that there is only one thing; 〜ばかりでなく adds a second thing on top.

title: ばかりに
meaning: simply because; all because of; on account of (leading to an unwelcome result)
summary: ばかりに points to a single cause and blames an unfortunate outcome on it — 'all because of just this, that bad thing happened.' It carries a note of regret or frustration, so the result is almost always negative. Typically the clause before ばかりに is a plain-form verb, often in the past (忘れたばかりに = all because I forgot).
structure: な-adjective＋ な／Noun＋ である ＋ ばかりに
pitfalls: The result is almost always something bad or regrettable; ばかりに doesn't fit happy outcomes.
It pins the blame on one single cause, unlike a neutral から／ので — the nuance is 'only because of this one thing, unfortunately...'.

examples.ja: 少し油断したばかりに、試合に負けてしまった。
examples.en: All because I let my guard down for a moment, I ended up losing the match.
examples.f: ｜少[すこ]し｜油断[ゆだん]したばかりに、｜試合[しあい]に｜負[ま]けてしまった。

examples.ja: パスポートを忘れたばかりに、旅行に行けなかった。
examples.en: Simply because I forgot my passport, I couldn't go on the trip.
examples.f: パスポートを｜忘[わす]れたばかりに、｜旅行[りょこう]に｜行[い]けなかった。

synonyms.note: せいで also blames a cause for a bad result; ばかりに stresses that it was just this one thing that caused it.

related.note: だけに means 'precisely because' and works for good or bad results; ばかりに points to a single cause and expects a bad one.

title: は別として
meaning: setting ~ aside; apart from ~; leaving aside whether ~
summary: は別として sets one matter aside as a separate issue so you can turn to the main point — 'putting X to one side, ...'. It attaches to a noun, and with a yes/no question it becomes 〜かどうかは別として ('leaving aside whether...'). It doesn't exclude members from a group; it just brackets off a topic for now.
structure: Sentence＋ かどうか ＋ は別として
pitfalls: It brackets a topic off as a separate issue; it doesn't mean 'except for' in the sense of excluding items — that is 以外.
For a yes/no point, use 〜かどうかは別として to mean 'leaving aside whether...'.

examples.ja: 味は別として、この店は値段が安くて助かる。
examples.en: Taste aside, this shop is cheap, which is a big help.
examples.f: ｜味[あじ]は｜別[べつ]として、この｜店[みせ]は｜値段[ねだん]が｜安[やす]くて｜助[たす]かる。

examples.ja: 参加するかどうかは別として、まず話だけ聞いてみよう。
examples.en: Leaving aside whether we'll join, let's first just hear them out.
examples.f: ｜参加[さんか]するかどうかは｜別[べつ]として、まず｜話[はなし]だけ｜聞[き]いてみよう。

synonyms.note: はともかく is very close in meaning ('setting aside'); は別として leans a little more on treating the matter as a distinct, separate issue.

related.note: 以外 excludes items from a set ('other than X'); は別として brackets a topic off to focus elsewhere.
ならともかく means 'if it were X, fine, but...'; は別として simply sets X aside without that conditional contrast.

title: はもちろん
meaning: ~ of course, and also ~; not to mention ~; not only ~ but also ~
summary: はもちろん presents X as the obvious, taken-for-granted case and then adds a further, more noteworthy item Y, usually marked with も — 'X goes without saying, and Y as well.' It attaches to a noun and often appears as はもちろんのこと. The point being added after it is the one that carries the real information.
structure: Noun＋ はもちろん（のこと）、〜も
pitfalls: The item before はもちろん is the expected/obvious one; the item added afterward (often with も) is the more surprising or noteworthy point.
It attaches to a noun; for 'not only... but also' after verbs or full clauses, だけでなく is the more general pattern.

examples.ja: この料理は子供はもちろん、大人にも大人気だ。
examples.en: This dish is hugely popular not only with kids but with adults too.
examples.f: この｜料理[りょうり]は｜子供[こども]はもちろん、｜大人[おとな]にも｜大人気[だいにんき]だ。

examples.ja: 彼は英語はもちろん、フランス語も話せる。
examples.en: He can speak French as well as English, of course.
examples.f: ｜彼[かれ]は｜英語[えいご]はもちろん、フランス｜語[ご]も｜話[はな]せる。

synonyms.note: だけでなく ('not only') is more general and attaches to verbs and clauses; はもちろん takes a noun and frames it as the obvious case.

related.note: はおろか is stronger ('let alone') and usually pairs with a negative or extreme; はもちろん is neutral and simply adds a second item.
もまた marks 'also, too' for one added item; はもちろん frames the first as obvious before adding the notable one.

title: 再び
meaning: again; once more; a second time
summary: 再び is an adverb meaning 'again' or 'once more'. It is more formal and written than the everyday また, and often appears in narration, news, or serious contexts. Place it before the verb or clause that repeats.
pitfalls: 再び is formal and written; in casual conversation people normally say また.
It is an adverb meaning 'once more'; don't confuse it with 二度と, which pairs with a negative to mean 'never again'.

examples.ja: 長い議論のあと、会議は再び始まった。
examples.en: After a long discussion, the meeting began once more.
examples.f: ｜長[なが]い｜議論[ぎろん]のあと、｜会議[かいぎ]は｜再[ふたた]び｜始[はじ]まった。

examples.ja: 彼とは卒業以来、再び会うことはなかった。
examples.en: I never met him again after graduation.
examples.f: ｜彼[かれ]とは｜卒業[そつぎょう]｜以来[いらい]、｜再[ふたた]び｜会[あ]うことはなかった。

related.note: また can mean everyday 'again' as well as 'moreover'; 再び is the more formal, written word specifically for 'once more'.
もう一度 means 'one more time' as a fresh repetition; 再び is a single adverb for 'once more', often after a long gap.

title: ふと
meaning: suddenly; without thinking; a thought or glance crossing one's mind unbidden
summary: ふと is an adverb for something that happens suddenly and without intention — especially a thought, feeling, or glance that crosses your mind on its own. 'It just occurred to me...', 'I happened to glance up...'. It pairs naturally with verbs of noticing, thinking, and looking.
pitfalls: ふと goes with verbs of thinking or noticing (思う, 見る, 思い出す); it isn't for a sudden loud physical event — for that use 急に or 突然.
It carries no sense of will: the thought or glance comes unbidden, not by choice.

examples.ja: ふと空を見上げると、大きな虹が出ていた。
examples.en: When I happened to glance up at the sky, a big rainbow was out.
examples.f: ふと｜空[そら]を｜見上[みあ]げると、｜大[おお]きな｜虹[にじ]が｜出[で]ていた。

examples.ja: 昔のことをふと思い出して、なつかしくなった。
examples.en: A memory of the old days suddenly came to me, and I felt nostalgic.
examples.f: ｜昔[むかし]のことをふと｜思い出[おもいだ]して、なつかしくなった。

related.note: つい is doing something unintentionally despite yourself; ふと is a thought or glance arising on its own, with no action you 'gave in' to.
いきなり is an abrupt event with no warning; ふと is quieter — something gently crossing your mind.

title: ぶりに
meaning: for the first time in (a span of time); after an interval of ~
summary: ぶり attaches to a length of time and says that much time passed before something happened again — 三年ぶりに = for the first time in three years. It highlights the gap since the last time the thing occurred. Often followed by に before a verb.
pitfalls: It needs a span of time (三年ぶり), not a point in time; it measures how long it had been.
ぶり highlights the interval since the last occurrence; 以来 instead marks the starting point from which something has continued.

examples.ja: 十年ぶりに高校の友達に会った。
examples.en: I met a friend from high school for the first time in ten years.
examples.f: ｜十[じゅう]｜年[ねん]ぶりに｜高校[こうこう]の｜友達[ともだち]に｜会[あ]った。

examples.ja: 二年ぶりに海外旅行に行った。
examples.en: I went abroad for the first time in two years.
examples.f: ｜二[に]｜年[ねん]ぶりに｜海外[かいがい]｜旅行[りょこう]に｜行[い]った。

related.note: て以来 marks the point since which a state has held ('ever since'); ぶり measures the length of the gap before something recurs.

title: ふりをする
meaning: to pretend; to act as if; to put on an act of ~
summary: ふりをする means to pretend or put on an act — to behave as if something were true when it isn't. 寝ているふりをする = pretend to be asleep; 知らないふりをする = pretend not to know. Verbs and い-adjectives attach plainly, while nouns and な-adjectives take の／な first.
structure: Verb［plain form］／い-adjective＋ ふりをする
な-adjective＋ な／Noun＋ の ＋ ふりをする
pitfalls: Use the ない form to pretend NOT to do something: 気づかないふりをする = pretend not to notice.
Nouns and な-adjectives take の／な before ふり: 病気のふりをする, 元気なふりをする.

examples.ja: 道で先生に会ったが、気づかないふりをした。
examples.en: I ran into my teacher on the street but pretended not to notice.
examples.f: ｜道[みち]で｜先生[せんせい]に｜会[あ]ったが、｜気[き]づかないふりをした。

examples.ja: 弟は寝ているふりをして、こっそり話を聞いていた。
examples.en: My little brother pretended to be asleep and was secretly listening to us.
examples.f: ｜弟[おとうと]は｜寝[ね]ているふりをして、こっそり｜話[はなし]を｜聞[き]いていた。

related.note: かのように describes an action as if something were the case; ふりをする is deliberately faking a state or behavior.
まるで sets up a 'just like' comparison; ふりをする is putting on a false act on purpose.

title: べきだ
meaning: should; ought to (the right or proper thing to do)
summary: べきだ says something is the right, proper, or expected thing to do — a firm sense of what one ought to do, based on principle or common sense. It attaches to the dictionary form of a verb. With する, both するべき and すべき are used.
structure: する → するべき／すべき
pitfalls: べきだ is stronger and more principled than 方がいい; it states what is right, not just a gentle suggestion.
Don't use べき for unavoidable rules or natural necessity ('you must be over 18') — that is なければならない; べき is about what is proper.
With する, both するべき and すべき are accepted.

examples.ja: 約束したのだから、最後まで責任を持つべきだ。
examples.en: Since you made a promise, you should take responsibility to the end.
examples.f: ｜約束[やくそく]したのだから、｜最後[さいご]まで｜責任[せきにん]を｜持[も]つべきだ。

examples.ja: 体調が悪いなら、無理をせず休むべきだよ。
examples.en: If you're not feeling well, you should rest instead of pushing yourself.
examples.f: ｜体調[たいちょう]が｜悪[わる]いなら、｜無理[むり]をせず｜休[やす]むべきだよ。

synonyms.note: 方がいい is a softer 'you'd better'; べきだ is a firmer statement of what is right or proper.

antonyms.note: べきではない is the negative — 'should not', the improper thing to do.

related.note: なければならない is unavoidable obligation ('must'); べきだ is about what is right or advisable.
はずだ is 'ought to be' as an expectation about facts; べきだ is 'ought to do' as a judgment about proper action.

title: べきではない
meaning: should not; ought not to (it's not the right thing to do)
summary: べきではない is the negative of べきだ — it says something is not the right or proper thing to do. It attaches to the dictionary form of a verb; casual speech uses べきじゃない. The past form べきではなかった expresses regret ('I shouldn't have...').
structure: Verb［dictionary form］＋ べきではない（べきじゃない）
pitfalls: The negative sits on べき, not on the main verb: 言うべきではない = 'shouldn't say' (dictionary-form verb + べきではない).
The past form べきではなかった means 'shouldn't have...' and voices regret.

examples.ja: 人の日記を勝手に読むべきではない。
examples.en: You shouldn't read someone's diary without permission.
examples.f: ｜人[ひと]の｜日記[にっき]を｜勝手[かって]に｜読[よ]むべきではない。

examples.ja: 相手の気持ちを考えず、そんなことを言うべきではなかった。
examples.en: I shouldn't have said such a thing without considering their feelings.
examples.f: ｜相手[あいて]の｜気持[きも]ちを｜考[かんが]えず、そんなことを｜言[い]うべきではなかった。

antonyms.note: べきだ is the affirmative — 'should do', the proper action.

related.note: てはいけない is a flat prohibition ('must not'); べきではない is a judgment that doing it is not right.
な after a verb is a blunt 'don't'; べきではない is a more reasoned 'you shouldn't'.

title: 別に〜ない
meaning: not particularly; not really; nothing in particular
summary: 別に leans on a following negative to mean 'not especially' or 'not really' — 別に嫌いじゃない = 'I don't particularly dislike it.' It's often used to play down or brush off, saying nothing stands out. As a bare one-word reply (別に), it can sound curt.
pitfalls: 別に in this sense needs a following negative to mean 'not especially'; used alone as a reply ('別に'), it can sound curt or evasive.
This is different from the ordinary 別に meaning 'separately' — here it is specifically 別に...ない.

examples.ja: 「どうしたの?」「別に何もないよ。」
examples.en: "What's wrong?" "Nothing in particular."
examples.f: 「どうしたの?」「｜別[べつ]に｜何[なに]もないよ。」

examples.ja: この映画は別に面白くなかった。
examples.en: This movie wasn't particularly interesting.
examples.f: この｜映画[えいが]は｜別[べつ]に｜面白[おもしろ]くなかった。

synonyms.note: あまり〜ない means 'not very'; 別に〜ない adds the nuance of 'nothing in particular / no special reason'.

related.note: 全く〜ない is a total 'not at all'; 別に〜ない is a milder 'not especially'.

title: ほど
meaning: to the extent that; so ~ that; about (an amount)
summary: ほど marks a degree or extent — it sets a vivid yardstick for how far a state goes: 立てないほど疲れた = 'so tired I couldn't stand.' The clause before ほど paints how extreme the situation is. After a number, ほど means 'about' (三十分ほど), much like くらい.
pitfalls: ほど often sets a striking measure for a degree (死ぬほど疲れた = 'dead tired'); the part before ほど shows how extreme the state is.
After a number, ほど means 'about/approximately' (三十分ほど), overlapping with くらい.

examples.ja: 立てないほど足が疲れてしまった。
examples.en: My legs got so tired that I couldn't stand.
examples.f: ｜立[た]てないほど｜足[あし]が｜疲[つか]れてしまった。

examples.ja: 泣きたいほど嬉しかった。
examples.en: I was so happy I could have cried.
examples.f: ｜泣[な]きたいほど｜嬉[うれ]しかった。

synonyms.note: くらい／ぐらい also marks extent and approximate amount and often swaps in for ほど; ほど is favored for a striking upper-limit yardstick.

related.note: ば〜ほど is 'the more... the more'; plain ほど here marks a single degree or extent.
ほど〜ない uses the same word in a comparison to mean 'not as... as'.

title: ほど〜ない
meaning: not as ~ as; not to the extent of ~
summary: In 〜ほど〜ない, the noun before ほど is a standard you fall short of: A は B ほど〜ない = 'A is not as ... as B.' B is the higher one, and A doesn't reach it. It always ends in a negative.
pitfalls: The item after ほど is the higher standard: A は B ほど〜ない means A falls short of B, so B is the greater one.
It requires a negative ending; drop the negative and ほど no longer means 'not as... as'.

examples.ja: 今年の夏は去年ほど暑くない。
examples.en: This summer isn't as hot as last year.
examples.f: ｜今年[ことし]の｜夏[なつ]は｜去年[きょねん]ほど｜暑[あつ]くない。

examples.ja: 数学は思っていたほど難しくなかった。
examples.en: Math wasn't as hard as I'd thought.
examples.f: ｜数学[すうがく]は｜思[おも]っていたほど｜難[むずか]しくなかった。

related.note: より states which side is more ('A is more... than B'); ほど〜ない says A falls short of B.
Plain ほど marks a degree or extent; the negative pattern ほど〜ない turns it into a comparison.

title: まさか
meaning: no way; surely not; you must be joking; don't tell me ~
summary: まさか flags something as too unexpected or unbelievable to be true — 'surely not', 'don't tell me...'. It often teams up with 〜とは or 〜なんて and a tone of surprise. As a standalone reply, まさか! means 'No way! / You're kidding!'.
structure: まさか ＋ Sentence（〜とは／〜なんて／〜ない）
pitfalls: まさか signals disbelief at something unexpected; it commonly pairs with 〜とは or 〜なんて and a surprised tone.
On its own, まさか! is a reply meaning 'No way! / You're kidding!'.

examples.ja: まさか彼が犯人だったとは、思ってもみなかった。
examples.en: I never dreamed that he was the culprit.
examples.f: まさか｜彼[かれ]が｜犯人[はんにん]だったとは、｜思[おも]ってもみなかった。

examples.ja: まさかこんな所で君に会うなんて、驚いたよ。
examples.en: Fancy meeting you in a place like this — I'm amazed.
examples.f: まさかこんな｜所[ところ]で｜君[きみ]に｜会[あ]うなんて、｜驚[おどろ]いたよ。

related.note: はずがない is a reasoned 'there's no way it's so'; まさか is a gut reaction of disbelief at something unexpected.
わけがない flatly denies a possibility on logical grounds; まさか voices surprised doubt, often before it turns out to be true.
とは marks a surprising fact; まさか often introduces the sentence that ends in 〜とは.

title: 又〜も
meaning: and also ~; moreover ~; ~ as well
summary: In this pattern また works as 'moreover / also', introducing a further fact, and a later も marks that added item as one more thing that holds too — 彼は医者であり、また作家でもある = 'He is a doctor, and also a writer.' It stacks a second point onto the first and is common in explanatory or written style.
pitfalls: Here また means 'moreover/also' and pairs with a later も to add a second point; this differs from また alone meaning 'again'.
It has an explanatory, somewhat written tone; in casual speech それに or a plain 〜も often does the same job.

examples.ja: 彼は医者であり、また作家でもある。
examples.en: He is a doctor, and also a writer.
examples.f: ｜彼[かれ]は｜医者[いしゃ]であり、また｜作家[さっか]でもある。

examples.ja: この温泉は体にいいし、またリラックスもできる。
examples.en: This hot spring is good for your health, and you can also relax.
examples.f: この｜温泉[おんせん]は｜体[からだ]にいいし、またリラックスもできる。

related.note: もまた marks one item as 'also, too'; また〜も leads with また ('moreover') and closes the added point with も.
それに ('besides, on top of that') adds a further point conversationally; また〜も does so in a more explanatory register.

title: 全く〜ない
meaning: not at all; completely not; not in the slightest
summary: 全く before a negative emphasizes a total, 100% denial — 全く分からない = 'I don't understand at all.' It is stronger than あまり〜ない ('not very'). Note that 全く can also precede a positive word to mean 'utterly/entirely' (全く同じ = exactly the same); the 'not at all' sense needs the following negative.
pitfalls: 全く〜ない is a total, 100% negation — stronger than あまり〜ない ('not very').
Before a positive word, 全く means 'utterly/entirely' (全く同じ = exactly the same); the 'not at all' sense depends on the following negative.

examples.ja: 彼の言っていることが全く分からない。
examples.en: I don't understand what he's saying at all.
examples.f: ｜彼[かれ]の｜言[い]っていることが｜全[まった]く｜分[わ]からない。

examples.ja: お金が全くないので、今月は旅行できない。
examples.en: I have no money at all, so I can't travel this month.
examples.f: お｜金[かね]が｜全[まった]くないので、｜今月[こんげつ]は｜旅行[りょこう]できない。

related.note: あまり〜ない is a partial 'not very'; 全く〜ない is a total 'not at all'.
別に〜ない is a mild 'not especially'; 全く〜ない is the strong, complete negation.
決して〜ない is 'never / by no means', stressing firm refusal; 全く〜ない stresses that the amount or degree is zero.

title: まるで
meaning: just like; as if; as though
summary: まるで sets up a vivid 'just like' comparison and normally finishes with ようだ／みたい／のように — まるで夢のようだ = 'It's just like a dream.' Leaving off that ending sounds incomplete. With a negative ending, まるで〜ない instead means 'not at all' (まるで違う = completely different).
structure: まるで ＋ 〜ようだ／みたいだ／のように
pitfalls: まるで normally pairs with a closing ようだ／みたい／のように; without that ending the sentence feels unfinished.
With a negative, まるで〜ない means 'not at all' (まるで違う = completely different), so the ending decides the meaning.

examples.ja: 彼女の部屋はまるでお店のようにきれいだ。
examples.en: Her room is as pretty as a shop.
examples.f: ｜彼女[かのじょ]の｜部屋[へや]はまるでお｜店[みせ]のようにきれいだ。

examples.ja: その子はまるで大人みたいな話し方をする。
examples.en: That child talks just like an adult.
examples.f: その｜子[こ]はまるで｜大人[おとな]みたいな｜話し方[はなしかた]をする。

related.note: ようだ ('seems like / is like') is the ending まるで usually leads into; まるで intensifies it to 'just like'.
みたい is the casual 'like'; まるで often teams with it for an emphatic 'just like'.
かのように is a more literary 'as if'; まるで is the everyday adverb that sets up the same comparison.

title: 〜み
meaning: -ness; the quality or felt sense of ~ (turns an adjective into a noun)
summary: 〜み attaches to an adjective stem to make a noun for the quality itself, often something you can feel or sense — 痛み = pain, 深み = depth, 温かみ = warmth. It works with a limited set of adjectives, not every one, and tends to name a felt quality rather than a measurable amount.
pitfalls: 〜み names a felt quality (痛み, 温かみ) and attaches only to a limited set of adjectives, not freely to all of them.
Compare 〜さ, which turns almost any adjective into a noun for degree (高さ = height); 〜み is less productive and more about a sensed quality.

examples.ja: 傷の痛みが少しずつやわらいできた。
examples.en: The pain from the wound has gradually eased.
examples.f: ｜傷[きず]の｜痛[いた]みが｜少[すこ]しずつやわらいできた。

examples.ja: この小説には深みがあって、何度も読みたくなる。
examples.en: This novel has depth, which makes you want to read it again and again.
examples.f: この｜小説[しょうせつ]には｜深[ふか]みがあって、｜何[なん]｜度[ど]も｜読[よ]みたくなる。

synonyms.note: 〜さ freely makes a degree noun from almost any adjective (高さ, 大きさ); 〜み names a felt quality and joins only certain adjectives.

related.note: 〜げ makes an adjective for how something looks or seems (寂しげ = looking lonely); 〜み makes a noun for the quality itself.
〜がり labels a person prone to a feeling (寒がり); 〜み names the quality or sensation, not a person.

title: 向き
meaning: suited to; suitable for; well-matched to (a group or purpose)
summary: N向き says something happens to suit or is convenient for a certain group or purpose — 初心者向き = suited to beginners. It suggests a natural fit rather than deliberate design. 向き also literally means 'facing (a direction)', as in 南向き (south-facing).
pitfalls: 向き suggests something naturally suits a group without being made for it; 向け means it was deliberately created or aimed at that target.
向き also literally means 'facing a direction' (南向き = south-facing).

examples.ja: この辞書は初心者向きで、説明が分かりやすい。
examples.en: This dictionary is suited to beginners; its explanations are easy to understand.
examples.f: この｜辞書[じしょ]は｜初心者[しょしんしゃ]｜向[む]きで、｜説明[せつめい]が｜分[わ]かりやすい。

examples.ja: あの映画は大人向きで、子供には少し難しい。
examples.en: That movie is geared to adults; it's a bit hard for children.
examples.f: あの｜映画[えいが]は｜大人[おとな]｜向[む]きで、｜子供[こども]には｜少[すこ]し｜難[むずか]しい。

related.note: 向け is deliberately made or aimed at a target; 向き is just a natural fit for that group.

title: 向け
meaning: intended for; aimed at; made for (a target audience)
summary: N向け says something was deliberately made, designed, or aimed at a particular target — 子供向けの番組 = a program made for children; 海外向けに販売する = sell for overseas markets. Unlike 向き, it stresses intentional targeting. It is often followed by の or に.
pitfalls: 向け stresses deliberate targeting ('made for'); 向き just says something happens to suit that group.
It is usually followed by の or に: 子供向けの番組, 海外向けに販売する.

examples.ja: この雑誌は若い女性向けに作られている。
examples.en: This magazine is made for young women.
examples.f: この｜雑誌[ざっし]は｜若[わか]い｜女性[じょせい]｜向[む]けに｜作[つく]られている。

examples.ja: 会社は海外向けの新しい商品を開発した。
examples.en: The company developed a new product aimed at overseas markets.
examples.f: ｜会社[かいしゃ]は｜海外[かいがい]｜向[む]けの｜新[あたら]しい｜商品[しょうひん]を｜開発[かいはつ]した。

related.note: 向き is a natural fit ('suits beginners'); 向け is deliberate targeting ('made for beginners').
にとって marks whose standpoint something matters from; 向け marks who a product or content is aimed at.

title: むしろ
meaning: rather; if anything; sooner (than the other option)
summary: むしろ weighs two possibilities and picks the second, less obvious one as the better fit — 'not so much A, rather B'. It often follows 〜より or 〜というより: 都会よりむしろ田舎がいい = 'I'd sooner have the countryside than the city.' It compares and prefers, rather than simply replacing one thing with another.
pitfalls: むしろ picks the second, less obvious choice as the better fit; it often follows 〜より or 〜というより.
It compares and prefers; it doesn't mean 'instead / in place of' the way 代わりに (kawari-ni) does.

examples.ja: 都会に住むより、むしろ田舎で静かに暮らしたい。
examples.en: Rather than living in the city, I'd sooner live quietly in the countryside.
examples.f: ｜都会[とかい]に｜住[す]むより、むしろ｜田舎[いなか]で｜静[しず]かに｜暮[く]らしたい。

examples.ja: 彼は怒っているというより、むしろ悲しそうだった。
examples.en: Rather than angry, he seemed, if anything, sad.
examples.f: ｜彼[かれ]は｜怒[おこ]っているというより、むしろ｜悲[かな]しそうだった。

related.note: というより ('rather than saying') rephrases a description; むしろ often follows it to point to the option you'd prefer.
より marks the standard being compared against; むしろ builds on that to pick the preferred side.
逆に flips to the opposite ('on the contrary'); むしろ leans toward a preferred alternative, not necessarily an opposite.

title: めったに〜ない
meaning: rarely; hardly ever (paired with a negative)
summary: めったに is an adverb that teams up with a negative ending to say something almost never happens — めったに怒らない = hardly ever gets angry. The negative ない／ません is obligatory; めったに carries the 'rarely' meaning only when it points at a negative predicate.
pitfalls: めったに must land on a negative ending; 「めったに行く」 is wrong — say めったに行かない.
It means 'almost never', stronger than あまり〜ない ('not very often').

examples.ja: 父はめったにお酒を飲みません。
examples.en: My father hardly ever drinks alcohol.
examples.f: ｜父[ちち]はめったにお｜酒[さけ]を｜飲[の]みません。

examples.ja: 彼はめったに人の悪口を言わない。
examples.en: He almost never speaks ill of others.
examples.f: ｜彼[かれ]はめったに｜人[ひと]の｜悪口[わるぐち]を｜言[い]わない。

synonyms.note: あまり〜ない is 'not very often'; めったに〜ない is much stronger — nearly never.

related.note: なかなか〜ない is 'not easily / not for a while'; めったに〜ない is about low frequency.
決して〜ない is an absolute 'never (I promise)'; めったに〜ない leaves room for rare exceptions.

title: も〜ば〜も
meaning: both ~ and ~; (with negatives) neither ~ nor ~
