summary: も〜ば〜も lists two parallel facts about one topic, using the ば conditional on the first predicate — 歌も歌えばギターも弾く = both sings and plays guitar. With negatives it becomes 'neither...nor'. It piles up matching items rather than stating a real condition.
structure: Noun ＋ も ＋ Verb／い-adjective［ば form］、Noun ＋ も 〜
pitfalls: The middle predicate takes ば form (多ければ, なければ); it is a listing device, not a genuine 'if'.
In a negative frame it reads as 'neither ~ nor ~': お金もなければ時間もない = have neither money nor time.

examples.ja: この店は品数も多ければ、値段も安い。
examples.en: This shop has a wide selection and low prices too.
examples.f: この｜店[みせ]は｜品数[しなかず]も｜多[おお]ければ、｜値段[ねだん]も｜安[やす]い。

examples.ja: 今はお金もなければ時間もない。
examples.en: Right now I have neither money nor time.
examples.f: ｜今[いま]はお｜金[かね]もなければ｜時間[じかん]もない。

related.note: だけでなく adds a second point onto a first; も〜ば〜も sets two items side by side as a balanced pair.
ばかりでなく is 'not only...but also'; も〜ば〜も simply lists two coexisting facts.

title: もしかしたら
meaning: perhaps; maybe; possibly (it could be that ~)
summary: もしかしたら opens a sentence to raise something as a possibility you are unsure about, and it usually pairs with かもしれない at the end — もしかしたら雨かもしれない = maybe it will rain. Variants もしかすると／もしかして carry the same feel.
structure: もしかしたら ＋ Sentence ＋ かもしれない／だろう
pitfalls: It normally leads to かもしれない／だろう, not a flat assertion; it marks a guess, not a certainty.
It is softer and less confident than おそらく ('most likely').

examples.ja: もしかしたら、彼はもう家に帰ったかもしれない。
examples.en: Maybe he's already gone home.
examples.f: もしかしたら、｜彼[かれ]はもう｜家[いえ]に｜帰[かえ]ったかもしれない。

examples.ja: もしかしたら、明日は雪になるかもしれません。
examples.en: Perhaps it will snow tomorrow.
examples.f: もしかしたら、｜明日[あした]は｜雪[ゆき]になるかもしれません。

synonyms.note: かもしれない is the sentence-ending 'might' that もしかしたら usually sets up at the front.

related.note: おそらく leans toward 'most likely'; もしかしたら is a more tentative 'perhaps, just possibly'.
でしょう offers a fairly confident guess; もしかしたら flags mere possibility.

title: もしも〜たら
meaning: if (supposing) ~; in the (unlikely) event that ~
summary: もしも strengthens the 'supposing' feel of a following conditional, usually たら — もしも宝くじが当たったら = if I ever won the lottery. It leans toward imagined or unlikely situations and is a more emphatic version of plain もし.
structure: もしも ＋ Verb／い-adjective［たら form］、Sentence
pitfalls: もしも only adds emphasis; the real condition is carried by たら (or なら／ば).
It tilts toward hypothetical or improbable scenarios, so it can sound dramatic in an everyday 'if'.

examples.ja: もしも宝くじが当たったら、世界中を旅行したい。
examples.en: If I ever won the lottery, I'd want to travel all over the world.
examples.f: もしも｜宝[たから]くじが｜当[あ]たったら、｜世界中[せかいじゅう]を｜旅行[りょこう]したい。

examples.ja: もしも困ったことがあったら、いつでも連絡してください。
examples.en: If you ever run into any trouble, contact me anytime.
examples.f: もしも｜困[こま]ったことがあったら、いつでも｜連絡[れんらく]してください。

synonyms.note: たら is the plain conditional; もしも just adds an emphatic 'supposing' at the front.

related.note: なら responds to a supposed premise; もしも〜たら sets up a hypothetical event and its result.
場合は is 'in the case that', more neutral and formal; もしも〜たら feels more hypothetical.

title: もっとも
meaning: that said; but then; though (adding a qualification)
summary: As a conjunction, もっとも starts a follow-up remark that partly limits what was just said — '..., though' / 'that said, ...'. It is often rounded off with が／けれど. This もっとも is different from the superlative adverb もっとも ('the most').
structure: Sentence。 ＋ もっとも、 ＋ Sentence（＋ が／けれど）
pitfalls: This もっとも joins sentences as a conjunction; don't confuse it with the adverb もっとも meaning 'the most'.
It qualifies or narrows the previous statement rather than flatly contradicting it.

examples.ja: 彼は毎日ジムに通っている。もっとも、体重はまだ変わっていないそうだが。
examples.en: He goes to the gym every day. That said, apparently his weight still hasn't changed.
examples.f: ｜彼[かれ]は｜毎日[まいにち]ジムに｜通[かよ]っている。もっとも、｜体重[たいじゅう]はまだ｜変[か]わっていないそうだが。

examples.ja: この店は安くておいしい。もっとも、いつも混んでいるけれど。
examples.en: This place is cheap and tasty — though it's always crowded.
examples.f: この｜店[みせ]は｜安[やす]くておいしい。もっとも、いつも｜混[こ]んでいるけれど。

related.note: ところが introduces an unexpected turn; もっとも adds a limiting side-note to what you just said.
ものの concedes 'although' within one sentence; もっとも opens a fresh qualifying sentence.

title: もの・もん
meaning: because ~ (a reason given emotionally, often as an excuse)
summary: Sentence-final もの (casual もん) gives a reason with feeling — justifying, excusing, or grumbling. It often answers a 'why?' and pairs with だって at the start of the reply. The tone is casual and can sound childish or defensive.
pitfalls: This is emotive, casual reason-giving; it's out of place in polite or formal speech.
It frequently follows a だって opener: 「だって〜だもん」.

examples.ja: 「どうして食べないの？」「だって、おなかがいっぱいだもん。」
examples.en: "Why aren't you eating?" "Because I'm full, that's why."
examples.f: 「どうして｜食[た]べないの？」「だって、おなかがいっぱいだもん。」

examples.ja: もう子供じゃないもの、ひとりで行けるよ。
examples.en: I'm not a child anymore, so I can go by myself.
examples.f: もう｜子供[こども]じゃないもの、ひとりで｜行[い]けるよ。

synonyms.note: ものだから also gives a heartfelt reason but connects mid-sentence; もの／もん closes the sentence.
もので is a softer, more polite excuse-giving connective; もん is blunter and more casual.

related.note: から is a neutral 'because'; もの／もん adds an emotional, self-justifying color.

title: ものだ
meaning: that's just how it is; one naturally does ~ (general truth or strong feeling)
summary: ものだ attaches to plain form to present something as a general, essential truth or the way things naturally are — 時間が経つのは早いものだ = time really does fly. It can also voice a heartfelt exclamation. It frames the idea as widely shared, not a one-off fact.
pitfalls: It states a general/essential truth or deep feeling, not one specific event; for a single concrete fact use plain だ.
Past 〜たものだ ('used to do') and 〜ものだから ('because') are separate patterns.

examples.ja: 年を取ると、昔のことが懐かしく思えるものだ。
examples.en: As you get older, you naturally come to feel nostalgic about the past.
examples.f: ｜年[とし]を｜取[と]ると、｜昔[むかし]のことが｜懐[なつ]かしく｜思[おも]えるものだ。

examples.ja: 子供は元気に遊ぶものだ。
examples.en: Children are meant to play with lots of energy — that's just how kids are.
examples.f: ｜子供[こども]は｜元気[げんき]に｜遊[あそ]ぶものだ。

related.note: 〜たものだ recalls a past habit ('used to'); ものだ states a timeless general truth.
〜ものではない says something is 'not to be done'; ものだ states how things naturally are.
〜ことだ gives direct advice ('you should'); ものだ describes a general truth or tendency.

title: ようがない
meaning: there's no way to ~; it's impossible to ~ (no means available)
summary: The ます-stem plus ようがない says there is no method or means to do something, so it simply can't be done — 連絡しようがない = there's no way to get in touch. It stresses a missing means rather than a lack of ability. Also written 〜ようもない.
structure: Verb［stem］＋ ようがない／ようもない
pitfalls: Attach it to the stem: 直しようがない, not 直すようがない.
It means 'no means to do it'; 'no way that [it's true]' (logical) is わけがない.

examples.ja: 住所がわからないので、手紙を送りようがない。
examples.en: I don't know the address, so there's no way to send the letter.
examples.f: ｜住所[じゅうしょ]がわからないので、｜手紙[てがみ]を｜送[おく]りようがない。

examples.ja: こんなに壊れていては、もう直しようがない。
examples.en: It's broken this badly — there's just no way to fix it now.
examples.f: こんなに｜壊[こわ]れていては、もう｜直[なお]しようがない。

related.note: わけがない denies that something could be true (logic); ようがない denies there's any means to do it.
ことができる is 'able to do'; ようがない is the flat 'no way to do it at all'.

title: ようとしたが
meaning: was about to / tried to ~, but ~ (and it didn't work out)
summary: The past volitional 〜ようとした plus が／けど marks that you were on the verge of doing something, or attempted it, but were interrupted or it failed — 出ようとしたが = I was about to leave, but... Because of が, a thwarted outcome usually follows.
structure: Verb［volitional］＋ とした ＋ が／けれど、Sentence
pitfalls: Built on the volitional (出よう, 言おう), not the dictionary form.
With が, an interrupted or failed result normally follows, so the subject is someone who meant to act.

examples.ja: 電車に乗ろうとしたが、目の前でドアが閉まってしまった。
examples.en: I was about to get on the train, but the doors closed right in front of me.
examples.f: ｜電車[でんしゃ]に｜乗[の]ろうとしたが、｜目[め]の｜前[まえ]でドアが｜閉[し]まってしまった。

examples.ja: 彼に本当のことを言おうとしたが、勇気が出なかった。
examples.en: I tried to tell him the truth, but I couldn't work up the courage.
examples.f: ｜彼[かれ]に｜本当[ほんとう]のことを｜言[い]おうとしたが、｜勇気[ゆうき]が｜出[で]なかった。

related.note: ようとする is the base 'try to / be about to'; ようとしたが adds a past attempt that fell through.
ところだった is 'was just about to (nearly)'; ようとしたが centers on an attempt that got blocked.
ようとしない is 'won't even try'; ようとしたが is 'did try, but failed'.

title: ようとしない
meaning: won't (even) try to ~; makes no effort to ~
summary: The negative of 〜ようとする: 〜ようとしない says someone shows no willingness to do something, often with a note of criticism or frustration — 話を聞こうとしない = won't even listen. It usually describes another person's stubborn refusal to act.
pitfalls: Uses the volitional stem (食べよう, 聞こう), not the dictionary form.
It implies they could act but choose not to — stronger than a plain 〜ない (which just states they don't).

examples.ja: 子供が野菜を食べようとしない。
examples.en: The child won't even try to eat his vegetables.
examples.f: ｜子供[こども]が｜野菜[やさい]を｜食[た]べようとしない。

examples.ja: 彼は私の話を聞こうとしなかった。
examples.en: He wouldn't even try to listen to what I had to say.
examples.f: ｜彼[かれ]は｜私[わたし]の｜話[はなし]を｜聞[き]こうとしなかった。

antonyms.note: ようとする is making the effort to do something; ようとしない is refusing to make any effort.

related.note: ようとしたが is 'tried but failed'; ようとしない is 'won't even attempt'.

title: ようとする
meaning: to try to ~; to be about to ~ (on the verge of)
summary: The volitional plus とする means either making an effort to do something (立ち上がろうとする = try to stand up) or being right on the point of something happening (日が暮れようとする = the sun is about to set). Context decides which reading applies.
pitfalls: Built on the volitional (帰ろう, 出よう), not the dictionary form.
Different from 〜と思う (stating an intention) and 〜つもり (a settled plan): ようとする is the attempt or the imminent moment itself.

examples.ja: 赤ちゃんが立ち上がろうとしている。
examples.en: The baby is trying to stand up.
examples.f: ｜赤[あか]ちゃんが｜立ち上[たちあ]がろうとしている。

examples.ja: 家を出ようとしたとき、電話が鳴った。
examples.en: Just as I was about to leave the house, the phone rang.
examples.f: ｜家[いえ]を｜出[で]ようとしたとき、｜電話[でんわ]が｜鳴[な]った。

antonyms.note: ようとしない is the negative — refusing to make the attempt that ようとする describes.

related.note: 〜ようと思う states an intention you've formed; ようとする is actually attempting or being on the verge.
〜るところだ is 'about to do' as a scheduled next step; ようとする can also mean caught in the very moment of starting.

title: ような気がする
meaning: to have a feeling that ~; it somehow feels like ~
summary: 〜ような気がする expresses a vague, intuitive impression — you sense something without solid proof. 忘れ物をしたような気がする = I have a feeling I forgot something. It is softer and more subjective than 〜と思う.
structure: Verb／い-adjective［plain form］＋ ような気がする
Noun ＋ の ＋ ような気がする
pitfalls: It voices an uncertain hunch, weaker than 〜と思う (a considered opinion).
With a noun, insert の: 学生のような気がする.

examples.ja: どこかで彼に会ったような気がする。
examples.en: I have a feeling I've met him somewhere before.
examples.f: どこかで｜彼[かれ]に｜会[あ]ったような｜気[き]がする。

examples.ja: 今日は何かいいことが起こるような気がする。
examples.en: I've got a feeling something good is going to happen today.
examples.f: ｜今日[きょう]は｜何[なに]かいいことが｜起[お]こるような｜気[き]がする。

related.note: ようだ draws a reasoned 'it seems' from evidence; ような気がする is a looser inner hunch.
ように見える is 'looks like' from what you can see; ような気がする is an inner impression, not a visual one.
みたいだ is a casual 'seems like'; ような気がする foregrounds your own gut feeling.

title: ように見える
meaning: to look ~; to appear ~ (judging from how it looks)
summary: 〜ように見える says something looks or appears a certain way to the observer, based on its visible appearance — 本物のように見える = looks like the real thing. The judgment comes from what you can actually see.
structure: Verb／い-adjective［plain form］＋ ように見える
な-adjective ＋ な／Noun ＋ の ＋ ように見える
pitfalls: It is grounded in visual appearance — 'it looks that way to the eye'.
Compare 〜ような気がする, which is an inner hunch rather than something you see.

examples.ja: この絵は本物のように見えるが、実はコピーだ。
examples.en: This painting looks like the real thing, but it's actually a copy.
examples.f: この｜絵[え]は｜本物[ほんもの]のように｜見[み]えるが、｜実[じつ]はコピーだ。

examples.ja: 彼女は少し疲れているように見えた。
examples.en: She looked a little tired.
examples.f: ｜彼女[かのじょ]は｜少[すこ]し｜疲[つか]れているように｜見[み]えた。

related.note: ようだ is a broad 'it seems' from any evidence; ように見える specifically means 'looks like' by sight.
みたいだ is the casual 'seems'; ように見える is more clearly tied to visible appearance.
ような気がする is a felt impression; ように見える is what your eyes tell you.

title: よりも
meaning: (more) than ~; rather than ~ (comparison, with emphasis)
summary: よりも is より 'than' with emphatic も, marking the standard of comparison and stressing the gap — 去年よりも暑い = even hotter than last year. The thing being compared against comes before よりも (Aよりも B = B, more than A).
pitfalls: よりも is より with added emphasis; largely interchangeable, but よりも highlights the contrast more.
The point of comparison sits before よりも, so 'A よりも B' means B outdoes A.

examples.ja: 今年の夏は去年よりもずっと暑い。
examples.en: This summer is much hotter than last year.
examples.f: ｜今年[ことし]の｜夏[なつ]は｜去年[きょねん]よりもずっと｜暑[あつ]い。

examples.ja: 電車で行くよりも、歩いたほうが早いですよ。
examples.en: Rather than going by train, walking is faster, you know.
examples.f: ｜電車[でんしゃ]で｜行[い]くよりも、｜歩[ある]いたほうが｜早[はや]いですよ。

synonyms.note: より is the plain 'than'; よりも is the same with emphasis on the difference.

related.note: 〜より〜ほうが frames a two-way choice ('B is more ~ than A'); よりも just marks the standard being beaten.
というより corrects a description ('rather than say A, it's B'); よりも compares degrees or preferences.

title: 連用形
meaning: the conjunctive (masu-stem) form used to link clauses in writing
summary: The 連用形 — the ます-stem of a verb (書き, 食べ) and the 〜く form of an い-adjective (良く) — can join clauses much like the て-form, but sounds more formal and literary. 朝早く起き、顔を洗い、家を出た links the actions in a written-style sequence.
pitfalls: This clause-linking use is formal and written; in speech the て-form (起きて、洗って) is normal.
It links actions in sequence or parallel, so the following clause continues the same subject's flow.

examples.ja: 朝六時に起き、軽く運動をしてから出かける。
examples.en: I get up at six, do some light exercise, and then head out.
examples.f: ｜朝[あさ]｜六[ろく]｜時[じ]に｜起[お]き、｜軽[かる]く｜運動[うんどう]をしてから｜出[で]かける。

examples.ja: この製品は品質も良く、値段も手頃だ。
examples.en: This product is high in quality and reasonably priced.
examples.f: この｜製品[せいひん]は｜品質[ひんしつ]も｜良[よ]く、｜値段[ねだん]も｜手頃[てごろ]だ。

related.note: The て-form links clauses in everyday speech; the 連用形 does the same job in a more formal, written register.

title: わけがない
meaning: there's no way that ~; it's impossible that ~ (logical impossibility)
summary: 〜わけがない strongly denies that something could be true, on the basis of reasoning — そんなことあるわけがない = there's no way that's true. It is more emphatic and logic-driven than はずがない. The casual form is わけない.
structure: Verb／い-adjective［plain form］＋ わけがない
な-adjective ＋ な／Noun ＋ の ＋ わけがない
pitfalls: It denies that something can be true (a logical conclusion); 'no means to do it' is ようがない.
It is a stronger, more confident version of はずがない.

examples.ja: あんなに勉強した彼が、試験に落ちるわけがない。
examples.en: There's no way he'd fail the exam after studying that hard.
examples.f: あんなに｜勉強[べんきょう]した｜彼[かれ]が、｜試験[しけん]に｜落[お]ちるわけがない。

examples.ja: 子供にこんな難しい問題が解けるわけがない。
examples.en: There's no way a child could solve a problem this difficult.
examples.f: ｜子供[こども]にこんな｜難[むずか]しい｜問題[もんだい]が｜解[と]けるわけがない。

synonyms.note: はずがない is a softer 'shouldn't / can't be'; わけがない is a more forceful, reasoned 'no way'.

related.note: わけではない is a partial 'it's not that ~'; わけがない is a full-on 'that's impossible'.
ようがない denies any means to do something; わけがない denies that something is true.

title: わけだ
meaning: that's why ~; so that means ~; no wonder ~ (a natural conclusion)
summary: 〜わけだ presents something as a logical consequence you've pieced together from what's known — どうりで寒いわけだ = no wonder it's cold. It can also restate or interpret ('so you're saying...'). It signals a conclusion that follows naturally from the facts.
structure: な-adjective ＋ な／Noun ＋ という ＋ わけだ
pitfalls: It draws a conclusion that follows from the situation, unlike から／ので, which simply supply a reason.
Keep it apart from わけではない (partial denial) and わけにはいかない (can't afford to).

examples.ja: 彼は十年もパリに住んでいた。どうりでフランス語が上手なわけだ。
examples.en: He lived in Paris for ten years. No wonder his French is so good.
examples.f: ｜彼[かれ]は｜十[じゅう]｜年[ねん]もパリに｜住[す]んでいた。どうりでフランス｜語[ご]が｜上手[じょうず]なわけだ。

examples.ja: 三時間も歩いたのか。それは疲れるわけだ。
examples.en: You walked for three hours? No wonder you're tired.
examples.f: ｜三[さん]｜時間[じかん]も｜歩[ある]いたのか。それは｜疲[つか]れるわけだ。

related.note: わけではない softly denies a conclusion; わけだ affirms one as the natural upshot.
ことになる is 'it works out / it's been decided that'; わけだ presents a conclusion drawn from reasoning.
ので simply states a reason; わけだ points to the conclusion that reason leads to.

title: わけではない
meaning: it doesn't (necessarily) mean that ~; it's not the case that ~ (partial denial)
summary: 〜わけではない gently denies a conclusion someone might jump to — 'that doesn't mean...', 'it's not that...'. 嫌いなわけではない = it's not that I dislike it. It denies part, not all, and often heads off a likely misunderstanding. Casual: わけじゃない.
structure: Verb／い-adjective［plain form］＋ わけではない
な-adjective ＋ な／Noun ＋ という ＋ わけではない
pitfalls: It's a soft, partial denial ('not necessarily so'), far weaker than わけがない ('no way that's true') or a flat 〜ない.
It typically corrects an assumption the listener might otherwise make.

examples.ja: 野菜が嫌いなわけではないが、あまり食べない。
examples.en: It's not that I dislike vegetables, but I don't eat many.
examples.f: ｜野菜[やさい]が｜嫌[きら]いなわけではないが、あまり｜食[た]べない。

examples.ja: 高いからといって、必ずおいしいわけではない。
examples.en: Just because it's expensive doesn't necessarily mean it's tasty.
examples.f: ｜高[たか]いからといって、｜必[かなら]ずおいしいわけではない。

synonyms.note: 必ずしも〜ない is 'not always/necessarily'; it often teams up with わけではない for the same partial-denial nuance.
というものではない denies that a general claim always holds; わけではない denies a specific inferred conclusion.

related.note: わけがない is a total 'impossible'; わけではない only chips away at part of a conclusion.
わけだ affirms a natural conclusion; わけではない denies one.

title: わけにはいかない
meaning: can't (bring myself to) ~; can't afford to ~ (for social or moral reasons)
summary: 〜わけにはいかない says you can't do something — not because it's physically impossible, but because duty, circumstances, or social pressure won't allow it. 休むわけにはいかない = I can't just take the day off. With a negative verb, 〜ないわけにはいかない flips to 'have no choice but to'.
structure: Verb［dictionary form］＋ わけにはいかない
Verb［ない form］＋ わけにはいかない（＝ must do）
pitfalls: The impossibility is social or psychological, not physical; for 'no means to do it' use ようがない.
The double negative 〜ないわけにはいかない means 'must do', so watch the form carefully.

examples.ja: 大事な会議があるので、今日は休むわけにはいかない。
examples.en: I have an important meeting, so I can't take the day off today.
examples.f: ｜大事[だいじ]な｜会議[かいぎ]があるので、｜今日[きょう]は｜休[やす]むわけにはいかない。

examples.ja: お世話になった先生の頼みだから、断るわけにはいかない。
examples.en: It's a request from a teacher I owe a lot to, so I can't turn it down.
examples.f: お｜世話[せわ]になった｜先生[せんせい]の｜頼[たの]みだから、｜断[ことわ]るわけにはいかない。

related.note: なければならない is a plain 'must'; 〜ないわけにはいかない is 'must' pushed by duty or obligation.
〜しかない is 'have no choice but to' from lack of options; わけにはいかない blocks an option on social grounds.
ようがない is physical/means-based impossibility; わけにはいかない is being unable for social or moral reasons.

title: わざと
meaning: on purpose; deliberately; intentionally
summary: わざと is an adverb saying an action was done on purpose, usually with awareness of the effect it would cause — often a teasing or negative one. 彼はわざと負けた = he lost on purpose.
pitfalls: It describes acting intentionally, often with a mischievous or unkind slant.
Don't confuse it with わざわざ ('go to the trouble of / go out of one's way'), which is about special effort, not sneaky intent.

examples.ja: 弟を笑わせようと、わざと変な顔をした。
examples.en: To make my little brother laugh, I made a silly face on purpose.
examples.f: ｜弟[おとうと]を｜笑[わら]わせようと、わざと｜変[へん]な｜顔[かお]をした。

examples.ja: 彼女はわざと私の質問を無視した。
examples.en: She deliberately ignored my question.
examples.f: ｜彼女[かのじょ]はわざと｜私[わたし]の｜質問[しつもん]を｜無視[むし]した。

related.note: わざわざ is going out of your way to do something with effort; わざと is doing something on purpose, often slyly.
〜つもりで is 'with the intention of'; わざと flags that the act itself was deliberate.

title: わざわざ
meaning: to go out of one's way to; to take the trouble of doing
summary: わざわざ is an adverb that marks an action as a special, deliberate effort — one that went beyond what was strictly needed, like making a special trip or taking extra trouble. It often acknowledges someone's kindness (thanks for going to the bother), and can also gently point out that such effort wasn't really necessary.
pitfalls: Don't confuse it with わざと ('on purpose'): わざわざ is about the extra trouble taken and is usually well-meant, while わざと is about acting deliberately to bring about a particular (often unwanted) result.
It frames the effort as beyond the minimum; using it can imply you notice the bother involved, so it carries a warmer or more pointed nuance than a plain verb.

examples.ja: 遠いところをわざわざ来てくれて、ありがとう。
examples.en: Thank you for going out of your way to come all the way out here.
examples.f: ｜遠[とお]いところをわざわざ｜来[き]てくれて、ありがとう。

examples.ja: わざわざ新しいのを買わなくても、これで十分ですよ。
examples.en: You don't have to go to the trouble of buying a new one; this is plenty.
examples.f: わざわざ｜新[あたら]しいのを｜買[か]わなくても、これで｜十分[じゅうぶん]ですよ。

related.note: わざと is doing something deliberately to cause a result (often a bad one); わざわざ stresses the extra trouble taken, usually with goodwill.
〜てまで frames effort as going 'so far as to' an extreme; わざわざ simply notes that a special effort was made.

title: 割に
meaning: considering ~; for ~; despite ~ (more/less than expected)
summary: 割に（は） compares something against a standard or expectation and points out that reality doesn't match it — X considering Y, or X despite Y. 値段の割においしい = tasty for the price. It weighs an amount or degree against what the first part would lead you to expect, and flags the gap.
pitfalls: It highlights a gap between expectation and reality; when the result actually fits what you'd expect (as befitting), use だけあって instead.
Unlike plain のに ('although'), 割に specifically measures a degree or amount against the standard the first part sets up.

examples.ja: このレストランは値段の割に量が多いです。
examples.en: For the price, this restaurant gives you a lot of food.
examples.f: このレストランは｜値段[ねだん]の｜割[わり]に｜量[りょう]が｜多[おお]いです。

examples.ja: 彼はたくさん練習した割に、あまり上手になっていない。
examples.en: Considering how much he practiced, he hasn't gotten very good.
examples.f: ｜彼[かれ]はたくさん｜練習[れんしゅう]した｜割[わり]に、あまり｜上手[じょうず]になっていない。

synonyms.note: のに simply marks 'although X, unexpectedly Y'; 割に weighs the result against the level X would lead you to expect.
くせに also flags an unexpected mismatch but adds blame or scorn; 割に stays neutral.

antonyms.note: だけあって says the result fits the standard ('just as you'd expect from X'); 割に says it runs against that standard.

title: を込めて
meaning: putting (feeling or effort) into; filled with ~
summary: を込めて attaches to a noun naming a feeling or energy and says the following action is carried out with that feeling poured into it — 心を込めて = with all one's heart, 感謝を込めて = with gratitude. The noun names the emotion or effort that fills the act.
pitfalls: The noun names a feeling or energy put into the act (心, 愛, 感謝, 願い); it is not used for physically filling a container with something.
Don't mix it up with だらけ ('covered in / full of'), which describes a surface littered with something unwanted; を込めて is about pouring emotion into an action, even though both can be glossed 'full of'.

examples.ja: 母に感謝を込めて手紙を書きました。
examples.en: I wrote a letter to my mother with heartfelt gratitude.
examples.f: ｜母[はは]に｜感謝[かんしゃ]を｜込[こ]めて｜手紙[てがみ]を｜書[か]きました。

examples.ja: 彼女は心を込めて歌を歌った。
examples.en: She sang the song with all her heart.
examples.f: ｜彼女[かのじょ]は｜心[こころ]を｜込[こ]めて｜歌[うた]を｜歌[うた]った。

related.note: 〜だらけ means a surface is covered in or full of something (usually unwanted); を込めて is about putting feeling into an action.

title: を中心に
meaning: centered on; with ~ at the center; mainly among ~
summary: を中心に（して） marks the thing that sits at the center of some activity, group, or arrangement — everything else gathers around it or is organized with it as the focus. 駅を中心に = centered on the station; 若者を中心に = mainly among young people.
structure: Noun ＋ を中心とした ＋ Noun
pitfalls: を中心に marks the focal point that other things arrange themselves around; it isn't a plain 'about (a topic)' — for simply discussing a subject, use について.

examples.ja: この町では、駅を中心に店が並んでいます。
examples.en: In this town, the shops are lined up centered around the station.
examples.f: この｜町[まち]では、｜駅[えき]を｜中心[ちゅうしん]に｜店[みせ]が｜並[なら]んでいます。

examples.ja: その歌手は若い人を中心に人気があります。
examples.en: That singer is popular mainly among young people.
examples.f: その｜歌手[かしゅ]は｜若[わか]い｜人[ひと]を｜中心[ちゅうしん]に｜人気[にんき]があります。

related.note: をめぐって centers a dispute or discussion around an issue; を中心に marks a focal point things are arranged around, without the sense of contention.
について marks the topic you talk or think about; を中心に marks what sits at the center of an activity or group.

title: を通じて・を通して
kana: をつうじて・をとおして
meaning: through; by way of; throughout
summary: を通じて / を通して marks a medium or intermediary that something passes through — a person, a channel, an experience — or a whole span of time or area over which something holds. 友達を通じて = through a friend; 一年を通して = all year round.
structure: Noun ＋ を通じて／を通して
pitfalls: Two senses share the form: with a person or means it reads 'by way of', with a time span or area it reads 'throughout'; the noun tells you which.
を通して leans slightly toward actively using the means, を通じて slightly toward the result or the span, but they overlap and are often interchangeable.

examples.ja: 私たちは共通の友達を通じて知り合いました。
examples.en: We got to know each other through a mutual friend.
examples.f: ｜私[わたし]たちは｜共通[きょうつう]の｜友達[ともだち]を｜通[つう]じて｜知り合[しりあ]いました。

examples.ja: この地方は一年を通して雨が多いです。
examples.en: This region gets a lot of rain throughout the year.
examples.f: この｜地方[ちほう]は｜一[いち]｜年[ねん]を｜通[とお]して｜雨[あめ]が｜多[おお]いです。

synonyms.note: によって marks the means or cause 'by which' something is done; を通じて marks a medium or intermediary the action passes through.

related.note: にわたって stresses the full extent of a range or period ('spanning'); を通じて in its time sense says something holds steadily throughout.

title: をはじめ
meaning: starting with ~; ~ and others like it; headed by ~
summary: をはじめ（として） singles out one representative, usually the most prominent, member of a group and implies a wider set follows it — X and others like it. 東京をはじめ、大都市では… = In big cities, starting with Tokyo… The named item heads a list that isn't spelled out in full.
structure: Noun ＋ をはじめとする ＋ Noun
pitfalls: The noun before をはじめ is the leading, most representative member of a group, not just a random example; it heads the list rather than being tucked into it.

examples.ja: この店では、りんごをはじめ、いろいろな果物を売っています。
examples.en: This shop sells all kinds of fruit, starting with apples.
examples.f: この｜店[みせ]では、りんごをはじめ、いろいろな｜果物[くだもの]を｜売[う]っています。

examples.ja: 校長先生をはじめ、多くの先生が卒業式に出席しました。
examples.en: Many teachers, headed by the principal, attended the graduation ceremony.
examples.f: ｜校長[こうちょう]｜先生[せんせい]をはじめ、｜多[おお]くの｜先生[せんせい]が｜卒業[そつぎょう]｜式[しき]に｜出席[しゅっせき]しました。

synonyms.note: など lists an item as one example among others ('and so on'); をはじめ presents its noun as the leading member the rest follow.

related.note: とか〜とか lists a couple of casual examples side by side; をはじめ names one prominent member standing in for a larger group.

title: んじゃない
meaning: don't ~! (blunt, casual prohibition)
summary: Attached to a verb in the dictionary form, 〜んじゃない（よ） is a forceful, spoken way to tell someone not to do something — the tone a parent might use scolding a child. 泣くんじゃない = Don't cry! It is blunter and more emotional than a flat 〜てはいけない.
structure: Verb［dictionary form］＋ んじゃない（よ）
pitfalls: Keep this apart from the suggestion 〜んじゃない（？） ('isn't it ~?; I'd say ~'), which sits on the plain form with a rising, questioning tone; as a prohibition it takes the dictionary form and a falling, commanding tone.
With the past た form, 〜んじゃなかった flips to regret ('I shouldn't have ~', 食べるんじゃなかった = I wish I hadn't eaten it), not a command.
It is rough, casual speech; don't aim it at superiors — use 〜ないでください instead.

examples.ja: 危ないから、そんな高いところに登るんじゃない。
examples.en: It's dangerous, so don't climb up somewhere that high.
examples.f: ｜危[あぶ]ないから、そんな｜高[たか]いところに｜登[のぼ]るんじゃない。

examples.ja: 人の物を勝手に使うんじゃないよ。
examples.en: Don't go using other people's things without asking.
examples.f: ｜人[ひと]の｜物[もの]を｜勝手[かって]に｜使[つか]うんじゃないよ。

synonyms.note: 〜な (行くな) is the terse, blunt 'don't'; 〜んじゃない carries the same force with a more emotional, scolding tone.

related.note: 〜ちゃいけない states that something must not be done as a rule; 〜んじゃない is a heated, on-the-spot order to stop.
〜てはいけない is the standard 'must not'; 〜んじゃない is its rough, spoken, scolding cousin.

title: んだって
meaning: I hear that ~; apparently ~ (casual, spoken hearsay)
summary: 〜んだって passes along something you heard as casual, spoken news or gossip — 'apparently', 'I hear'. It is built from the explanatory のだ (→ んだ) plus the quoting って, so it reports the information with a 'the story is that ~' flavor. 田中さん、結婚するんだって = Apparently Tanaka is getting married.
structure: な-adjective／Noun ＋ な ＋ んだって
pitfalls: After a noun or な-adjective, insert な: 学生なんだって, 静かなんだって — not 学生だんだって.
Don't confuse it with sentence-initial だって ('because; but; after all'); 〜んだって sits at the end of the clause and reports hearsay.
It is colloquial; for neutral or written reporting of what you heard, use 〜そうだ instead.

examples.ja: 山田さん、来週から北海道に引っ越すんだって。
examples.en: I hear Yamada is moving to Hokkaido starting next week.
examples.f: ｜山田[やまだ]さん、｜来週[らいしゅう]から｜北海道[ほっかいどう]に｜引っ越[ひっこ]すんだって。

examples.ja: あの新しいカフェ、コーヒーがすごくおいしいんだって。
examples.en: Apparently that new cafe's coffee is really good.
examples.f: あの｜新[あたら]しいカフェ、コーヒーがすごくおいしいんだって。

synonyms.note: 〜そうだ reports hearsay in a neutral, often written tone; 〜んだって is its casual, spoken counterpart with an explanatory の flavor.
〜って quotes or reports speech bare; 〜んだって adds the explanatory んだ, framing it as 'the story is that ~'.
〜らしい reports with a touch of inference or distance ('it seems'); 〜んだって passes on what was actually said more directly.

related.note: んです is the explanatory のだ that 〜んだって is built on — んだ plus the quoting って.
んだけど・んですが is another colloquial extension of explanatory んだ, used to soften a lead-in rather than report hearsay.
